KNOWING THIS CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM IS IMPORTANT BECAUSE MANAGEMENT DIFFERS SUBSTANTIALLY BY GROUP - SPECIFIC PULMONARY VASODILATOR THERAPIES (used in Group 1 PAH) ARE GENERALLY NOT INDICATED, AND CAN EVEN BE HARMFUL, IN GROUP 2 OR GROUP 3 DISEASE, WHERE THE FOCUS IS INSTEAD ON TREATING THE UNDERLYING LEFT HEART DISEASE OR LUNG DISEASE/HYPOXAEMIA RESPECTIVELY.
One_Line: Group 3 pulmonary hypertension is caused by chronic lung disease and hypoxaemia - COPD and pulmonary fibrosis are the classic examples.

Question: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and cough for 6 weeks. He is a heavy smoker. 2 weeks ago, he started having headaches and noticed swelling of his face. Physical examination reveals prominent non-pulsating neck veins, puffiness of the face and edema of the upper limbs (see report). Chest X-ray: Shows a prominence of the right hilum. Which of the following types of lung cancer is the most commonly associated with this clinical presentation?
Explanation_A: Wrong. Adenocarcinoma is typically PERIPHERALLY located and is the commonest lung cancer subtype OVERALL (and particularly in non-smokers), but it is NOT the type MOST SPECIFICALLY AND COMMONLY ASSOCIATED WITH SVC OBSTRUCTION, which more classically arises from CENTRAL, HILAR tumours.
Explanation_B: Wrong. Carcinoid tumours are typically SLOW-GROWING, and while they can occasionally cause SVC obstruction if centrally located, this is not their classic, most common association.
Explanation_C: Wrong, though squamous cell carcinoma IS also typically a CENTRAL, hilar tumour type (unlike adenocarcinoma) and CAN cause SVC obstruction - however, SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER IS THE TYPE MOST CLASSICALLY AND STRONGLY ASSOCIATED WITH THIS PRESENTATION, given its typical CENTRAL location and RAPID GROWTH/PROPENSITY FOR EARLY, BULKY MEDIASTINAL LYMPHADENOPATHY.
Explanation_D: CORRECT. THE CLASSIC PRESENTATION DESCRIBED - RAPIDLY PROGRESSIVE SYMPTOMS OVER JUST WEEKS, WITH PROMINENT NON-PULSATING NECK VEIN DISTENSION, FACIAL PUFFINESS/SWELLING, AND UPPER LIMB OEDEMA, TOGETHER WITH A CENTRAL/HILAR MASS ON CHEST X-RAY - IS SUPERIOR VENA CAVA (SVC) OBSTRUCTION SYNDROME, MOST COMMONLY CAUSED BY LUNG CANCER, AND SPECIFICALLY MOST STRONGLY ASSOCIATED WITH SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER, GIVEN ITS CHARACTERISTIC CENTRAL LOCATION AND RAPID, AGGRESSIVE GROWTH WITH EARLY, BULKY MEDIASTINAL LYMPH NODE INVOLVEMENT THAT CAN QUICKLY COMPRESS THE ADJACENT SVC.
High_Yield_Must_Know: SUPERIOR VENA CAVA OBSTRUCTION SYNDROME - RECOGNISE THE CLASSIC PRESENTATION AND ITS STRONGEST MALIGNANT ASSOCIATION. CLINICAL FEATURES OF SVC OBSTRUCTION: reflecting IMPAIRED VENOUS DRAINAGE FROM THE HEAD, NECK, AND UPPER LIMBS due to obstruction of the SVC (most commonly from EXTERNAL COMPRESSION by a mediastinal/hilar mass or bulky lymphadenopathy, though intraluminal thrombosis, e.g., from an indwelling central line, is another cause) - PROMINENT, DISTENDED, NON-PULSATING NECK VEINS (NON-PULSATILE distinguishes venous distension from arterial pulsation seen in other conditions), FACIAL SWELLING/PUFFINESS (particularly noticeable periorbitally, and WORSE IN THE MORNING/ON LYING FLAT), UPPER LIMB OEDEMA, HEADACHE (from venous congestion/raised intracranial venous pressure), DYSPNOEA, AND SOMETIMES VISIBLE DILATED COLLATERAL VEINS ACROSS THE CHEST WALL (as the body attempts to establish alternative venous drainage pathways bypassing the obstruction). CAUSES: THE MAJORITY OF CASES ARE CAUSED BY MALIGNANCY, WITH LUNG CANCER BEING THE SINGLE COMMONEST OVERALL CAUSE - AND AMONG LUNG CANCER SUBTYPES, SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER IS THE TYPE MOST STRONGLY AND CLASSICALLY ASSOCIATED WITH SVC OBSTRUCTION, given its typical CENTRAL/HILAR location (arising from central bronchi) combined with its CHARACTERISTICALLY RAPID GROWTH RATE AND EARLY, EXTENSIVE MEDIASTINAL LYMPHADENOPATHY - THESE FEATURES MEAN SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER CAN CAUSE SIGNIFICANT, RAPIDLY PROGRESSIVE EXTERNAL COMPRESSION OF THE ADJACENT SVC RELATIVELY EARLY IN ITS COURSE, EXPLAINING WHY THIS PRESENTATION (OVER JUST WEEKS, AS HERE) IS PARTICULARLY CHARACTERISTIC. SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA IS ALSO TYPICALLY CENTRALLY LOCATED AND CAN CAUSE SVC OBSTRUCTION, BUT SMALL CELL IS THE MORE CLASSICALLY, STRONGLY ASSOCIATED SUBTYPE GIVEN ITS PARTICULARLY AGGRESSIVE GROWTH PATTERN. MANAGEMENT: URGENT DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP (CT CHEST, TISSUE DIAGNOSIS) AND TREATMENT OF THE UNDERLYING MALIGNANCY (CHEMOTHERAPY IS OFTEN PARTICULARLY EFFECTIVE AND RAPID-ACTING FOR SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER SPECIFICALLY, GIVEN ITS CHEMOSENSITIVITY), WITH ENDOVASCULAR SVC STENTING AS AN OPTION FOR RAPID SYMPTOM RELIEF IN SEVERE OR REFRACTORY CASES, ALONGSIDE SUPPORTIVE MEASURES (HEAD ELEVATION, SOMETIMES CORTICOSTEROIDS TO REDUCE PERITUMOURAL OEDEMA).
One_Line: Rapid neck vein distension, facial swelling, and arm oedema over weeks with a central lung mass is SVC obstruction, and small cell lung cancer is its classic, most aggressive cause.

Question: An asymptomatic 60-year-old man, non-smoker presents for a routine annual physical check-up. A chest X-ray showed an opacity, which is less than 3 cm in the left upper lobe. Which of the following is the next best step in the management?
Explanation_A: Wrong as the IMMEDIATE next step. Surgical resection is premature before establishing whether this represents a new, concerning finding requiring further workup, or a stable, long-standing benign finding.
Explanation_B: CORRECT. FOR AN INCIDENTALLY DISCOVERED SOLITARY PULMONARY NODULE (UNDER 3CM, IN AN ASYMPTOMATIC PATIENT), THE ESSENTIAL, SIMPLEST, AND MOST INFORMATIVE FIRST STEP IS TO REVIEW ANY PRIOR/OLD CHEST IMAGING - IF THE SAME OPACITY WAS PRESENT AND UNCHANGED IN SIZE/APPEARANCE ON IMAGING FROM 2 OR MORE YEARS AGO, THIS STRONGLY SUGGESTS A BENIGN, STABLE PROCESS, AND NO FURTHER WORKUP IS TYPICALLY NEEDED - THIS SIMPLE, LOW-COST STEP CAN AVOID UNNECESSARY, MORE INVASIVE INVESTIGATION.
Explanation_C: Wrong as the IMMEDIATE first step, though CT chest is often a reasonable NEXT step if old imaging is unavailable or shows the nodule is new/changed. Reviewing existing prior imaging first is simpler, faster, and potentially avoids the need for further imaging/investigation altogether.
Explanation_D: Wrong as the immediate first step. Biopsy is invasive and is reserved for nodules with concerning features on imaging or growth on serial imaging - it is premature before first establishing basic stability/growth information from prior imaging or further characterisation.
High_Yield_Must_Know: SOLITARY PULMONARY NODULE WORKUP - ALWAYS START BY LOOKING FOR OLD IMAGING TO ASSESS STABILITY. THE SOLITARY PULMONARY NODULE (SPN) IS A COMMON INCIDENTAL FINDING, AND THE APPROACH TO WORKUP IS GUIDED BY SIZE, PATIENT RISK FACTORS (AGE, SMOKING HISTORY), AND, CRUCIALLY, WHETHER PRIOR IMAGING IS AVAILABLE FOR COMPARISON. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT, SIMPLEST FIRST STEP IN EVALUATING ANY NEWLY DISCOVERED PULMONARY NODULE IS TO ACTIVELY SEEK OUT AND REVIEW ANY PRIOR CHEST IMAGING (X-RAY OR CT) THE PATIENT MAY HAVE HAD FOR ANY REASON IN THE PAST - THIS IS BASED ON THE WELL-ESTABLISHED PRINCIPLE THAT A NODULE THAT HAS REMAINED COMPLETELY STABLE IN SIZE FOR 2 YEARS OR MORE IS OVERWHELMINGLY LIKELY TO BE BENIGN (given the DOUBLING TIME of most malignant nodules being generally faster than this, typically ranging from about 20 days to 400 days depending on tumour type - a nodule stable beyond 2 years essentially excludes a rapidly growing malignancy, though VERY SLOW-GROWING malignancies such as certain adenocarcinoma subtypes can occasionally be an exception, warranting some clinical judgement) - IF STABLE, OLD IMAGING CAN OFTEN OBVIATE THE NEED FOR ANY FURTHER, MORE COSTLY OR INVASIVE INVESTIGATION. IF NO PRIOR IMAGING IS AVAILABLE, OR IF COMPARISON SHOWS THE NODULE IS NEW OR HAS GROWN, FURTHER WORKUP PROCEEDS BASED ON SIZE AND RISK FACTORS - TYPICALLY CT CHEST FOR BETTER CHARACTERISATION (SIZE, MARGINS, DENSITY/CALCIFICATION PATTERN - CERTAIN CALCIFICATION PATTERNS SUCH AS DIFFUSE, CENTRAL, OR 'POPCORN' PATTERNS SUGGEST BENIGNITY), SOMETIMES PET-CT (FOR METABOLIC ACTIVITY ASSESSMENT IN NODULES OF INDETERMINATE SIZE/RISK), SERIAL SURVEILLANCE IMAGING FOR SMALL, LOW-RISK NODULES, OR TISSUE SAMPLING (BIOPSY OR RESECTION) FOR NODULES WITH HIGHER-RISK FEATURES OR DEMONSTRATED GROWTH.
One_Line: Before doing anything else with an incidental lung nodule, find and compare old chest imaging - stability over 2 years essentially rules out cancer.

Question: A 55-year old man with stable COPD, presents with sudden onset left-sided pleuritic chest pain and exertional dyspnea. On examination, he is not in distress. the trachea is central and breath sounds are equal in both sides with occasional mild expiratory wheezes (see report). Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, Heart rate 80 /min, Respiratory rate 22 /min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 93 %. Chest X-ray: Shows a left sided pneumothorax measuring 2 cm between the lung and chest wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Explanation_A: Wrong as the standard first-line step for THIS presentation, given his relative clinical stability (not in distress, stable vital signs) and small pneumothorax size - the general trend in current guidance is towards conservative management for small, minimally symptomatic pneumothoraces.
Explanation_B: Wrong as the FIRST step, though it remains an option if he deteriorates or the pneumothorax is/becomes larger or symptomatic. Given his current clinical stability and the RELATIVELY SMALL size (2cm), CONSERVATIVE management is the appropriate initial approach.
Explanation_C: Wrong. Pleurodesis is a procedure to PREVENT RECURRENCE, typically used after RECURRENT episodes of pneumothorax or in specific high-risk situations - it is not appropriate acute management for a FIRST, small, currently stable pneumothorax.
Explanation_D: CORRECT. IN A CLINICALLY STABLE PATIENT (NOT IN SIGNIFICANT RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, REASONABLE VITAL SIGNS, MILD HYPOXIA) WITH A RELATIVELY SMALL (2CM) SECONDARY (COPD-ASSOCIATED) PNEUMOTHORAX, CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT WITH SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN (WHICH INCREASES THE RATE OF PLEURAL AIR REABSORPTION) AND CLOSE OBSERVATION/MONITORING IS AN APPROPRIATE, GUIDELINE-SUPPORTED FIRST-LINE APPROACH, AVOIDING UNNECESSARY INVASIVE INTERVENTION.
High_Yield_Must_Know: PNEUMOTHORAX MANAGEMENT - SIZE AND CLINICAL STABILITY GUIDE THE APPROACH, WITH INCREASING SUPPORT FOR CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT EVEN IN SOME SECONDARY (COPD-ASSOCIATED) CASES WHEN CLINICALLY STABLE. TRADITIONAL TEACHING HAS EMPHASISED MORE AGGRESSIVE INTERVENTION FOR SECONDARY PNEUMOTHORAX (occurring in patients with UNDERLYING LUNG DISEASE such as COPD, given their reduced pulmonary reserve) COMPARED WITH PRIMARY SPONTANEOUS PNEUMOTHORAX (occurring in otherwise healthy, typically young, tall, thin individuals without underlying lung disease) - HOWEVER, CONTEMPORARY GUIDELINES INCREASINGLY SUPPORT A MORE INDIVIDUALISED, CONSERVATIVE APPROACH BASED ON THE SPECIFIC CLINICAL PICTURE: FOR A PATIENT WHO IS CLINICALLY STABLE (AS HERE - NOT IN SIGNIFICANT DISTRESS, ACCEPTABLE VITAL SIGNS DESPITE MILD HYPOXIA), WITH A RELATIVELY SMALL PNEUMOTHORAX (GENERALLY UNDER 2-3CM BY VARIOUS SIZE CRITERIA), CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT WITH SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN (WHICH ACCELERATES REABSORPTION OF THE PLEURAL AIR BY REDUCING THE PARTIAL PRESSURE OF NITROGEN IN THE BLOOD, CREATING A FAVOURABLE GRADIENT FOR NITROGEN, AND THEREFORE AIR, TO DIFFUSE OUT OF THE PLEURAL SPACE) AND CLOSE OBSERVATION WITH SERIAL IMAGING IS AN APPROPRIATE, INCREASINGLY SUPPORTED FIRST-LINE APPROACH, EVEN IN SECONDARY PNEUMOTHORAX, PROVIDED THE PATIENT REMAINS STABLE. NEEDLE ASPIRATION OR CHEST TUBE INSERTION WOULD BE INDICATED IF: THE PATIENT IS SYMPTOMATIC/IN SIGNIFICANT DISTRESS, THE PNEUMOTHORAX IS LARGE, THERE IS EVIDENCE OF TENSION PHYSIOLOGY (MEDIASTINAL SHIFT, HAEMODYNAMIC COMPROMISE - REQUIRING IMMEDIATE NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION AS A TRUE EMERGENCY), OR IF CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT FAILS WITH PROGRESSIVE ENLARGEMENT OR WORSENING SYMPTOMS ON FOLLOW-UP.
One_Line: A clinically stable patient with a small pneumothorax gets oxygen and observation first - not automatic drainage.
Accuracy_Review: Accurate as reflecting increasingly supported, individualised conservative management; some more traditional teaching would still favour chest tube insertion for any secondary (COPD-associated) pneumothorax regardless of size or stability, so this represents an evolving area of practice worth checking against the specific guideline your exam follows.

Question: A 20-year-old woman presents to the Out-Patient Department with mild dyspnea, malaise, low-grade fever and arthralgia. Physical examination showed tender erythematous nodules measuring 2-3 cm in both shins. Chest auscultation revealed fine basal crackles. Which of the following is the next best action in management?
Explanation_A: Wrong as the most directly relevant next step. Blood cultures would be relevant if there were strong suspicion of a bacterial/septic process, but this presentation (erythema nodosum, arthralgia, mild systemic symptoms, basal crackles) points more specifically towards a different underlying process requiring chest imaging first.
Explanation_B: Wrong as the immediate next step, and premature before establishing the underlying diagnosis/cause - treatment should follow, not precede, appropriate diagnostic workup.
Explanation_C: CORRECT. TENDER ERYTHEMATOUS NODULES ON THE SHINS (CLASSIC ERYTHEMA NODOSUM) TOGETHER WITH ARTHRALGIA, MILD RESPIRATORY SYMPTOMS, AND BASAL CRACKLES STRONGLY SUGGESTS AN UNDERLYING SYSTEMIC CONDITION, MOST CLASSICALLY SARCOIDOSIS (OR, IN AN ENDEMIC AREA, TUBERCULOSIS) - THE APPROPRIATE, SIMPLE, HIGH-YIELD NEXT STEP IS A CHEST X-RAY, SPECIFICALLY LOOKING FOR BILATERAL HILAR LYMPHADENOPATHY (THE CLASSIC FINDING IN SARCOIDOSIS, PARTICULARLY WHEN COMBINED WITH ERYTHEMA NODOSUM AND ARTHRALGIA - TOGETHER FORMING LOFGREN SYNDROME).
Explanation_D: Wrong as the immediate next step. Skin biopsy of the nodules could theoretically be performed, but erythema nodosum has a fairly CHARACTERISTIC clinical appearance, and the more useful, higher-yield, simpler next step to identify the SPECIFIC UNDERLYING SYSTEMIC CAUSE is chest imaging, given the classic clinical picture strongly suggesting sarcoidosis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: ERYTHEMA NODOSUM WITH ARTHRALGIA AND RESPIRATORY FINDINGS - THINK LOFGREN SYNDROME (ACUTE SARCOIDOSIS) AND GET A CHEST X-RAY. ERYTHEMA NODOSUM IS A PANNICULITIS (INFLAMMATION OF SUBCUTANEOUS FAT) PRESENTING AS TENDER, ERYTHEMATOUS, typically BILATERAL NODULES, CLASSICALLY OVER THE ANTERIOR SHINS - IT IS A REACTIVE, HYPERSENSITIVITY-TYPE SKIN MANIFESTATION OF AN UNDERLYING SYSTEMIC PROCESS RATHER THAN A PRIMARY SKIN DISEASE ITSELF, WITH NUMEROUS POSSIBLE UNDERLYING CAUSES - SARCOIDOSIS, TUBERCULOSIS, STREPTOCOCCAL INFECTION, INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE, CERTAIN DRUGS (SULFONAMIDES, ORAL CONTRACEPTIVES), AND PREGNANCY, AMONG OTHERS. LOFGREN SYNDROME IS A SPECIFIC, RECOGNISABLE, ACUTE PRESENTATION OF SARCOIDOSIS DEFINED BY THE CLASSIC TRIAD OF: ERYTHEMA NODOSUM, BILATERAL HILAR LYMPHADENOPATHY (ON CHEST IMAGING), AND POLYARTHRALGIA/ARTHRITIS (CLASSICALLY AFFECTING THE ANKLES) - OFTEN WITH ACCOMPANYING MILD FEVER AND MALAISE, ESSENTIALLY EXACTLY THE PICTURE DESCRIBED IN THIS PATIENT. LOFGREN SYNDROME HAS A GENERALLY GOOD PROGNOSIS WITH A HIGH RATE OF SPONTANEOUS RESOLUTION, AND IS CONSIDERED SUFFICIENTLY CLINICALLY CHARACTERISTIC THAT A TISSUE BIOPSY IS OFTEN NOT REQUIRED FOR DIAGNOSIS WHEN THE FULL CLASSIC TRIAD IS PRESENT WITH TYPICAL BILATERAL HILAR ADENOPATHY ON IMAGING. THE APPROPRIATE, SIMPLE, HIGH-YIELD NEXT DIAGNOSTIC STEP IS THEREFORE A CHEST X-RAY, SPECIFICALLY LOOKING FOR THE CHARACTERISTIC BILATERAL HILAR LYMPHADENOPATHY THAT WOULD SUPPORT THE DIAGNOSIS OF SARCOIDOSIS/LOFGREN SYNDROME AND HELP GUIDE FURTHER MANAGEMENT (WHICH, FOR CLASSIC LOFGREN SYNDROME, OFTEN INVOLVES SIMPLE SYMPTOMATIC TREATMENT WITH NSAIDs GIVEN THE GENERALLY SELF-LIMITING NATURE, RATHER THAN IMMEDIATE SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS).
One_Line: Erythema nodosum plus arthralgia plus basal crackles suggests Lofgren syndrome sarcoidosis - a chest X-ray for bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is the simple, high-yield next step.

Question: Which of the following is the best oxygen delivery system in a patient with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease?
Explanation_A: Wrong. A simple face mask does not provide PRECISE, CONTROLLED oxygen concentration delivery - the actual FiO2 delivered varies with the patient's breathing pattern, which is undesirable in COPD where PRECISE oxygen titration is important.
Explanation_B: Wrong. A rebreathing bag (non-rebreather mask) is used to deliver HIGH-CONCENTRATION oxygen for patients requiring maximal oxygenation (such as in severe hypoxaemia from other causes) - in COPD, UNCONTROLLED HIGH-FLOW/HIGH-CONCENTRATION oxygen risks SUPPRESSING RESPIRATORY DRIVE AND WORSENING CO2 RETENTION in patients who are CHRONICALLY CO2-RETAINING and may rely relatively more on HYPOXIC DRIVE to breathe.
Explanation_C: Wrong as the BEST option, though nasal cannula is commonly used and reasonable for STABLE, LOWER-FLOW oxygen needs. It still does not provide the same PRECISE, CONTROLLED, PREDICTABLE FiO2 DELIVERY that a Venturi mask specifically offers, which is the goal in COPD.
Explanation_D: CORRECT. THE VENTURI MASK IS CONSIDERED THE BEST OXYGEN DELIVERY SYSTEM SPECIFICALLY FOR COPD PATIENTS, BECAUSE IT PROVIDES A PRECISE, FIXED, CONTROLLED CONCENTRATION OF INSPIRED OXYGEN (FiO2), REGARDLESS OF THE PATIENT'S VARIABLE BREATHING PATTERN/RATE - THIS ALLOWS CAREFUL, DELIBERATE TITRATION OF OXYGEN TO THE LOWEST EFFECTIVE LEVEL NEEDED TO CORRECT HYPOXAEMIA WITHOUT SIGNIFICANTLY SUPPRESSING RESPIRATORY DRIVE OR WORSENING CO2 RETENTION, WHICH IS THE KEY SAFETY CONCERN IN COPD PATIENTS.
High_Yield_Must_Know: OXYGEN DELIVERY IN COPD - WHY PRECISE, CONTROLLED (VENTURI MASK) DELIVERY IS PREFERRED. THE CENTRAL CONCERN IN COPD, PARTICULARLY IN PATIENTS WITH ESTABLISHED CHRONIC CO2 RETENTION (as discussed in the 'BLUE BLOATER' pattern elsewhere in this bank), IS THAT UNCONTROLLED, EXCESSIVE SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN CAN WORSEN HYPERCAPNIA (CO2 RETENTION) THROUGH SEVERAL MECHANISMS - INCLUDING BLUNTING OF THE (RELATIVELY BLUNTED, PARTIALLY HYPOXIA-DEPENDENT) RESPIRATORY DRIVE IN SOME CHRONIC CO2-RETAINERS, WORSENING VENTILATION-PERFUSION MISMATCH (BY REVERSING PROTECTIVE HYPOXIC PULMONARY VASOCONSTRICTION IN POORLY VENTILATED AREAS, REDIRECTING BLOOD FLOW TO THESE POORLY VENTILATED REGIONS), AND THE HALDANE EFFECT (OXYGEN DISPLACING CO2 FROM HAEMOGLOBIN, INCREASING THE AMOUNT OF DISSOLVED/PARTIAL PRESSURE CO2 IN THE BLOOD) - THIS IS WHY OXYGEN THERAPY IN COPD MUST BE CAREFULLY, DELIBERATELY TITRATED TO ACHIEVE A TARGET OXYGEN SATURATION RANGE (TYPICALLY AROUND 88-92% IN KNOWN OR AT-RISK CO2 RETAINERS, RATHER THAN THE HIGHER TARGETS APPROPRIATE FOR MOST OTHER ACUTELY UNWELL PATIENTS), RATHER THAN SIMPLY MAXIMISING OXYGEN DELIVERY. THE VENTURI MASK ACHIEVES THIS PRECISE CONTROL THROUGH ITS DESIGN - IT USES SPECIFICALLY SIZED, COLOUR-CODED ADAPTORS THAT ENTRAIN A FIXED, PREDICTABLE RATIO OF ROOM AIR TO SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN FLOW, DELIVERING A CONSISTENT, KNOWN FiO2 (COMMONLY AVAILABLE IN GRADED OPTIONS SUCH AS 24%, 28%, 31%, 35%, 40%, 60%) REGARDLESS OF THE PATIENT'S OWN RESPIRATORY RATE OR DEPTH OF BREATHING - THIS PREDICTABILITY AND PRECISE CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES IT THE PREFERRED, SAFEST CHOICE FOR CAREFULLY TITRATING OXYGEN IN COPD, ALLOWING CLINICIANS TO DELIVER THE LOWEST FiO2 NEEDED TO ACHIEVE THE TARGET SATURATION RANGE WHILE MINIMISING THE RISK OF CO2 RETENTION.
One_Line: For controlled, titratable oxygen in COPD, the Venturi mask is preferred - it delivers a precise, known FiO2 that avoids over-oxygenating and worsening CO2 retention.

Question: A 65-year-old man known to have COPD presented to the Emergency Department with increasing dyspnea, cough, expectoration and fever. Initial assessment revealed fully conscious patient with mild distress, central cyanosis and bilateral wheezing on chest auscultation. The patient was started on high flow oxygen and salbutamol nebulizer but 1 hour later, his level of consciousness is reduced (see lab result). ABG HCO3- 36 (22-28 mmol/L), ABG PCO2 9 (4.7-6.0 kPa), pH 7.18 (7.36-7.45), ABG PO2 15 (10.6-14.2 kPa). Which of the following is the best initial step in management?
Explanation_A: Wrong as the FIRST, immediate step, though mechanical ventilation may ultimately be needed if the situation does not rapidly improve. The IMMEDIATE, CORRECTABLE cause of his deterioration should be addressed FIRST, before escalating to invasive ventilation.
Explanation_B: CORRECT. THIS IS A CLASSIC PRESENTATION OF OXYGEN-INDUCED CO2 NARCOSIS IN A COPD PATIENT - HIGH-FLOW, UNCONTROLLED OXYGEN THERAPY HAS CAUSED MARKED WORSENING HYPERCAPNIA (PCO2 RISEN TO 9, MARKEDLY ELEVATED) WITH RESULTING RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS (pH 7.18, SEVERELY ACIDOTIC) AND A REDUCED LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS (CO2 NARCOSIS) - NOTABLY, HIS OXYGENATION IS NOW EXCESSIVE (PO2 15, ABOVE THE NORMAL RANGE, REFLECTING OVER-OXYGENATION FROM THE HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN) - THE APPROPRIATE, IMMEDIATE FIRST STEP IS TO REDUCE THE OXYGEN FLOW/CONCENTRATION (TARGETING A MORE APPROPRIATE, CONTROLLED SATURATION RANGE, TYPICALLY 88-92% IN THIS CONTEXT) TO ALLOW HIS RESPIRATORY DRIVE AND VENTILATION TO IMPROVE.
Explanation_C: Wrong as the initial step. There is no specific indication for an urgent brain CT (no focal neurological deficit or trauma history described) - his reduced consciousness is readily explained by the clear, acute biochemical derangement (severe CO2 narcosis), which should be addressed FIRST.
Explanation_D: Wrong. Naloxone reverses OPIOID-induced respiratory depression - there is no indication of opioid use/overdose in this stem, and his clinical and biochemical picture is fully explained by oxygen-induced hypercapnia/CO2 narcosis, not an opioid effect.
High_Yield_Must_Know: OXYGEN-INDUCED CO2 NARCOSIS IN COPD - A CLASSIC, DANGEROUS COMPLICATION OF UNCONTROLLED HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN THERAPY. AS COVERED IN THE PRECEDING QUESTION REGARDING VENTURI MASK USE, COPD PATIENTS, PARTICULARLY THOSE WITH CHRONIC CO2 RETENTION, ARE AT RISK OF WORSENING HYPERCAPNIA WITH EXCESSIVE, UNCONTROLLED SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN - THIS PATIENT WAS STARTED ON HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN (RATHER THAN CONTROLLED, TITRATED OXYGEN VIA A VENTURI MASK), AND WITHIN JUST 1 HOUR HAS DEVELOPED A CLASSIC PICTURE OF ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS WITH REDUCED CONSCIOUSNESS ('CO2 NARCOSIS' - CO2 IS A POTENT CEREBRAL VASODILATOR AND, AT SUFFICIENTLY HIGH LEVELS, DIRECTLY DEPRESSES CONSCIOUSNESS/CNS FUNCTION). THE KEY DIAGNOSTIC CLUE: HIS PO2 IS NOW 15 kPa, ABOVE THE NORMAL RANGE (10.6-14.2), CONFIRMING HE HAS BEEN OVER-OXYGENATED BY THE HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN THERAPY - COMBINED WITH THE MARKEDLY ELEVATED PCO2 (9 kPa) AND SEVERELY LOW pH (7.18, INDICATING SEVERE, ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS - NOTE THE BICARBONATE IS ALREADY CHRONICALLY ELEVATED AT 36, REFLECTING HIS UNDERLYING CHRONIC COPD/CO2 RETENTION, BUT THE pH HAS NOW DROPPED SIGNIFICANTLY DESPITE THIS COMPENSATION, INDICATING A SUPERIMPOSED ACUTE WORSENING). MANAGEMENT: THE IMMEDIATE, FIRST STEP IS TO REDUCE THE OXYGEN FLOW/FiO2, TARGETING A MORE CONTROLLED, APPROPRIATE SATURATION RANGE (TYPICALLY 88-92% FOR KNOWN OR AT-RISK CO2 RETAINERS) RATHER THAN THE HIGHER SATURATION TARGETS APPROPRIATE FOR MOST OTHER ACUTELY UNWELL PATIENTS - THIS OFTEN ALLOWS RAPID, SIGNIFICANT IMPROVEMENT IN THE RESPIRATORY DRIVE AND VENTILATION, IMPROVING THE HYPERCAPNIA AND ACIDOSIS, AND OFTEN AVOIDS THE NEED FOR MORE INVASIVE INTERVENTION - HOWEVER, IF REDUCING OXYGEN AND OPTIMISING OTHER THERAPY (BRONCHODILATORS, TREATING ANY UNDERLYING TRIGGER SUCH AS THE APPARENT CHEST INFECTION HERE WITH APPROPRIATE ANTIBIOTICS) DOES NOT RAPIDLY IMPROVE THE SITUATION, ESCALATION TO NON-INVASIVE VENTILATION (NIV, TYPICALLY BiPAP) OR, IF THAT FAILS OR IS CONTRAINDICATED, INVASIVE MECHANICAL VENTILATION WOULD THEN BE THE NEXT STEPS - BUT THE FIRST, IMMEDIATE, SIMPLE, POTENTIALLY REVERSIBLE ACTION IS TO CORRECT THE IATROGENIC OVER-OXYGENATION THAT HAS PRECIPITATED THIS ACUTE DETERIORATION.
One_Line: His PO2 is now too HIGH and his CO2 has shot up with a falling level of consciousness - this is CO2 narcosis from too much oxygen; turn the flow down first.

Question: A 30-year-old postpartum woman is admitted to the General Ward with diagnosis of right leg DVT. She was started on enoxaparin 80 mg bid, but in the same day of admission, she developed sudden onset dyspnea and right pleuritic chest pain. On examination, she was dyspneic and apprehensive. Heart sounds showed loud P2 and lungs were clear to auscultation (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 125/70 mmHg, Heart rate 100 /min, Respiratory rate 22 /min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 95 %. ABG HCO3- 22 (22-28 mmol/L), ABG PCO2 4.2 (4.7-6.0 kPa), pH 7.48 (7.36-7.45), ABG PO2 12 (10.6-14.2 kPa). Spiral CT chest: Thrombus in the right lower pulmonary artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
Explanation_A: Wrong. There is no specific indication to switch from enoxaparin (a low molecular weight heparin) to unfractionated heparin here - she is haemodynamically STABLE, and her presentation (a small, confirmed segmental PE) does not require this specific change.
Explanation_B: Wrong. Thrombolytic therapy is reserved for MASSIVE (HIGH-RISK) PE WITH HAEMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY (as discussed in an earlier related question in this bank) - THIS PATIENT IS HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE (normal blood pressure, oxygen saturation only mildly reduced at 95%, and importantly her CLINICAL SYMPTOMS DEVELOPED WHILE ALREADY ON THERAPEUTIC ANTICOAGULATION, suggesting this represents a SMALL, LOW-RISK PE rather than a massive, life-threatening event) - thrombolysis would be inappropriate, disproportionate, and carries unnecessary bleeding risk for this presentation.
Explanation_C: CORRECT. SHE DEVELOPED THIS (RELATIVELY SMALL, SEGMENTAL) PULMONARY EMBOLUS WHILE ALREADY RECEIVING THERAPEUTIC-DOSE ANTICOAGULATION (ENOXAPARIN 80MG TWICE DAILY, AN APPROPRIATE THERAPEUTIC DOSE) FOR HER KNOWN DVT - SHE REMAINS HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE THROUGHOUT (NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE, ONLY MILDLY REDUCED OXYGEN SATURATION, CLEAR LUNGS) - THE APPROPRIATE MANAGEMENT FOR THIS LOW-RISK, ALREADY-ANTICOAGULATED PRESENTATION IS SIMPLY TO CONTINUE THE SAME, ALREADY-APPROPRIATE THERAPEUTIC ANTICOAGULATION REGIMEN, SINCE SHE IS ALREADY RECEIVING ADEQUATE, EFFECTIVE TREATMENT FOR HER VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLIC DISEASE.
Explanation_D: Wrong. Invasive (surgical or catheter-directed mechanical) thrombectomy is reserved for MASSIVE PE WITH HAEMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY WHERE THROMBOLYSIS IS CONTRAINDICATED OR HAS FAILED - this is a disproportionate, unnecessary intervention for a stable patient with a small PE already on adequate anticoagulation.
High_Yield_Must_Know: LOW-RISK PULMONARY EMBOLISM DEVELOPING ON THERAPEUTIC ANTICOAGULATION - CONTINUE THE SAME TREATMENT IF THE PATIENT REMAINS STABLE. THIS QUESTION TESTS RECOGNITION THAT NOT EVERY NEW PE, EVEN ONE OCCURRING 'DESPITE' ANTICOAGULATION, REQUIRES ESCALATION OF THERAPY - THE KEY IS ASSESSING OVERALL RISK/SEVERITY, SPECIFICALLY HAEMODYNAMIC STABILITY. THIS PATIENT'S CLINICAL PICTURE IS REASSURING FOR A LOW-RISK EVENT: SHE IS HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE (NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE, HEART RATE ONLY MILDLY ELEVATED), HER OXYGEN SATURATION IS ONLY MILDLY REDUCED (95%), HER LUNGS ARE CLEAR (NO SIGNIFICANT PULMONARY COMPROMISE), AND CRITICALLY, THE CT CONFIRMS ONLY A THROMBUS IN A SEGMENTAL (LOWER LOBE) PULMONARY ARTERY BRANCH RATHER THAN A MASSIVE, CENTRAL, SADDLE-TYPE EMBOLUS (CONTRAST THIS WITH THE EARLIER, DIFFERENT QUESTION IN THIS BANK DESCRIBING AN UNSTABLE PATIENT WITH A SADDLE EMBOLUS REQUIRING THROMBOLYSIS - THAT WAS A MASSIVE, HIGH-RISK PE; THIS IS A SMALL, LOW-RISK ONE). THE RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS SEEN ON HER ABG (LOW PCO2, RAISED pH) IS A COMMON, EXPECTED FINDING IN PE FROM ANXIETY-DRIVEN HYPERVENTILATION/TACHYPNOEA, NOT A MARKER OF SEVERITY IN ITSELF. GIVEN SHE IS ALREADY RECEIVING APPROPRIATE, THERAPEUTIC-DOSE ANTICOAGULATION (enoxaparin at an appropriate treatment dose, not merely a prophylactic dose) FOR HER UNDERLYING DVT, AND REMAINS STABLE DESPITE THIS NEW, SMALL, SEGMENTAL PE, THE MOST APPROPRIATE MANAGEMENT IS SIMPLY TO CONTINUE THE SAME EFFECTIVE ANTICOAGULATION REGIMEN AND MONITOR CLOSELY - THERE IS NO INDICATION TO ESCALATE TO THROMBOLYSIS, MECHANICAL THROMBECTOMY, OR EVEN NECESSARILY SWITCH ANTICOAGULANT AGENTS, SINCE THE CURRENT THERAPY IS APPROPRIATE AND SHE REMAINS CLINICALLY WELL.
One_Line: A small, low-risk PE occurring on already-therapeutic anticoagulation in a stable patient just means continue the same treatment - it does not automatically mean escalate to thrombolysis.

Question: A 40-year-old man with paraplegia following road traffic accident one year ago is brought to the Emergency Department because of sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain. On examination, he is in severe distress and cyanosed. He has left parasternal heave and loud P2. Chest is clear to auscultation (see lab results and reports). Blood pressure 80/55 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Respiratory rate 30 /min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 86 %. ABG HCO3- 22 (22-28 mmol/L), ABG PCO2 4.2 (4.7-6.0 kPa), pH 7.4 (7.36-7.45), ABG PO2 8.6 (10.6-14.2 kPa). Echocardiogram: Dilated right ventricle with pulmonary artery pressure of 55 mmHg. Venous Doppler: Confirmed DVT in the left leg extending to the thigh. Which of the following is the best line of management?
Explanation_A: Wrong as the PRIMARY, immediate management, though an IVC filter might be considered as an ADJUNCT in specific circumstances (such as a contraindication to anticoagulation). It does not address the IMMEDIATE, LIFE-THREATENING haemodynamic compromise from the current massive PE - it only prevents FUTURE emboli, not the current crisis.
Explanation_B: CORRECT. THIS IS A MASSIVE (HIGH-RISK) PULMONARY EMBOLISM WITH HAEMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY (HYPOTENSIVE AT 80/55, SEVERE HYPOXIA AT 86%, SEVERE DISTRESS/CYANOSIS, ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC EVIDENCE OF SIGNIFICANT RIGHT VENTRICULAR STRAIN/DILATION WITH SIGNIFICANTLY ELEVATED PULMONARY ARTERY PRESSURE) IN A PATIENT WITH A CONFIRMED, EXTENSIVE (PROXIMAL, EXTENDING TO THE THIGH) DVT - AS ESTABLISHED IN AN EARLIER, ANALOGOUS QUESTION IN THIS BANK, MASSIVE, HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE PE REQUIRES IMMEDIATE SYSTEMIC THROMBOLYSIS (ALTEPLASE) TO RAPIDLY DISSOLVE THE CLOT BURDEN AND RESTORE HAEMODYNAMIC STABILITY.
Explanation_C: Wrong as the SOLE, primary management for THIS severity of presentation. Standard-intensity anticoagulation alone (without thrombolysis) is appropriate for STABLE PE, but is INSUFFICIENT AS THE SOLE TREATMENT for this haemodynamically UNSTABLE, life-threatening massive PE, which requires the more rapid, aggressive clot-dissolving action of thrombolysis.
Explanation_D: Wrong. Warfarin is an ORAL agent for LONGER-TERM, OUTPATIENT anticoagulation management once a patient is stabilised - it has no role in the IMMEDIATE management of an acute, life-threatening massive PE.
High_Yield_Must_Know: MASSIVE (HIGH-RISK) PULMONARY EMBOLISM - REPEATED, HIGH-YIELD RECOGNITION OF THE NEED FOR IMMEDIATE THROMBOLYSIS. THIS QUESTION CLOSELY PARALLELS AN EARLIER ONE IN THIS BANK (THE PYELONEPHRITIS PATIENT WITH A SADDLE EMBOLUS), REINFORCING THE SAME CRITICAL PRINCIPLE: WHEN A PATIENT WITH CONFIRMED PE IS HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE (HYPOTENSIVE, SEVERE HYPOXIA, SIGNIFICANT DISTRESS), WITH ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC EVIDENCE OF SIGNIFICANT ACUTE RIGHT VENTRICULAR STRAIN (DILATED RV, SIGNIFICANTLY ELEVATED PULMONARY ARTERY PRESSURE, AS SEEN HERE), THIS IS A MASSIVE/HIGH-RISK PE REQUIRING IMMEDIATE SYSTEMIC THROMBOLYSIS (ALTEPLASE), NOT SIMPLY STANDARD ANTICOAGULATION ALONE. ADDITIONAL RISK FACTOR NOTED IN THIS PATIENT: CHRONIC PARAPLEGIA (FROM HIS PRIOR TRAUMATIC INJURY) IS ITSELF A SIGNIFICANT, RECOGNISED RISK FACTOR FOR VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM, GIVEN PROLONGED IMMOBILITY AND VENOUS STASIS IN THE PARALYSED LIMBS - THIS PROVIDES THE UNDERLYING PREDISPOSING CONTEXT FOR HIS EXTENSIVE, PROXIMAL DVT AND THE RESULTING MASSIVE PE. THE MECHANISTIC PRINCIPLE REMAINS THE SAME AS DISCUSSED PREVIOUSLY IN THIS BANK: STANDARD ANTICOAGULATION (HEPARIN, ENOXAPARIN, WARFARIN) ONLY PREVENTS FURTHER CLOT FORMATION/EXTENSION BUT DOES NOT ACTIVELY DISSOLVE THE EXISTING, ALREADY LIFE-THREATENING CLOT BURDEN - IN A PATIENT WHOSE RIGHT VENTRICLE IS ACUTELY FAILING FROM THE SUDDEN PRESSURE OVERLOAD, THERE IS SIMPLY NOT ENOUGH TIME TO WAIT FOR THE BODY'S OWN NATURAL FIBRINOLYSIS TO GRADUALLY CLEAR THE CLOT - THROMBOLYTIC THERAPY IS NEEDED TO RAPIDLY DISSOLVE THE OBSTRUCTING CLOT AND RESTORE ADEQUATE PULMONARY BLOOD FLOW AND RIGHT VENTRICULAR FUNCTION BEFORE CARDIOVASCULAR COLLAPSE ENSUES.
One_Line: Unstable, hypoxic, with echo evidence of acute right heart strain from a massive PE - this needs alteplase now, standard anticoagulation alone will not act fast enough.

Question: A 50-year-old woman presented with fever, dyspnea and weight loss. Physical examination showed evidence of pleural effusion in the left hemithorax (see report). Pleural fluid analysis: Shows exudative fluid with high gamma interferon level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Wrong. Empyema is a FRANKLY PURULENT pleural collection, typically with LOW pH, LOW GLUCOSE, and organisms visible/culturable on Gram stain/culture - the specific finding of an elevated ADENOSINE DEAMINASE/GAMMA INTERFERON (interferon-gamma) level is not the characteristic marker for simple empyema.
Explanation_B: Wrong. Mesothelioma (associated with asbestos exposure) causes a pleural effusion, but does NOT specifically produce this characteristic ELEVATED GAMMA INTERFERON marker.
Explanation_C: Wrong. A parapneumonic effusion (from an underlying pneumonia) is exudative, but does not specifically show the elevated gamma interferon level that is characteristic of tuberculous effusion specifically.
Explanation_D: CORRECT. AN EXUDATIVE PLEURAL EFFUSION WITH A HIGH GAMMA INTERFERON (INTERFERON-GAMMA) LEVEL IS HIGHLY CHARACTERISTIC OF TUBERCULOUS PLEURAL EFFUSION - INTERFERON-GAMMA IS RELEASED BY SENSITISED T-LYMPHOCYTES IN RESPONSE TO MYCOBACTERIAL ANTIGENS, AND ITS ELEVATION IN PLEURAL FLUID IS A WELL-ESTABLISHED, HIGH-YIELD DIAGNOSTIC MARKER FOR TB PLEURITIS (ALONGSIDE THE RELATED, ALSO CLASSICALLY TESTED, ELEVATED ADENOSINE DEAMINASE/ADA LEVEL).
High_Yield_Must_Know: TUBERCULOUS PLEURAL EFFUSION - RECOGNISE THE CHARACTERISTIC PLEURAL FLUID BIOMARKERS. TB PLEURAL EFFUSION TYPICALLY PRESENTS WITH SUBACUTE/CHRONIC CONSTITUTIONAL SYMPTOMS - FEVER, WEIGHT LOSS, NIGHT SWEATS, DYSPNOEA, AND SOMETIMES PLEURITIC CHEST PAIN - REFLECTING A HYPERSENSITIVITY REACTION TO MYCOBACTERIAL ANTIGENS IN THE PLEURAL SPACE (RATHER THAN NECESSARILY ACTIVE, HEAVILY BACILLARY PLEURAL DISEASE, WHICH IS WHY DIRECT SMEAR MICROSCOPY OF THE PLEURAL FLUID FOR ACID-FAST BACILLI IS OFTEN NEGATIVE/LOW YIELD, AND CULTURE, WHILE MORE SENSITIVE, TAKES WEEKS). PLEURAL FLUID CHARACTERISTICS: EXUDATIVE (BY LIGHT'S CRITERIA), TYPICALLY LYMPHOCYTE-PREDOMINANT ON CELL COUNT, AND MOST DISTINCTIVELY, ELEVATED LEVELS OF TWO SPECIFIC BIOMARKERS REFLECTING THE UNDERLYING CELL-MEDIATED IMMUNE RESPONSE TO MYCOBACTERIAL ANTIGENS: ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) - AN ENZYME RELEASED BY ACTIVATED LYMPHOCYTES AND MACROPHAGES, WITH GOOD SENSITIVITY AND SPECIFICITY FOR TB PLEURITIS WHEN SIGNIFICANTLY ELEVATED (THE MOST WIDELY USED, CLASSIC MARKER); AND INTERFERON-GAMMA - RELEASED BY SENSITISED T-LYMPHOCYTES SPECIFICALLY RESPONDING TO MYCOBACTERIAL ANTIGENS, ALSO HIGHLY SENSITIVE AND SPECIFIC FOR TB PLEURAL EFFUSION WHEN ELEVATED, AND INCREASINGLY USED (SOMETIMES REFERRED TO IN THE CONTEXT OF PLEURAL FLUID INTERFERON-GAMMA RELEASE ASSAYS) - EITHER OR BOTH OF THESE ELEVATED BIOMARKERS, IN THE CORRECT CLINICAL CONTEXT, STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE DIAGNOSIS OF TB PLEURITIS, OFTEN ALLOWING PRESUMPTIVE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT INITIATION WITHOUT NEEDING TO AWAIT SLOWER, LESS SENSITIVE CULTURE RESULTS, PARTICULARLY IN TB-ENDEMIC SETTINGS. CONFIRMATORY TESTING (WHERE FEASIBLE) INCLUDES PLEURAL BIOPSY (SHOWING CASEATING GRANULOMAS) AND/OR CULTURE/PCR-BASED TESTING OF PLEURAL FLUID OR TISSUE.
One_Line: An exudative pleural effusion with a high interferon-gamma level is the classic marker for tuberculous pleuritis.

Question: A 55-year-old man with COPD, presented with increasing dyspnea, cough and bilateral lower limb swelling. Physical examination showed elevated JVP, hepatomegaly and pitting edema in both lower limbs. Chest auscultation revealed scattered rhonchi in both sides. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Option_D: High resolution CT scan of chest
Explanation_A: Wrong as the immediate priority. Spirometry assesses/confirms his ALREADY-KNOWN underlying COPD severity, but does not address or explain the NEW finding of right heart failure signs (elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, bilateral leg oedema), which is the more clinically pressing issue requiring urgent characterisation.
Explanation_B: CORRECT. THE NEW FINDINGS OF ELEVATED JVP, HEPATOMEGALY, AND BILATERAL PITTING LEG OEDEMA IN A KNOWN COPD PATIENT SUGGEST DEVELOPING COR PULMONALE (RIGHT HEART FAILURE SECONDARY TO CHRONIC LUNG DISEASE/PULMONARY HYPERTENSION) - AN ECHOCARDIOGRAM IS THE APPROPRIATE, ESSENTIAL NEXT STEP TO ASSESS RIGHT VENTRICULAR SIZE/FUNCTION, ESTIMATE PULMONARY ARTERY PRESSURE, AND ALSO IMPORTANTLY TO ASSESS LEFT VENTRICULAR FUNCTION (TO EXCLUDE OR IDENTIFY A CONCURRENT LEFT-SIDED CARDIAC CONTRIBUTION TO HIS PRESENTATION).
Explanation_C: Wrong as the FIRST, most appropriate NEXT step, though it could be a reasonable ADJUNCT if a DVT/PE were specifically suspected as contributing to his BILATERAL leg swelling. However, his OVERALL clinical picture (elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, BILATERAL leg swelling together) more strongly and directly suggests systemic/right heart failure (cor pulmonale) rather than primarily a venous thromboembolic process, making cardiac assessment the more directly relevant next step.
Explanation_D: Wrong as the most appropriate immediate next step. HRCT would further characterise underlying parenchymal lung disease, but does not directly address or characterise the ACUTE, new finding of right heart failure signs, which is better and more directly assessed by echocardiography.
High_Yield_Must_Know: COR PULMONALE - RECOGNISE THE CLINICAL SIGNS AND KNOW THAT ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY IS THE KEY NEXT INVESTIGATION. COR PULMONALE REFERS TO RIGHT VENTRICULAR ENLARGEMENT/DYSFUNCTION SECONDARY TO A PRIMARY DISORDER OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM (MOST COMMONLY CHRONIC LUNG DISEASE SUCH AS COPD CAUSING CHRONIC PULMONARY HYPERTENSION, ALTHOUGH THE TERM SPECIFICALLY EXCLUDES RIGHT HEART FAILURE FROM PRIMARY LEFT HEART DISEASE OR CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE) - THE UNDERLYING MECHANISM IS CHRONIC HYPOXIA-DRIVEN PULMONARY VASOCONSTRICTION AND VASCULAR REMODELLING (AS DISCUSSED IN THE WHO GROUP 3 PULMONARY HYPERTENSION CLASSIFICATION ELSEWHERE IN THIS BANK), PROGRESSIVELY INCREASING RIGHT VENTRICULAR AFTERLOAD UNTIL THE RIGHT VENTRICLE CAN NO LONGER COMPENSATE, LEADING TO DILATION, FAILURE, AND SYSTEMIC VENOUS CONGESTION. CLINICAL SIGNS OF DEVELOPING/ESTABLISHED COR PULMONALE (RIGHT HEART FAILURE), AS SEEN IN THIS PATIENT: ELEVATED JUGULAR VENOUS PRESSURE, HEPATOMEGALY (FROM HEPATIC VENOUS CONGESTION), AND PERIPHERAL (BILATERAL LOWER LIMB) PITTING OEDEMA - ALL REFLECTING SYSTEMIC VENOUS/RIGHT-SIDED CONGESTION, RATHER THAN PRIMARILY PULMONARY/LEFT-SIDED CONGESTION (WHICH WOULD MORE CLASSICALLY CAUSE PULMONARY OEDEMA, ORTHOPNOEA, AND BASAL CRACKLES). ONCE COR PULMONALE IS CLINICALLY SUSPECTED, ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY IS THE KEY, ESSENTIAL NEXT INVESTIGATION - IT ALLOWS DIRECT ASSESSMENT OF RIGHT VENTRICULAR SIZE, WALL THICKNESS, AND FUNCTION, ESTIMATION OF PULMONARY ARTERY SYSTOLIC PRESSURE (VIA THE TRICUSPID REGURGITANT JET VELOCITY), AND CRITICALLY, ASSESSMENT OF LEFT VENTRICULAR FUNCTION AND ANY VALVULAR DISEASE - THIS LAST POINT IS IMPORTANT BECAUSE IT HELPS DISTINGUISH TRUE COR PULMONALE (PRIMARILY PULMONARY/RIGHT-SIDED CAUSE) FROM A SCENARIO WHERE UNDERLYING, POSSIBLY UNRECOGNISED, LEFT HEART DISEASE IS CONTRIBUTING TO OR EXPLAINING THE OVERALL PICTURE, WHICH WOULD SIGNIFICANTLY CHANGE THE MANAGEMENT APPROACH. MANAGEMENT OF CONFIRMED COR PULMONALE FOCUSES ON TREATING THE UNDERLYING LUNG DISEASE (OPTIMISING COPD MANAGEMENT, LONG-TERM OXYGEN THERAPY IF HYPOXAEMIC, AS DISCUSSED ELSEWHERE IN THIS BANK REGARDING SURVIVAL BENEFIT IN COPD WITH COR PULMONALE) AND MANAGING FLUID OVERLOAD SYMPTOMATICALLY (DIURETICS).
One_Line: New signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, big liver, leg swelling) in a COPD patient suggest cor pulmonale - echocardiogram is the key next test to assess the right heart and pulmonary pressures.

Question: In a patient with COPD and cor pulmonale, which of the following improves survival?
Highlighted: COPD and cor pulmonale, improves survival
Explanation_A: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist used in asthma, not shown to improve survival in COPD.
Explanation_B: Inhaled steroids can reduce exacerbations in severe COPD but do not confer a mortality benefit.
Explanation_C: Correct. Long term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is the only intervention proven to improve survival in hypoxemic COPD patients (along with smoking cessation).
Explanation_D: Long acting beta agonists improve symptoms and quality of life but do not independently improve survival in COPD.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The only two interventions proven to decrease mortality in COPD are smoking cessation and long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) for those with resting severe hypoxemia (PaO2 <= 55 mmHg or SaO2 <= 88%, or PaO2 <= 59 with cor pulmonale).
One_Line: LTOT and smoking cessation are the only proven mortality-lowering therapies in COPD.

Question: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated for a 6-month history of recurrent dyspnea, cough, and wheezing. She is awakened with asthma symptoms 6-8 nights a month. Her current medication is salbutamol inhaler. On examination, there are wheezes in both lung fields. Which of the following is the most appropriate next best step in management?
Option_D: Inhaled budesonide and inhaled albuterol as needed
Highlighted: 6-8 nights a month, current medication is salbutamol
Explanation_A: Montelukast is an alternative, but not the preferred step-up therapy compared to inhaled corticosteroids.
Explanation_B: LABAs should never be used as monotherapy in asthma due to increased risk of asthma-related death.
Explanation_C: Correct. The patient has moderate persistent asthma (or uncontrolled on SABA alone). The preferred next step is low-dose ICS/LABA (budesonide/formoterol) as maintenance and reliever therapy.
Explanation_D: While ICS is needed, adding a LABA is preferred over PRN SABA alone for symptom control based on recent guidelines.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Frequent nighttime awakenings (>4/month) indicate moderate persistent asthma, requiring step-up to ICS-LABA therapy (e.g., budesonide-formoterol) which provides both maintenance and quick relief.
One_Line: Uncontrolled asthma on SABA alone requires step-up to an ICS/LABA combination.

Question: A 30-year-old woman complains of recurrent attacks of sudden onset dyspnea, chest and throat tightness. Inhaled salbutamol is of little help; however, her symptoms improves suddenly. On examination, she is found to have inspiratory wheeze during dyspnea spells. Which of the following is the likely cause of symptoms?
Highlighted: sudden onset dyspnea, throat tightness, inspiratory wheeze, poor response to salbutamol
Explanation_A: Asthma typically presents with expiratory wheezing and responds to bronchodilators.
Explanation_B: Foreign body can cause localized wheezing but would not typically present as recurrent brief attacks that resolve suddenly without intervention.
Explanation_C: GERD can trigger asthma or microaspiration but wouldn't primarily cause sudden inspiratory stridor/wheeze as an isolated finding.
Explanation_D: Correct. Vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) mimics asthma but classically presents with throat tightness, inspiratory wheeze (stridor), and failure to respond to asthma medications.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Vocal cord dysfunction involves paradoxical closure of the vocal cords during inspiration, leading to inspiratory stridor and throat tightness, often misdiagnosed as refractory asthma.
One_Line: Inspiratory wheeze + throat tightness + failure of albuterol = Vocal cord dysfunction.

Question: A 55-year-old obese non-smoker man with hypertension presents with exertional dyspnea for 2 years. His wife stated that he is uncomfortable while sleeping at night and produces loud snores. Examination revealed central cyanosis, suffused conjunctivae and clear chest. BMI 40 kg/m2. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
Highlighted: obese, daytime somnolence, loud snores, central cyanosis
Explanation_A: Spirometry may show restrictive pattern due to obesity but cannot diagnose sleep apnea.
Explanation_B: Spiral CT is used for pulmonary embolism, not sleep apnea.
Explanation_C: Correct. Polysomnography (sleep study) is the gold standard diagnostic test for Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA).
Explanation_D: Methacholine challenge tests for asthma hyperresponsiveness, not sleep apnea.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is strongly suspected in obese patients with loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime sleepiness, and is definitively diagnosed with nocturnal polysomnography.
One_Line: Polysomnography is the diagnostic study of choice for Obstructive Sleep Apnea.

Question: A 55-year-old obese non-smoker man presents with loud snoring, daytime somnolence and exertional dyspnea for 4 years. Examination revealed central cyanosis: suffused conjunctivae and clear chest (see lab results). BMI 40 kg/m2. ABG HCO3- 38 (22-28 mmol/L), ABG PCO2 6.9 (4.7-6.0 kPa), pH 7.38 (7.36-7.45), ABG PO2 9 (10.6-14.2 kPa). Which of the following is the best treatment after polysomnography?
Highlighted: loud snoring, daytime somnolence, ABG PCO2 6.9, pH 7.38
Explanation_A: Oxygen alone may worsen hypercapnia in patients with obesity hypoventilation syndrome.
Explanation_B: Tiotropium is for COPD, not sleep apnea or obesity hypoventilation.
Explanation_C: Correct. Nasal CPAP (or BiPAP) is the primary treatment for OSA and Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome to keep airways open and improve gas exchange.
Explanation_D: Prednisone has no role in the treatment of OSA or Obesity Hypoventilation.
High_Yield_Must_Know: In Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) and severe OSA, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) acts as a pneumatic splint to prevent upper airway collapse, improving hypoxia and hypercapnia.
One_Line: Nasal CPAP is the first-line treatment for Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Obesity Hypoventilation.

Question: A 65-year-old man with idiopathic bronchiectasis presents with persistent cough of large amount of mucoid sputum and dyspnea on exertion. He is compliant with his medications, which include azithromycin. Physical examination showed finger clubbing and mild bilateral coarse crackles. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
Highlighted: idiopathic bronchiectasis, persistent cough of large amount of mucoid sputum
Explanation_A: Prednisone is not indicated for routine bronchiectasis management unless there is ABPA.
Explanation_B: N-Acetylcysteine has weak evidence for bronchiectasis compared to airway clearance techniques.
Explanation_C: Saline nebulizer can help thin secretions, but physical clearance is the mainstay.
Explanation_D: Correct. Chest physiotherapy and postural drainage are the cornerstone of bronchiectasis management to clear secretions and prevent infection.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The cornerstone of daily management for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is mechanical airway clearance (postural drainage, chest physiotherapy) to prevent mucus plugging and superinfections.
One_Line: Postural sputum drainage is the mainstay non-pharmacologic treatment for bronchiectasis.

Question: A 60-year-old man known to have COPD refused the advice to stop smoking. What is the best statement should be given to him during a communication session?
Option_A: You better stop smoking otherwise you will die
Option_B: We will do everything to help you stop smoking
Option_C: We have to talk to your family about this refusal
Option_D: If you don't stop smoking we will stop seeing you in the clinic
Highlighted: refused the advice to stop smoking, best statement
Explanation_A: Confrontational and threatening language destroys the doctor-patient relationship.
Explanation_B: Correct. Expressing support and offering resources aligns with motivational interviewing and maintains a therapeutic alliance.
Explanation_C: Violates patient autonomy and confidentiality; adult patients have the right to refuse.
Explanation_D: Abandonment of the patient is unethical.
High_Yield_Must_Know: When counseling patients who refuse behavior change, physicians should employ motivational interviewing, express empathy, avoid confrontation, and leave the door open for future discussions.
One_Line: Always use supportive and empathetic statements when counseling non-compliant patients.

Question: A 56-year-old man who has chronic productive cough underwent a CT chest, which was consistent with bronchiectasis. He came today to discuss his disease. Which of the following would convey the diagnostic information to him?
Option_A: Read to him the CT report
Option_B: Show him the chest X-ray film
Option_C: Inform him that he has bronchiectasis
Option_D: Tell him that his air tubules are inflamed and damaged
Highlighted: convey the diagnostic information to him
Explanation_A: Reading a technical radiologist report will confuse the patient with medical jargon.
Explanation_B: Showing the film without simple explanation is not helpful to a layperson.
Explanation_C: Using the medical term 'bronchiectasis' without explaining it does not ensure understanding.
Explanation_D: Correct. Explaining the pathophysiology in simple layman's terms ('air tubules are inflamed and damaged') ensures the patient comprehends the condition.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Effective medical communication requires translating complex medical terminology into simple, easily understandable concepts tailored to the patient's health literacy level.
One_Line: Always use simple, jargon-free language to explain medical conditions to patients.

Question: A young patient has poorly controlled asthma and her doctor decided to start her on oral steroids. She is uncomfortable about that decision. When counselling this patient, what is the most important communication aspect should be addressed?
Option_D: The scientific basis of using steroids
Highlighted: uncomfortable about that decision, most important communication aspect
Explanation_A: Living conditions are less immediately relevant than addressing her specific anxiety about the drug.
Explanation_B: Correct. Eliciting and addressing the patient's specific fears (e.g., weight gain, side effects) is paramount to ensure adherence and build trust.
Explanation_C: She is described as uncomfortable, not necessarily angry; exploring concerns comes first.
Explanation_D: Scientific facts alone rarely alleviate emotional concerns or fears about side effects.
High_Yield_Must_Know: In patient-centered care, exploring the patient's beliefs, fears, and concerns regarding a new medication is the most effective way to improve compliance.
One_Line: Address the patient's specific concerns before explaining the scientific basis of a treatment.

Question: A 74-year-old man, who smokes for 40 years, underwent a CT chest, which showed a large lung mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to break the bad news?
Option_A: Avoid wasting time and tell him directly that he has lung cancer
Option_B: Inform him that this is nothing to worry about
Option_C: Inform him that he should stop smoking
Option_D: Deliver the information in small steps
Explanation_A: Being overly direct without preparation can be psychologically traumatic.
Explanation_B: Minimizing the issue gives false hope and damages trust.
Explanation_C: Focusing on smoking cessation ignores the acute, severe issue of a potential lung cancer diagnosis.
Explanation_D: Correct. Breaking bad news should follow structured protocols like SPIKES, delivering information in digestible chunks (small steps) and checking for understanding.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news emphasizes giving a warning shot, delivering information in small pieces, and assessing the patient's emotional response.
One_Line: Break bad news in small, digestible steps to allow the patient to process the information.

Question: A patient with interstitial lung disease has repeated admissions for pneumonia. His son is worried about antibiotics induced diarrhoea. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to address this situation?
Option_A: Tell him that the diarrhea is not serious
Option_B: Stress that the hospital infection control policy will be implemented
Option_C: Agree with him that the antibiotics should be stopped
Option_D: Apologize for repeatedly using antibiotics to treat his father
Explanation_A: Dismissing concerns minimizes the son's valid worry (C. diff can be severe).
Explanation_B: Correct. Reassuring the family that proper infection control protocols (like monitoring, isolation, hygiene) are in place addresses the root of their anxiety.
Explanation_C: Stopping antibiotics for pneumonia could be fatal to the patient.
Explanation_D: Apologizing implies a mistake was made, but treating pneumonia with antibiotics is standard of care.
High_Yield_Must_Know: When families express valid fears of hospital-acquired complications (like C. diff), the best approach is to explain the proactive preventive measures the hospital uses.
One_Line: Address valid fears of medical complications by explaining the preventive protocols in place.

Question: A 28-year-old man, who is a known drug addict, is found in deep coma and cyanosed. Blood pressure 100/55 mmHg, Heart rate 55 /min, Respiratory rate 8 /min, Oxygen saturation 85 %. Which of the following is the most important initial management?
Option_A: Obtain detailed history from the family
Highlighted: deep coma, cyanosed, Respiratory rate 8 /min, Oxygen saturation 85 %
Explanation_A: History is secondary to securing the airway and breathing in an unstable patient.
Explanation_B: Correct. The patient has severe respiratory depression (RR 8) and hypoxia (cyanosis, SpO2 85%) causing coma, requiring immediate airway protection and mechanical ventilation (ABCs first).
Explanation_C: Gastric lavage is contraindicated in a comatose patient without a protected airway due to aspiration risk.
Explanation_D: A CT scan may be needed later, but airway and breathing take precedence over diagnostic imaging.
High_Yield_Must_Know: In any toxicology or trauma patient presenting with a GCS < 8 or severe respiratory depression (RR < 10), securing the airway and assisting ventilation is the absolute first step (ABCs).
One_Line: Always secure the airway and support ventilation (ABCs) before pursuing diagnostic testing.

Question: A 53-year-old man with liver cirrhosis presents with several episodes of vomiting of blood and black tarry stool. Blood pressure: Supine 105/60 mmHg, Sitting 85/50 mmHg. Heart rate: Supine 90 /min, Sitting 110 /min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Option_D: Intravenous infusion of H2 receptor antagonists
Highlighted: liver cirrhosis, vomiting of blood, Sitting 85/50 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min
Explanation_A: NG tubes are generally avoided or used with extreme caution in suspected variceal bleeding, and are not the first step.
Explanation_B: Endoscopy is definitive but the patient is hemodynamically unstable and must be resuscitated first.
Explanation_C: Correct. The patient has massive upper GI bleeding with orthostatic hypotension (shock). IV fluid resuscitation is always the most critical first step.
Explanation_D: H2 blockers have no role in acute variceal bleeding; octreotide and antibiotics would be used, but after IV fluids.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Initial management of acute variceal hemorrhage requires establishing large-bore IV access and restoring intravascular volume with fluids and blood products before performing endoscopy.
One_Line: Hemodynamic resuscitation with IV fluids is always the first step in acute GI bleeding.

Question: An elderly man, known to have COPD is brought to Emergency Department with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis and drowsiness. His upper airways were full of secretions (see lab results). Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 38.0 C, Oxygen saturation 74 %. ABG HCO3- 36 (22-28 mmol/L), ABG PCO2 7.99 (4.7-6.0 kPa), pH 7.24 (7.36-7.45), ABG PO2 8.99 (10.6-14.2 kPa). Which of the following is the best option in management?
Highlighted: drowsiness, upper airways were full of secretions, pH 7.24
Explanation_A: NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) is contraindicated in patients with impaired consciousness (drowsiness) and inability to clear secretions.
Explanation_B: Correct. The patient has hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH 7.24, PCO2 7.99) with altered mental status and copious secretions, requiring invasive mechanical ventilation.
Explanation_C: Aminophylline is a third-line agent and does not address the acute need for airway protection.
Explanation_D: Face mask oxygen will not correct the severe hypercapnia and hypoventilation in this comatose patient.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Contraindications to non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in COPD exacerbations include altered mental status (drowsiness/coma), high aspiration risk, and inability to clear respiratory secretions.
One_Line: Altered mental status and copious secretions in severe COPD exacerbation require intubation, not NIV.

Question: A 40-year-old woman is admitted with diagnosis of Guillain Barre Syndrome. Which of the following would be the most appropriate method for monitoring ventilatory impairment?
Highlighted: Guillain Barre Syndrome, monitoring ventilatory impairment
Explanation_A: RSBI is used to assess readiness for extubation, not to monitor progressive neuromuscular weakness.
Explanation_B: Serial ABGs are painful and a late indicator of respiratory failure; waiting for hypercapnia is dangerous.
Explanation_C: Correct. Bedside forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF) are the standard methods to monitor impending respiratory failure in neuromuscular diseases.
Explanation_D: Oxygen saturation only drops late in the course of neuromuscular hypoventilation; it misses early hypercapnia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome require frequent bedside monitoring of Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) and Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF). An FVC < 20 mL/kg is an indication for intubation.
One_Line: Monitor respiratory status in GBS using bedside vital capacity and negative inspiratory force.

Question: A 60-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and ischemic heart disease is admitted to the Critical Care Unit in shock. The following parameters are obtained from pulmonary artery catheterization (see table). Right atrial pressure 2 (2-8 mmHg), Pulmonary artery pressure 15/3 (16-24/5-12 mmHg), Wedge pressure 4 (5-12 mmHg), Cardiac output 2.5 (4-6 L/min), Systemic vascular resistance 1800 (800-1200 dyne/s/cm5). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Highlighted: Right atrial pressure 2, Pulmonary artery pressure 15/3, Wedge pressure 4, Cardiac output 2.5
Explanation_A: Cardiogenic shock would show high filling pressures (high RAP and high Wedge pressure).
Explanation_B: Septic shock (distributive) characteristically presents with low systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and high cardiac output.
Explanation_C: Correct. Low right atrial pressure, low pulmonary artery pressure, low wedge pressure, low cardiac output, and a compensatory high SVR perfectly describe hypovolemic shock.
Explanation_D: Pulmonary embolism typically causes high right atrial pressure and high pulmonary artery pressure (right heart strain) with a low wedge pressure.
High_Yield_Must_Know: In hypovolemic shock, all cardiac filling pressures (CVP/RAP, PAP, PCWP) are markedly decreased due to volume loss, leading to low cardiac output and reflexly elevated SVR.
One_Line: Low CVP, low wedge pressure, and low cardiac output with high SVR indicate hypovolemic shock.

Question: A 45-year-old man is just admitted to the Critical Care Unit with polytrauma following road traffic accident because of hypotension. He is sedated and mechanically ventilated. His heart sounds are distant with no added sounds. Lung auscultation showed equal air entry to both sides with no added sounds (see report). Blood pressure 85/55 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Temperature 36.0 C, Oxygen saturation 100 %. Central venous pressure: Right atrial pressure 15 mmHg. Chest radiograph: Cardiomegaly and fractured sternum. Both lungs are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Highlighted: hypotension, distant heart sounds, Right atrial pressure 15, Cardiomegaly
Explanation_A: Fat embolism causes hypoxemia and lung infiltrates, not isolated high CVP with distant heart sounds and cardiomegaly.
Explanation_B: Septic shock typically has low to normal CVP and bounding pulses, without cardiomegaly or muffled heart sounds.
Explanation_C: Hypovolemia would present with a low CVP/Right atrial pressure.
Explanation_D: Correct. Beck's triad (hypotension, distant heart sounds, elevated JVP/CVP) plus cardiomegaly on X-ray in a trauma setting points strongly to cardiac tamponade.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Cardiac tamponade restricts diastolic filling, equalizing diastolic pressures across all chambers. It manifests clinically as Beck's Triad: hypotension, elevated JVP (or high CVP), and muffled heart sounds.
One_Line: Hypotension + muffled heart sounds + high CVP = Cardiac Tamponade.

Question: A 35-year-old man is evaluated in the Orthopedic Ward because of dyspnea, tachycardia and confusion. The patient had fractured left femur for which he undergone internal fixation 2-days ago. He is on enoxaparin as prophylaxis and pain-killer as needed. On examination, the heart sounds are normal and there are scattered crepitations in both lung fields. Petechial rash around the neck and axillae are noticed (see lab result and reports). Blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Respiratory rate 26 /min, Temperature 37.8 C, Oxygen saturation 85 %. ABG HCO3- 22 (22-28 mmol/L), ABG PCO2 4.7 (4.7-6.0 kPa), pH 7.26 (7.36-7.45), ABG PO2 9.5 (10.6-14.2 kPa). Chest radiograph: Bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrate. Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Highlighted: fractured left femur, confusion, Petechial rash around the neck
Explanation_A: Pulmonary embolism does not typically cause a petechial rash or diffuse bilateral infiltrates.
Explanation_B: Correct. The classic triad of fat embolism syndrome is hypoxemia, neurologic abnormalities (confusion), and a petechial rash, occurring 24-72 hours after a long bone fracture.
Explanation_C: Aspiration pneumonia causes lung infiltrates and hypoxia but would not explain the petechial rash.
Explanation_D: Septicemia could cause confusion and rash, but the timing post-femur fracture and classic triad strongly point to fat embolism.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Fat Embolism Syndrome typically presents 24-72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fractures. Look for the classic triad: respiratory distress (hypoxia), neurological dysfunction (confusion), and a petechial rash (especially axillary/neck).
One_Line: Long bone fracture + hypoxia + confusion + petechial rash = Fat Embolism Syndrome.

Question: A 65-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus and old myocardial infarction is admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with urosepsis and septic shock. Her blood pressure did not respond to fluid challenge for which she is started on norepinephrine infusion. She has hypoxia despite optimizing the ventilator parameters and FiO2 of 100% (see table and report). Right atrial pressure 3 (2-8 mmHg), Pulmonary artery pressure 13/3 (16-24/5-12 mmHg), Wedge pressure 5 (5-12 mmHg), Cardiac output 4 (4-6 L/min). Chest X-ray: Bilateral lung infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the lung infiltrate?
Highlighted: septic shock, Wedge pressure 5, Bilateral lung infiltrate
Explanation_A: Correct. ARDS is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema triggered by systemic inflammation (like urosepsis), characterized by bilateral infiltrates and a normal/low wedge pressure (<18 mmHg).
Explanation_B: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is ruled out by the low wedge pressure (5 mmHg), which would be elevated (>18 mmHg) in left heart failure.
Explanation_C: PE rarely causes bilateral diffuse lung infiltrates.
Explanation_D: Volume overload would elevate the PCWP (wedge pressure).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) presents with severe hypoxemia and bilateral alveolar infiltrates on imaging, with a normal PCWP (<18 mmHg), distinguishing it from cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
One_Line: Bilateral infiltrates + normal wedge pressure in a septic patient = ARDS.

Question: A 50-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension, presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset left sided body weakness for 4 hours. On examination, he has left sided upper motor neuron facial palsy and left sided hemiparesis. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
Highlighted: left sided body weakness for 4 hours, best next step
Explanation_A: Aspirin shouldn't be given until hemorrhagic stroke is ruled out.
Explanation_B: MRI is more sensitive for ischemia but CT is faster and is the standard of care to rapidly rule out hemorrhage in the acute setting.
Explanation_C: Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet and should not be given until bleeding is ruled out.
Explanation_D: Correct. A non-contrast head CT is the most critical first step in suspected acute stroke to differentiate between ischemic and hemorrhagic causes before deciding on thrombolysis/antiplatelets.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The absolute first step in the management of a suspected acute stroke is a non-contrast CT scan of the head to rule out intracranial hemorrhage, dictating eligibility for tPA.
One_Line: Non-contrast CT head is the best initial step for sudden focal neurological deficits.

Question: A 16-year-old boy presents with a several days history of progressive arm and leg weakness. No diplopia or loss of sphincter control. He has been well except for an upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. On examination, his breathing is slow and shallow. His heart rate and blood pressure are fluctuant. There is symmetrical weakness of the face and all four extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are absent, and sensations are intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Highlighted: progressive arm and leg weakness, upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago, Deep tendon reflexes are absent
Explanation_A: Polymyositis presents with proximal muscle weakness but reflexes are typically preserved, and it does not usually present acutely post-infection.
Explanation_B: Myasthenia gravis features fatiguable weakness, prominent ocular symptoms (diplopia, ptosis), and preserved reflexes.
Explanation_C: Transverse myelitis presents with a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia) below the lesion.
Explanation_D: Correct. Ascending symmetric paralysis and areflexia following a respiratory or GI infection are the classic hallmarks of Guillain-Barré Syndrome.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) classically presents with rapidly progressive, ascending, symmetric flaccid paralysis and areflexia, often triggered by a preceding Campylobacter jejuni or viral infection.
One_Line: Ascending weakness + areflexia post-infection = Guillain-Barré Syndrome.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents with an 8-week history of severe headache. The headaches have occurred at the same time each day, about 2 a.m. and last around 30 minutes. Headaches are accompanied by lacrimation and redness of the right eye. Which of the following is the best to prevent this type of headache?
Highlighted: headache at the same time each day, lacrimation and redness of the right eye, prevent this type
Explanation_A: Correct. The patient has cluster headaches. Verapamil (a calcium channel blocker) is the first-line medication for the prevention/prophylaxis of cluster headaches.
Explanation_B: Propranolol is used for migraine prophylaxis, not cluster headaches.
Explanation_C: Sumatriptan is an abortive treatment for acute cluster headache attacks, not for prevention.
Explanation_D: 100% Oxygen is the first-line abortive treatment for acute attacks, not a prophylactic measure.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Cluster headaches manifest as severe, unilateral, orbital/supraorbital pain with autonomic symptoms (tearing, ptosis). Acute attacks are treated with 100% O2 and triptans; Verapamil is used for prophylaxis.
One_Line: Verapamil prevents cluster headaches; 100% oxygen aborts them.

Question: A 55-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension complains of pain in the right eye and double vision when looking to the left. On examination, there is ptosis, limited adduction, elevation, and depression of the right eye. The pupils are equal and reactive in both sides. Fundoscopy and other cranial nerve are normal as well as the rest of neurological examination of the upper and lower limbs. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
Highlighted: ptosis, limited adduction, elevation, and depression, pupils are equal and reactive
Explanation_A: PCoA aneurysms typically compress the superficial parasympathetic fibers of CN III first, presenting with a dilated, non-reactive pupil (pupil-involving).
Explanation_B: Correct. Diabetic CN III neuropathy is an ischemic mononeuropathy that classically spares the parasympathetic pupillary fibers located on the periphery of the nerve, causing a 'pupil-sparing' CN III palsy.
Explanation_C: Cavernous sinus thrombosis would likely involve multiple cranial nerves (III, IV, V1, V2, VI) and present with chemosis and proptosis.
Explanation_D: Midbrain tumors would present with other brainstem signs (e.g., contralateral hemiparesis - Weber syndrome).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Ischemic CN III palsies (commonly due to diabetes) typically spare the pupil because the inner somatic fibers are infarcted while the peripheral parasympathetic pupillary fibers receive collateral blood supply.
One_Line: Pupil-sparing CN III palsy in an older patient with vascular risk factors is usually due to diabetic ischemic neuropathy.

Question: An 18-year-old boy known to have grand mal epilepsy since childhood is brought to the Emergency Department after having repeated tonic-clonic seizures at home. He is compliant with his medication, which is sodium valproate. In the Emergency Department, he is unconscious and continuously convulsing. After oxygenation and securing the airway, which of the following intravenous drugs should be administered?
Highlighted: unconscious and continuously convulsing, intravenous drugs
Explanation_A: Phenytoin is used as a second-line agent to prevent recurrence but acts too slowly to be the initial drug to break status epilepticus.
Explanation_B: Correct. The patient is in status epilepticus. Intravenous benzodiazepines (like diazepam or lorazepam) are the first-line treatment to rapidly abort the seizure.
Explanation_C: Thiopental or propofol are used for refractory status epilepticus requiring intubation, not as a first-line drug.
Explanation_D: Phenobarbital is used in neonatal seizures or refractory status epilepticus, not as first-line for adults.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Status epilepticus (continuous seizure >5 mins or recurrent without returning to baseline) requires immediate management: ABCs followed by rapid administration of an IV benzodiazepine (Lorazepam or Diazepam).
One_Line: First-line medical treatment for status epilepticus is an IV benzodiazepine.

Question: In a patient with Guillain Barre Syndrome, which of the following is the best treatment option?
Explanation_A: Steroids (oral or IV pulse) have no proven benefit in Guillain-Barré Syndrome and may actually worsen outcomes.
Explanation_B: Cyclosporine is an immunosuppressant used in transplants and other autoimmune diseases, not GBS.
Explanation_C: Correct. Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) or Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) are the primary disease-modifying treatments for GBS, accelerating recovery.
Explanation_D: Cyclophosphamide is used for vasculitis and severe systemic autoimmune diseases, not acute GBS.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The mainstay of disease-modifying therapy for Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is either Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) or Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange). Glucocorticoids are strictly not indicated.
One_Line: Treat Guillain-Barré Syndrome with IVIG or Plasmapheresis, never with steroids.

Question: Which of the following agents has been shown to reduce mortality in patients with congestive heart failure?
Explanation_A: Digitalis decreases hospitalization rates and provides symptom relief by increasing cardiac contractility, but it does NOT reduce overall mortality.
Explanation_B: Enalapril (an ACE inhibitor) reduces afterload and preload, and prevents deleterious cardiac remodeling, which has been definitively shown to reduce mortality in HFrEF.
Explanation_C: Furosemide is a loop diuretic excellent for fluid overload and congestion symptom relief, but it has no proven mortality benefit in heart failure.
Explanation_D: Procainamide is an antiarrhythmic agent not indicated for heart failure mortality reduction and may actually worsen heart failure or cause arrhythmias.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Drugs that provide a mortality benefit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, Beta-blockers, Aldosterone antagonists, and ARNIs. Diuretics and digoxin only improve symptoms.
One_Line: ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in CHF, whereas loop diuretics like furosemide only provide symptomatic relief.

Question: Which of the following is a recognized side effect of furosemide in congestive heart failure?
Explanation_A: Hypokalaemia is a very common and classic side effect of loop diuretics due to increased potassium excretion in the distal tubule.
Explanation_B: Bronchospasm is not a recognized side effect of furosemide; it is typically associated with beta-blockers.
Explanation_C: Furosemide can occasionally cause hyperglycemia and impaired glucose tolerance, not hypoglycemia.
Explanation_D: Haemolytic anaemia is exceptionally rare and not a classic or primarily recognized side effect of furosemide.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Loop diuretics (Furosemide) inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Major side effects include Hypokalemia, Hypomagnesemia, Hypocalcemia, Ototoxicity, and Hyperuricemia.
One_Line: Furosemide is a loop diuretic classically known to cause hypokalemia.

Question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with vomiting and generalized abdominal pain. She does not know her medications. She states that her vision has been slightly yellow tinged recently (see image). Blood pressure 90/50 mmHg Heart rate 60 /min Respiratory rate 16 /min Temperature 37° C Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Anterolateral MI can cause nausea and hypotension, but it does not cause yellow-tinged vision.
Explanation_B: Digoxin toxicity classically presents with gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea/vomiting), bradycardia, and visual disturbances, most notably yellow-green halos (xanthopsia).
Explanation_C: Hypokalaemia can cause weakness, arrhythmias, and predisposes patients to digoxin toxicity, but does not cause yellow vision directly.
Explanation_D: Hypothermia is ruled out as the patient's temperature is normal (37° C).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Digoxin toxicity presents with GI distress, confusion, visual changes (xanthopsia), and dangerous arrhythmias. It is highly exacerbated by hypokalemia.
One_Line: Yellow-tinged vision (xanthopsia) combined with GI distress and bradycardia is the classic hallmark of digoxin toxicity.

Question: A 60-year-old patient with a previous ischaemic stroke presents with a regular narrow complex tachycardia. The patient is hemodynamically stable. The decision is made to administer IV adenosine. In the presence of which of the following should the dose of adenosine be reduced?
Explanation_A: Theophylline is an adenosine receptor antagonist; it requires a HIGHER dose of adenosine for efficacy, not lower.
Explanation_B: Dipyridamole inhibits the cellular uptake of adenosine, significantly prolonging its half-life and intensifying its effects. The adenosine dose MUST be reduced.
Explanation_C: Adenosine is rapidly metabolized by erythrocytes and endothelial cells in the blood; renal impairment does not significantly affect its clearance.
Explanation_D: Significant mitral regurgitation is a valvular issue and does not directly alter adenosine's pharmacokinetics.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Dipyridamole and carbamazepine potentiate adenosine by blocking its nucleoside transporter uptake. In patients taking these, the starting dose of adenosine should be reduced.
One_Line: Dipyridamole inhibits adenosine cellular uptake, potentiating its effect, thus necessitating a reduced dose.

Question: Which of the following drugs used in the treatment of chronic heart failure has been shown to increase survival?
Explanation_A: Digoxin improves symptoms and reduces hospitalizations but does NOT increase survival.
Explanation_B: Enalapril (ACE inhibitor) reduces cardiac remodeling and is proven to increase survival in patients with chronic heart failure.
Explanation_C: Furosemide is used for volume overload (symptom control) but does not increase survival.
Explanation_D: Hydralazine alone is less effective than ACE inhibitors for survival; it is usually combined with nitrates for specific populations.
High_Yield_Must_Know: ACE inhibitors decrease angiotensin II and aldosterone production, reducing afterload and preload, preventing deleterious cardiac remodeling, and thereby increasing survival.
One_Line: ACE inhibitors like enalapril have a proven mortality benefit in chronic heart failure.

Question: A 39-year-old man presents to the clinic with unexplained fever 19 days after an attack of acute rheumatic fever. Several of his teeth have been extracted prior to the hospital admission. Clinical examination confirms a systolic murmur and splenomegaly (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values WBC 14.0 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Neutrophils 72 40-60% Urinalysis: Erythrocytes 25 0-2 per HPF Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Floppy mitral valve (MVP) does not explain the prolonged fever, splenomegaly, or hematuria.
Explanation_B: Bacterial endocarditis typically occurs when oral flora enter the blood during a dental extraction and settle on damaged valves (e.g., from prior rheumatic fever). It presents with fever, murmurs, splenomegaly, and immune complex phenomena (hematuria).
Explanation_C: Acute myocardial infarction presents with chest pain, not prolonged fever, splenomegaly, or microscopic hematuria.
