Blood pressure 120/75 mmH Heart rate 80 /min Respiratory rate 17 /min Temperature 37.1° C Test Result Normal Values Thyroxine (T4 free) 19.5 8.5 - 15.2 pmol/L Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone 8.7 0.4-5.0 mU/L Which of the following is the most appropriate radiological imaging?
Explanation_A: The patient has hyperthyroidism (high free T4) with an inappropriately elevated TSH (8.7), pointing to a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma. The co-existing galactorrhea and amenorrhea suggest either co-secretion of prolactin or stalk compression. A Pituitary MRI is required.
Explanation_B: Thyroid ultrasound is useful for goiters or primary hyperthyroidism, but does not address the central (pituitary) cause of the inappropriately high TSH.
Explanation_C: Ovarian ultrasound does not investigate the central endocrine derangement.
Explanation_D: Mammogram is not indicated for systemic endocrine galactorrhea.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Central hyperthyroidism (TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma) presents with elevated Free T4 and an inappropriately normal or elevated TSH. Imaging of choice is a Pituitary MRI.
One_Line: Elevated free T4 with a non-suppressed, high TSH indicates central hyperthyroidism requiring a pituitary MRI.

Question: A 50-year-old woman with major depression, complains of excessive urination and thirst for 2 months. She had a right mastectomy 1 year ago. 3 months before, lung metastases was diagnosed. The physical examination is normal except for the surgical scar (see lab results). Blood pressure 115/75 mmHg Heart rate 80/min Respiratory rate 16 /min Temperature 37.1° C Test Result Normal Values Sodium 150 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 3.8 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Urea 6.7 2.75-7.4 mmol/L Creatinine 111 44-115 mol/L Fasting blood sugar 6.8 3.5-6.5 mmol/L 24 Urine Analysis Test Result Normal Values Osmolality 110 280-910 mOsm/Kg H20 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Diabetes insipidus (DI) presents with polyuria, polydipsia, hypernatremia (Na=150), and dilute urine (osm=110). Given her lung metastasis, she likely has central DI due to metastatic infiltration of the posterior pituitary/hypothalamus.
Explanation_B: Adipsic hypernatremia involves a lack of thirst, but this patient complains of excessive thirst.
Explanation_C: Psychogenic polydipsia presents with polyuria and dilute urine, but patients are HYPOnatremic, not hypernatremic, due to excessive water intake washing out sodium.
Explanation_D: Option omitted in source.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Central DI can be caused by metastatic disease to the brain (commonly lung or breast cancer). It presents with polyuria, hypernatremia, and dilute urine.
One_Line: Hypernatremia with very dilute urine in a patient with cancer metastases points to Central Diabetes Insipidus.

Question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painful neck swelling for the last week. The swelling has been increasing over time. She has a sore throat and difficulty in swallowing. She has frequent bowel motions. On a physical examination, there is a diffuse tender anterior neck swelling and both hands show a fine tremor (see lab results). Blood pressure 140/90 mmHg Heart rate 105 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 38.1° C Test Result Normal Values Thyroxine (T4 free) 26.4 8.5 - 15.2 pmol/L Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone 0.03 0.4 - 5.0 mU/L ESR 58 3-15 mm/h Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
Explanation_A: The patient has Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, characterized by a painful goiter, thyrotoxicosis, and a high ESR. It is a self-limiting inflammatory condition. Severe pain is treated with NSAIDs or Prednisone.
Explanation_B: Methimazole is an anti-thyroid drug. It is ineffective here because the hyperthyroidism is caused by the release of preformed hormone from destroyed follicles, not overproduction.
Explanation_C: Propylthiouracil is ineffective for the same reason as methimazole.
Explanation_D: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated as iodine uptake is universally suppressed in subacute thyroiditis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis presents with a painful thyroid, hyperthyroidism, and a very high ESR. Treatment is symptomatic with NSAIDs or corticosteroids for severe pain.
One_Line: Anti-thyroid drugs do not work for subacute thyroiditis; treat severe neck pain with corticosteroids (Prednisone) or NSAIDs.

Question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a follow-up. She was started on levothyroxine for treatment of hypothyroidism 2 weeks before (see lab result). Test Result Normal Value TSH 7.5 0.4-6.5 mU/L Which of the following would be the best treatment plan?
Option_A: Same dose, check TSH level in 1 to 2 months
Option_B: Reduce dose, check TSH level in 1 to 2 months
Option_C: Reduce dose, check TSH level in 48 to 72 hours
Option_D: Stop treatment until TSH normal, and then restart
Explanation_A: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) takes 4 to 6 weeks to reach a new steady state after initiating or changing a levothyroxine dose. Checking at 2 weeks is too early. Keep the same dose and recheck later.
Explanation_B: Reducing the dose based on a 2-week premature lab value is incorrect management.
Explanation_C: 48-72 hours is far too short to see TSH changes.
Explanation_D: Stopping treatment is inappropriate, as the patient requires replacement.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Levothyroxine has a long half-life (7 days). It takes 4 to 6 weeks for the pituitary axis to stabilize; therefore, TSH should not be rechecked before 6 weeks.
One_Line: Never adjust a levothyroxine dose based on a TSH level drawn less than 4-6 weeks after starting therapy.

Question: A patient has presented with a 2 cm solid thyroid nodule on the Ultrasound. Which of the following is the best next step in the management?
Explanation_A: A 2 cm solid thyroid nodule is large enough to warrant immediate investigation to rule out malignancy, not watchful waiting.
Explanation_B: A thyroid scan is primarily indicated if the TSH is suppressed (to check for a 'hot' toxic nodule), but biopsy is the gold standard for tissue diagnosis.
Explanation_C: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) is the most accurate, cost-effective, and definitive initial diagnostic step for a suspicious or large (>1-1.5 cm) solid thyroid nodule.
Explanation_D: CT neck is used for evaluating local invasion or planning surgery for known cancers, not for initial diagnosis of a nodule.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Any solid thyroid nodule ≥ 1 cm (or smaller with highly suspicious ultrasound features) with normal or high TSH should be evaluated with Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) biopsy.
One_Line: Fine needle aspiration is the gold standard initial tissue test for evaluating a solid thyroid nodule.

Question: A 26-year-old woman has become increasingly tired for the past 2 months. During the past week she has noted purple blotches on her skin. On physical examination, there are petechial haemorrhages on her trunk and extremities (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 72 120-160 g/L HCT 0.22 0.37-0.48 MCV 92 80-95 fl WBC 1.5 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Platelet count 10 150-400 x 109/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Aplastic anemia causes severe pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) leading to fatigue, infections, and bleeding (petechiae), matching this patient's profile.
Explanation_B: Sickle cell anemia causes hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusive crises, not uniform pancytopenia.
Explanation_C: Hemolytic anemia causes low Hb, but typically normal/high WBC and normal platelets, accompanied by jaundice and reticulocytosis.
Explanation_D: Iron deficiency anemia presents with microcytic anemia, normal WBC, and often normal/elevated platelets (reactive thrombocytosis), not severe pancytopenia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Aplastic anemia is bone marrow failure leading to pancytopenia. Patients present with anemia (fatigue), thrombocytopenia (bleeding/petechiae), and leukopenia (infections).
One_Line: Pancytopenia presenting as fatigue, petechiae, and low cell counts across all lineages is diagnostic of aplastic anemia.

Question: A 26-year-old woman presents for pre-marital counselling (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 110 120-160 g/L HCT 0.33 0.37-0.48 MCV 67 80-95 fl Hb A2 4.5 <3.5 % Sickling Negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Beta Thalassemia minor (trait) presents as an asymptomatic, mild microcytic anemia (MCV < 80) with an elevated HbA2 level (>3.5%).
Explanation_B: Beta Thalassemia major presents in early childhood with severe, life-threatening, transfusion-dependent anemia.
Explanation_C: Sickle beta thalassemia would show a positive sickling test or HbS on electrophoresis.
Explanation_D: Beta Thalassemia intermedia causes moderate to severe anemia, usually symptomatic, unlike this asymptomatic patient presenting for pre-marital counseling.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Beta-thalassemia minor is characterized by mild microcytic anemia, a normal to high RBC count, normal RDW, and an elevated HbA2 (> 3.5%) on hemoglobin electrophoresis.
One_Line: An asymptomatic patient with microcytic anemia and elevated HbA2 has Beta Thalassemia minor.

Question: A 55-year-old man presents to the clinic with headaches and increased tiredness for the last 4 months. On physical examination he is febrile and his spleen tip is palpable (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values Hb 200 130-170 g/L HCT 0.67 0.42-0.52 MCV 93 80-95 f1 WBC 12 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Platelets 420 150-400 x 1099/L The serum erythropoietin: Very low levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Myelofibrosis causes massive splenomegaly, but typically presents with teardrop cells, anemia, and variable platelets, not massive polycythemia.
Explanation_B: Polycythemia rubra vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driving autonomous overproduction of RBCs (Hb 200), WBCs, and platelets. The autonomous production suppresses endogenous Erythropoietin (EPO).
Explanation_C: Congenital heart disease causes secondary polycythemia due to chronic hypoxia, which would result in HIGH, not low, erythropoietin.
Explanation_D: Essential thrombocythemia features massively elevated platelets without the massive erythrocytosis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Polycythemia Vera is defined by elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit, splenomegaly, and a suppressed (low) serum EPO level, due to a JAK2 V617F mutation.
One_Line: A high hemoglobin, high platelets, splenomegaly, and very low EPO level is classic for Polycythemia Vera.

Question: A 26-year-old man has been diagnosed with sarcoidosis 2 years before, he now presents with mild pallor (see lab results and report) Test Result Normal Values Hb 100 130-170 g/L HCT 0.29 0.42-0.52 MCV 79 80-95 fl WBC 7.5 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Platelet count 200 150-400 x 109/L Ferritin 915 22-561 ng/L Haemoglobin electrophoresis: Normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Sideroblastic anemia can be microcytic, but ferritin is high, and it is less related to chronic inflammatory conditions like sarcoidosis.
Explanation_B: Beta Thalassemia minor has normal ferritin and elevated HbA2.
Explanation_C: Iron deficiency anemia presents with low ferritin, whereas this patient has a high ferritin (915), marking an acute phase response.
Explanation_D: Anemia of chronic disease (ACD) is common in chronic inflammatory states (like sarcoidosis). It features normocytic or mild microcytic anemia with high ferritin and low TIBC (hepcidin sequesters iron).
High_Yield_Must_Know: In Anemia of Chronic Disease, hepcidin traps iron in macrophages, resulting in low serum iron, low TIBC, and normal-to-high serum ferritin.
One_Line: A mild microcytic or normocytic anemia with a high ferritin level in a patient with a chronic inflammatory condition points to Anemia of Chronic Disease.

Question: A 30-year-old man comes to the Outpatient Clinic because of the recent development of marked peripheral edema. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he has 4+ edema of the lower extremities (see lab results and reports). Blood pressure 105/80 mmHg Test Result Normal Values Albumin 18 34-56 g/L Urea 5 2.8-8.9 mmol/L Creatinine 85 44-115 mol/L Dipstick analysis: 4+ proteins. Urinalysis: Oval fat bodies, and some hyaline casts and occasional RBCs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Interstitial nephritis causes eosinophiluria, white cell casts, and mild proteinuria, not 4+ proteinuria, oval fat bodies, or severe hypoalbuminemia.
Explanation_B: Nephritic syndrome is characterized by hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, and mild-moderate proteinuria.
Explanation_C: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria (>3.5g/day or 4+ on dipstick), severe hypoalbuminemia, severe peripheral edema, and oval fat bodies (lipiduria).
Explanation_D: Ischemic nephropathy causes chronic renal failure, not acute severe nephrotic syndrome.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The classic tetrad of Nephrotic Syndrome: Massive proteinuria (>3.5g/day), Hypoalbuminemia, Generalized edema, and Hyperlipidemia (causing oval fat bodies in urine).
One_Line: Edema, profound hypoalbuminemia, 4+ proteinuria, and oval fat bodies are the hallmarks of Nephrotic Syndrome.
Accuracy_Review: Corrected  answer in source (A). The correct answer is C (Nephrotic syndrome).

Question: A 30-year-old overweight man presents to the general physician with 6-month of intermittent epigastric burning pain. He has also noted that for the past 2 months he has been experiencing episodes of nausea, an unpleasant taste in the mouth, hoarseness, and a nocturnal cough. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain, but it doesn't typically cause hoarseness, unpleasant mouth taste, and nocturnal cough (which are extraesophageal signs of reflux).
Explanation_B: Atypical angina is cardiac; it doesn't cause bad taste, hoarseness, or epigastric burning primarily.
Explanation_C: Chronic cholelithiasis causes right upper quadrant colicky pain, often post-prandial, not burning reflux symptoms.
Explanation_D: GERD classically causes retrosternal burning pain (heartburn). Extraesophageal manifestations include hoarseness, chronic nocturnal cough, and acid regurgitation/sour taste.
High_Yield_Must_Know: GERD can present with typical symptoms (heartburn, regurgitation) and atypical/extraesophageal symptoms (chronic cough, hoarseness, asthma exacerbations, dental erosions).
One_Line: Epigastric burning, acid taste, hoarseness, and a nocturnal cough are the classic typical and atypical symptoms of GERD.

Question: A 40-year-old man with Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease presents to the general physician with 3-month history of intermittent retrosternal burning pain, worse on bending, nausea, regurgitation with an unpleasant taste in the mouth, and a nocturnal cough. The patient has been using over the counter antacids with no relief. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
Explanation_A: Surgery (Nissen fundoplication) is reserved for refractory cases that fail maximal medical therapy.
Explanation_B: Antibiotics are used for H. pylori eradication in peptic ulcer disease, not primary GERD.
Explanation_C: Lifestyle modifications are important but insufficient for a patient who has failed OTC antacids and has persistent, distressing symptoms.
Explanation_D: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are the most effective medical therapy for GERD and are the first-line prescription treatment when antacids fail.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Patients with classic GERD symptoms that do not resolve with lifestyle changes or OTC H2 blockers/antacids should be started on a once-daily Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) trial for 8 weeks.
One_Line: Proton pump inhibitors are the definitive first-line pharmacological therapy for persistent GERD.

Question: An individual who has received all 3 doses of hepatitis B vaccine and has never had hepatitis B virus infection. Which of the following serologic markers is expected to be positive?
Explanation_A: HBcAb (Hepatitis B core antibody) is only positive following natural infection. It is never positive from vaccination.
Explanation_B: HBsAb (Hepatitis B surface antibody) is the ONLY positive marker in a successfully vaccinated individual.
Explanation_C: HBeAb indicates clearing of an active infection and lower infectivity; not seen in vaccinated people.
Explanation_D: HBeAb and HBsAb together would indicate past infection, not vaccination.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The Hepatitis B vaccine contains only HBsAg. Therefore, successful vaccination results in isolated Anti-HBs (HBsAb) positivity, with negative Anti-HBc and HBsAg.
One_Line: Isolated HBsAb (Anti-HBs) positivity is the serological hallmark of Hepatitis B immunity via vaccination.

Question: A 53-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department. She has been unwell for 6 months with arthralgia, fever, weight loss and more recently has developed pleuritic chest pains. She also has synovitis of the small joints of the hands. There were no rashes or nail fold infarcts. Heart sounds are normal (see lab results and reports). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 70 /min Respiratory rate 18/min Test Result Normal Values Hb 89 120-160 g/L WBC 3.2 4-10.5 x 109/L Platelets count 99 150-400 × 109/L Neutrophils 80 40-60% Lymphocytes 17 20-40 % MCV 90 80-95 f1 C-reactive peptide 99 <8.2 mg/L ESR 56 3-15 mm/h Clotting time 7 5-10 min Ferritin 920 22-340 pg/L ANA 1:320 =1:40 Pulmonary Angiography CT: Confirms a small left pleural effusion. There is no consolidation, pulmonary embolus and no lymphadenopathy. ECG: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Infective endocarditis could cause fever and pleuritic pain (septic emboli), but doesn't explain the strongly positive ANA or classic synovitis.
Explanation_B: Adult-onset Still's disease causes fever, salmon-colored rash, and arthritis, but typically features a very high ferritin, leukocytosis, and a negative ANA.
Explanation_C: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) predominantly affects women and presents with systemic inflammation: serositis (pleuritic pain), non-erosive arthritis (synovitis), cytopenias, and a high ANA titer (1:320).
Explanation_D: Rheumatoid arthritis causes synovitis, but does not typically present with severe cytopenias, serositis, and a high ANA without prominent erosive joint findings.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The diagnosis of SLE requires multiple clinical criteria (arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, rashes) and strong immunologic criteria (positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm).
One_Line: A young to middle-aged woman with cytopenias, pleuritis, synovitis, and a strongly positive ANA has Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).

Question: What is the immunological status of a patient with negative HBsAg, positive anti-HBc and positive anti-HBs?
Option_A: Immune due to hepatitis B vaccination
Explanation_A: Vaccination induces ONLY anti-HBs. Anti-HBc is negative in vaccinated individuals.
Explanation_B: Natural infection exposes the immune system to all viral antigens, resulting in both anti-HBs (surface antibody = immunity) and anti-HBc (core antibody = past exposure).
Explanation_C: Chronic infection features a persistently positive HBsAg (surface antigen) for >6 months.
Explanation_D: Acute infection features positive HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Immunity from a past natural Hepatitis B infection is denoted by positive Anti-HBs AND positive Anti-HBc (IgG). Immunity from vaccination has positive Anti-HBs ONLY.
One_Line: Positive anti-HBc and anti-HBs with negative HBsAg proves immunity from a past natural Hepatitis B infection.

Question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of episodes of pain with swelling and warmth of her hands and feet for the past 3 weeks. During these episodes, lasting hours to days, it is difficult for her to walk or to prepare meals. On physical examination, she has painful 1 cm subcutaneous nodules on the extensor surfaces of her elbows. Over the next 6 years, her hands become deformed so that it is difficult to perform tasks as simple as opening a door or buttoning her blouse. Which of the following laboratory findings would confirm the diagnosis?
Explanation_A: HLA-B27 is associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies (Ankylosing spondylitis, Reactive arthritis), not Rheumatoid Arthritis.
Explanation_B: ANA is non-specific and primarily indicates SLE, though it can be positive in RA, it is not confirming.
Explanation_C: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP) antibodies are highly specific (95%) for Rheumatoid Arthritis and confirm the diagnosis.
Explanation_D: Decreased complement is seen in SLE and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not typically RA.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is sensitive but not highly specific. Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for Rheumatoid Arthritis and often predict a more aggressive disease course.
One_Line: Anti-CCP antibodies are the most specific diagnostic marker for Rheumatoid Arthritis.

Question: A 43-year-old patient man presents with headache and neck stiffness (see reports). CSF Analysis: Appearance cloudy Glucose low Protein high White cells 100 /mm3 (70% polymorphs) CT Brain: Normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the infection?
Explanation_A: Cryptococcal meningitis usually shows a lymphocytic predominance with normal or slightly low glucose, primarily in HIV patients.
Explanation_B: Tuberculous meningitis shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, and very high protein.
Explanation_C: Bacterial meningitis classically presents with cloudy CSF, low glucose, high protein, and a polymorphonuclear (neutrophil) predominance.
Explanation_D: Viral meningitis presents with clear CSF, normal glucose, normal or slightly high protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: CSF patterns: Bacterial (Polymorphs, low glucose, high protein). Viral (Lymphocytes, normal glucose, normal/high protein). Fungal/TB (Lymphocytes, low glucose, high protein).
One_Line: Cloudy CSF with low glucose, high protein, and a neutrophil predominance is the hallmark of bacterial meningitis.

Question: A 22-year-old man presents with altered sensorium for the last 2 days and headaches for 5 days, with a history of fever for the preceding month. On examination, there is nuchal rigidity (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 100 130-170 g/L WBC 11 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Glucose, fasting 7.22 3.5-6.5 mmol/L Cerebrospinal Fluid: Test Result Normal Values Appearance turbid clear Cells 240 0-3 /uL Total protein 3.6 0.22-0.33 g/L Glucose 2.7 2.50-3.89 mmol/L Neutrophils 23 0-1% Lympocytes 73 0-1% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Septicaemia alone does not define the CSF findings. Bacterial meningitis would have a polymorphonuclear (neutrophil) predominance.
Explanation_B: A one-month history of fever with subacute onset of meningitis, paired with CSF showing low glucose, high protein, and a lymphocytic predominance (73%), is classic for Tuberculous meningitis.
Explanation_C: Phylogenetic meningitis is not a standard clinical term.
Explanation_D: Viral meningoencephalitis has a lymphocytic predominance but typically features a NORMAL CSF glucose.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Subacute to chronic meningitis (weeks) with lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein, and low CSF glucose is characteristic of Tuberculous or Fungal meningitis.
One_Line: A subacute meningitis with lymphocytic CSF and low glucose strongly points to TB meningitis.

Question: A 29-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department with vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps. It started within 4 hours of eating a steak in a local restaurant. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
Explanation_A: E. coli gastroenteritis usually has an incubation period of 1-3 days, not 4 hours.
Explanation_B: Salmonella has an incubation of 6-48 hours.
Explanation_C: Campylobacter jejuni causes inflammatory diarrhea after an incubation of 2-5 days.
Explanation_D: Staphylococcus aureus causes rapid-onset food poisoning (within 1-6 hours) due to preformed enterotoxins, classically after eating meats, mayonnaise, or creamy foods.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Food poisoning occurring within 1 to 6 hours is due to preformed toxins. The most common pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus (meats, dairy) and Bacillus cereus (fried rice).
One_Line: Vomiting and diarrhea within hours of a meal points to preformed toxin from Staphylococcus aureus.

Question: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with fever, night sweating and cough for 2 weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
Option_B: Send sputum for Acid fast bacilli
Option_C: Isolate in a single, negative pressure room
Option_D: Appointment in outpatient clinic after 2 weeks
Explanation_A: Bronchoscopy may be needed later, but the immediate public health priority is preventing transmission of potential tuberculosis.
Explanation_B: Sending sputum for AFB is the correct diagnostic step, but infection control takes immediate precedence.
Explanation_C: A patient presenting with a chronic cough, fever, and night sweats is highly suspicious for active pulmonary tuberculosis. The immediate action is airborne isolation in a negative pressure room.
Explanation_D: Discharging the patient to the outpatient clinic endangers the public.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Any patient with symptoms highly suspicious for active pulmonary tuberculosis (fever, night sweats, weight loss, chronic cough) must be immediately placed in airborne isolation.
One_Line: Immediate airborne isolation is required for any patient suspected of having active pulmonary tuberculosis.

Question: A 47-year-old patient presents with 12-hour of severe pain and swelling of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. On examination, the affected joint is erythematous and tender. Blood pressure 110/ 65 mmHg Heart rate 105 /min Respiratory rate 12 /min Temperature 38°C Which of the following is the most likely cause?
Explanation_A: Acute, severe monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is the classic presentation of gout, which is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals.
Explanation_B: Staphylococcus aureus causes septic arthritis, which usually targets larger joints like the knee and is less likely to present classically at the 1st MTP.
Explanation_C: Disseminated gonorrhea causes migratory polyarthralgia and tenosynovitis.
Explanation_D: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals cause pseudogout, which most commonly affects the knee or wrist, not the 1st MTP joint.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Gout classically presents as severe, acute monoarticular arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) due to needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals.
One_Line: Severe, sudden pain and swelling of the big toe (podagra) is caused by monosodium urate crystals.

Question: A 52-year-old patient presents with isolated pain and swelling of the left knee. Arthrocentesis demonstrates innumerable needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
Explanation_A: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent used for long-term chronic gout management, not for acute flares.
Explanation_B: Methotrexate is used for Rheumatoid Arthritis, not gout.
Explanation_C: The crystals are monosodium urate (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent), confirming acute gout. First-line treatment for acute gout flares is NSAIDs, such as Indomethacin.
Explanation_D: Sulfinpyrazone is a uricosuric used for chronic prevention, not acute attacks.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Acute gout flares are treated with NSAIDs (Indomethacin), Colchicine, or Corticosteroids. Urate-lowering therapy (Allopurinol, Probenecid) should never be started during an acute attack.
One_Line: Indomethacin (an NSAID) is the first-line treatment for an acute attack of gout.

Question: A 32-year-old woman complains of severe joint pain in the fingers of both hands, especially in the morning during the winter months. Examination confirms deformity of her fingers (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Gout typically affects the MTP joint of the big toe or the knee, and features acute episodic flares, not chronic symmetrical finger deformities.
Explanation_B: Haemophilia causes hemarthrosis (bleeding into large joints like knees/ankles) in males.
Explanation_C: Rheumatoid arthritis classically presents in young/middle-aged women with symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands (MCP, PIP) with significant morning stiffness and eventual deformity.
Explanation_D: Osteoarthritis primarily affects weight-bearing joints and the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) with minimal morning stiffness (<30 mins).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Rheumatoid arthritis typically involves the MCP and PIP joints of the hands symmetrically, sparing the DIP joints, and causes prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour).
One_Line: Symmetrical involvement of hand joints with prolonged morning stiffness and deformity is classic Rheumatoid Arthritis.

Question: A 74-year-old woman complains of a deep, aching pain of the hip which is aggravated by walking. She states that after a busy day, the pain keeps her awake at night, and each morning her hip is stiff for several hours. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pain?
Explanation_A: Depression does not cause isolated mechanically aggravated hip pain.
Explanation_B: Osteomyelitis causes acute fever, bone tenderness, and severe constant pain, not chronic activity-related pain.
Explanation_C: Osteoporosis is painless unless a fracture has occurred.
Explanation_D: Osteoarthritis is characterized by deep, aching joint pain exacerbated by use/weight-bearing and relieved by rest. (Note: The prompt mentions 'stiff for several hours' which is atypical for OA, as OA morning stiffness is usually <30 mins, but the mechanical nature of the hip pain in an elderly patient points to OA overall in this question's context).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease characterized by pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest, typically affecting weight-bearing joints (hips, knees) in the elderly.
One_Line: Deep, aching joint pain that worsens with walking in an elderly patient is classic for osteoarthritis.

Question: A 60-year-old woman complains of pain in her right knee for the last 3 years. The pain is worse with activity and relieved by rest and analgesics. Physical examination reveals that she has a varus knee deformity and tenderness over the medial joint line (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Inflammatory arthritis (like Rheumatoid) usually presents with prolonged morning stiffness, symmetry, and systemic symptoms, not mechanical pain worsened by activity.
Explanation_B: A medial meniscus tear causes acute pain, locking, or clicking, often with a history of trauma, rather than chronic 3-year progressive pain.
Explanation_C: Septic arthritis is acute, severe, with fever and a warm, swollen joint, not a chronic 3-year history.
Explanation_D: Osteoarthritis is characterized by chronic joint pain worsened by weight-bearing/activity and relieved by rest. Medial compartment narrowing is common, leading to a varus (bow-legged) deformity.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Osteoarthritis of the knee frequently involves the medial compartment more than the lateral, leading to a varus (bow-legged) deformity.
One_Line: Chronic knee pain worsened by activity with a varus deformity indicates osteoarthritis.

Question: A 58-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Clinic with very severe pain, swelling and redness of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Some joint fluid is withdrawn (see lab results and reports). Test Result Normal Values Colour yellow clear Clarity opaque transparent WBC per mm3 100,000 < 200 PMNs 75 < 25% Fluid Exam: Negatively birefringent rate crystals are seen on polarizing examination of the synovial fluid. Hands X-ray: Juxta-articular punched-out sclerotic erosions involving the first metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints with associated periarticular soft tissue swelling. Which of the following treatments should be avoided in the current situation?
Explanation_A: NSAIDs (like Indomethacin) are the first-line treatment for acute gout attacks.
Explanation_B: Colchicine is an effective alternative or adjunct for acute gout flares.
Explanation_C: Allopurinol is a urate-lowering therapy used to prevent future attacks. It should NEVER be initiated during an acute attack, as fluctuating uric acid levels can worsen and prolong the flare.
Explanation_D: Corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular) are highly effective for acute gout flares, especially if NSAIDs/Colchicine are contraindicated.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Urate-lowering therapies (Allopurinol, Febuxostat) should not be initiated during an acute gout flare, as rapid changes in uric acid levels will exacerbate the inflammation.
One_Line: Allopurinol must be avoided during an acute attack of gout.

Question: Which of the following crystals is responsible for the arthritic symptoms of pseudogout?
Explanation_A: Calcium urate is not a standard crystal; monosodium urate causes gout.
Explanation_B: Calcium oxalate crystals are found in kidney stones.
Explanation_C: Calcium chloride does not cause crystal arthropathy.
Explanation_D: Pseudogout is caused by Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate (CPPD) crystals, which are rhomboid-shaped and weakly positively birefringent.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Pseudogout is caused by Calcium Pyrophosphate crystals (rhomboid-shaped, positive birefringence), while Gout is caused by Monosodium Urate crystals (needle-shaped, negative birefringence).
One_Line: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals cause pseudogout.

Question: A 29-year-old woman is diagnosed with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Which of the following pathological changes is characteristic of this diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Dilated proximal tubules with inflammation is characteristic of Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) or Interstitial Nephritis, not RPGN.
Explanation_B: Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a clinical syndrome characterized by a rapid loss of renal function and the histologic hallmark of crescent formation in Bowman's space.
Explanation_C: IgA deposition defines IgA Nephropathy (Berger's disease), which can rarely present as RPGN but is not the defining universal histologic feature of RPGN itself.
Explanation_D: Fat globules are seen in nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic RPGN.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The histologic hallmark of Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is the formation of 'crescents' within Bowman's space, consisting of fibrin, macrophages, and epithelial cells.
One_Line: Crescent formation in Bowman's space is the defining pathologic lesion of Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis.

Question: A young man comes into the clinic with intermittent haemoptysis for 2 months, associated with some blood in his urine. He is a non-smoker and was previously in excellent health. He also describes a weight gain of 20 kg over the past 3 weeks, with "puffy eyes" in the morning. He has an elevated serum creatinine concentration (see report). Lung Biopsy: Serum immunoglobulin on basement membranes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Myocardial infarction does not cause hemoptysis, hematuria, or linear IgG deposits on basement membranes.
Explanation_B: Goodpasture syndrome is a pulmonary-renal syndrome caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies. It presents with hemoptysis (pulmonary hemorrhage) and hematuria (glomerulonephritis). Biopsy shows linear IgG deposition.
Explanation_C: DiGeorge syndrome is a congenital immunodeficiency (thymic aplasia, hypocalcemia).
Explanation_D: Graves' disease causes hyperthyroidism, not pulmonary hemorrhage and renal failure.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Goodpasture syndrome involves anti-GBM antibodies attacking the type IV collagen in the basement membranes of the lungs (causing hemoptysis) and kidneys (causing RPGN/hematuria).
One_Line: Hemoptysis, hematuria, and linear IgG deposition on basement membranes define Goodpasture syndrome.

Question: Which of the following sites is the best to aspirate a sample of right pleural effusion with a syringe and needle?
Explanation_A: The midclavicular line is rarely used due to the risk of liver/spleen injury and because fluid pools dependently.
Explanation_B: The 6th intercostal space may be too high to safely drain a dependent effusion without risking lung puncture.
Explanation_C: The ideal site for thoracentesis is the 7th to 9th intercostal space in the midaxillary or posterior axillary line, allowing access to dependent fluid while avoiding the diaphragm.
Explanation_D: Parasternal spaces are never used for thoracentesis due to the risk of injuring the internal mammary vessels or the heart.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Thoracentesis is typically performed in the mid-to-posterior axillary line between the 7th and 9th intercostal spaces, inserting the needle just SUPERIOR to the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
One_Line: The best site for thoracentesis is the midaxillary line at the 7th to 9th intercostal space.

Question: A 45-year-old man presents with difficulty in breathing and a nocturnal cough for the last 3 weeks. Spirometry results show a forced vital capacity and the FEV/FVC ratio lower than normal. Which of the following consistent with these findings?
Explanation_A: Reduced muscle strength causes a restrictive pattern (low FVC, normal FEV1/FVC).
Explanation_B: Decreased lung compliance (pulmonary fibrosis) causes a restrictive pattern (low FVC, normal FEV1/FVC).
Explanation_C: Increased lung compliance occurs in emphysema, but the spirometric findings directly reflect resistance.
Explanation_D: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (< 0.70) is the hallmark of an obstructive lung disease (e.g., asthma, COPD), which is driven by increased airway resistance preventing rapid exhalation.
High_Yield_Must_Know: An FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70 defines obstructive lung disease, which is characterized by increased airway resistance and air trapping.
One_Line: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio indicates increased airway resistance (obstructive lung disease).

Question: What is the optimal treatment for community-acquired pneumonia in an otherwise healthy patient?
Explanation_A: Respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are used for patients with comorbidities, recent antibiotic use, or severe CAP, not as first-line for otherwise healthy adults.
Explanation_B: Macrolides (like Azithromycin) or Doxycycline are the first-line treatment for outpatient community-acquired pneumonia in previously healthy patients without recent antibiotic use.
Explanation_C: Vancomycin is reserved for severe inpatient pneumonia with suspected MRSA.
Explanation_D: Dicloxacillin is used for MSSA skin infections, not pneumonia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: For an otherwise healthy outpatient with Community Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) and no recent antibiotic use, a Macrolide (Azithromycin) or Doxycycline is the first-line therapy.
One_Line: Azithromycin is the optimal first-line treatment for CAP in an otherwise healthy outpatient.

Question: What is the optimal duration of anticoagulation following an initial episode of pulmonary embolism?
Explanation_A: 6 weeks is too short for a provoked PE, and certainly too short for an unprovoked PE.
Explanation_B: 3 months is the standard minimum for a first episode of PROVOKED pulmonary embolism (e.g., post-surgery). (Source states 6 months, but 3 months is often standard for provoked; however, in many older exams 6 months is accepted).
Explanation_C: While 3 months is often the minimum for provoked, 6 months is frequently cited as the standard duration for a first episode of unprovoked or general PE in many testing algorithms.
Explanation_D: 12 months or lifelong is reserved for recurrent PEs or those with severe thrombophilia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The standard duration of anticoagulation for a first episode of pulmonary embolism is 3 to 6 months. (Provoked is often 3 months; unprovoked is often 6 months or longer).
One_Line: Anticoagulation is typically continued for 3 to 6 months following an initial pulmonary embolism.
Accuracy_Review: Corrected  is C (6 months). Current guidelines often say 3 months for provoked, 3-6+ for unprovoked. Will mark as Correct based on older standard.

Question: In which of the following conditions is interstitial pneumonitis a characteristic histopathologic finding?
Explanation_A: Viral pneumonias (and atypical bacterial pneumonias like Mycoplasma) classically cause an interstitial pneumonitis, where inflammation is confined to the alveolar septae rather than the alveolar spaces.
Explanation_B: Lobar pneumonia (typical of Strep pneumo) fills the alveolar spaces with exudate.
Explanation_C: Bronchopneumonia causes patchy consolidation in the alveoli.
Explanation_D: Secondary tuberculosis causes caseating granulomas and cavitation, usually in the upper lobes.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Atypical pneumonias (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella, Viruses) cause an interstitial infiltrate (inflammation of the alveolar septae) leading to a 'reticulonodular' pattern on CXR with a dry cough.
One_Line: Viral and atypical pneumonias classically present with interstitial pneumonitis.

Question: Which of the following pneumoconiosis will commonly predispose to the development of pulmonary tuberculosis?
Explanation_A: Silicosis profoundly impairs the function of alveolar macrophages, making patients highly susceptible to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis).
Explanation_B: Asbestosis predisposes to bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma, not TB.
Explanation_C: Anthracosis (coal worker's pneumoconiosis) can cause massive pulmonary fibrosis but does not have the same severe TB predisposition as silicosis.
Explanation_D: Farmer's lung is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not associated with TB.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Silicosis is unique among pneumoconioses because silica particles are toxic to alveolar macrophages, resulting in a significantly increased risk of Tuberculosis.
One_Line: Silicosis severely impairs macrophage function, predisposing patients to pulmonary tuberculosis.

Question: A 38-year-old woman with pleurisy requires a thoracentesis. The needle should be placed on the midaxillary line of the affected side. Which rib level should the needle penetrate through?
Explanation_A: The 4th intercostal space is too high.
Explanation_B: The 5th intercostal space is the site for chest tube insertion (triangle of safety), but thoracentesis for fluid is usually lower.
Explanation_C: 6th/7th is acceptable but slightly high.
Explanation_D: Thoracentesis is safely and most commonly performed between the 7th, 8th, or 9th intercostal spaces in the mid-to-posterior axillary line to access dependent fluid while avoiding the diaphragm/liver/spleen.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Thoracentesis should be performed in the midaxillary or posterior axillary line between the 7th and 9th ribs. The needle must go over the superior border of the lower rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
One_Line: Thoracentesis is best performed between the 8th and 10th ribs in the midaxillary line.

Question: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with fever, night sweats and cough for 2 weeks (see report). Chest X-ray: Right upper lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
Option_B: Admit the patient to the Intensive Unit
Option_D: Isolate the patient in a single, negative pressure room
Explanation_A: Bronchoscopy may be diagnostic if sputum is negative, but infection control is the first priority.
Explanation_B: Admitting to the ICU is not necessary unless the patient is hemodynamically unstable or in respiratory failure.
Explanation_C: A 2-week follow up allows the patient to infect others.
Explanation_D: Right upper lobe consolidation with chronic fever, cough, and night sweats is highly suspicious for active pulmonary TB. The immediate priority is airborne isolation in a negative pressure room.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Patients with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis must be immediately isolated in a negative pressure room to prevent airborne transmission before any diagnostic testing continues.
One_Line: Immediate airborne isolation is the required first step for any patient with suspected active tuberculosis.

Question: Which of the following can improve survival in patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
Explanation_A: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce exacerbations but do not increase overall survival in COPD.
Explanation_B: Long-term supplemental oxygen therapy (LTOT) is one of the very few interventions proven to decrease mortality and improve survival in patients with severe resting hypoxemic COPD.
Explanation_C: Smoking cessation improves survival, but for severe hypoxic COPD, oxygen is a direct medical intervention proven to prolong life.
Explanation_D: Beta agonists improve symptoms and bronchodilation but do not improve mortality.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Only two interventions have been proven to reduce mortality in COPD: Smoking cessation and Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT) for those with resting hypoxemia (PaO2 ≤ 55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤ 88%).
One_Line: Supplemental oxygen and smoking cessation are the only interventions proven to improve survival in COPD.

Question: A 25-year-old patient with moderate persistent asthma is currently on a low-dose, inhaled corticosteroid but needs to use a beta-2 agonist rescue inhaler at least once a day. Which of the following should be added to the current treatment?
Option_B: Leukotriene inhibitor to the steroid regimen
Option_C: Long-acting beta-2 agonist to steroid regimen
Explanation_A: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and many side effects; it is a last resort.
Explanation_B: Leukotriene inhibitors are alternatives to ICS, but LABAs are the preferred add-on.
Explanation_C: According to asthma guidelines, if a patient is not controlled on a low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS), the next step is to add a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA).
Explanation_D: Ipratropium is a short-acting anticholinergic used for acute exacerbations, not chronic step-up therapy.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Asthma Step-up Therapy: Step 1: PRN SABA. Step 2: Daily low-dose ICS. Step 3: Low-dose ICS + LABA (or medium-dose ICS). Never use a LABA without an ICS in asthma.
One_Line: For asthma uncontrolled on low-dose ICS, the next step is adding a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA).

Question: A 55-year-old patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presents with shortness of breath. The patient is in severe respiratory distress and hypoxemic with decreased breath sounds and a prolonged expiration phase. There is no improvement after bronchodilators. The patient is conscious with a pH of 7.3. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
Explanation_A: Aminophylline is no longer recommended for acute COPD exacerbations due to toxicity.
Explanation_B: IV Corticosteroids are standard for acute exacerbations, but this patient is in severe respiratory distress with acidemia (pH 7.3), requiring immediate ventilatory support.
Explanation_C: Repeating bronchodilators is part of the regimen, but ventilatory support is the critical next step for impending failure.
Explanation_D: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV/BiPAP) is indicated for severe COPD exacerbations with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35) and effectively reduces the need for intubation and improves mortality.
High_Yield_Must_Know: NIPPV (BiPAP) is the treatment of choice for COPD exacerbations complicated by hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 45), significantly reducing mortality and intubation rates.
One_Line: Non-invasive ventilation is indicated for COPD exacerbations with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35).

Question: Which of the following is the most effective treatment for adults with obstructive sleep apnea?
Option_B: Maintain a BMI less than 30 kg/m2
Explanation_A: Modafinil treats daytime sleepiness but does not fix the underlying airway obstruction.
Explanation_B: Weight loss is recommended but takes time; CPAP provides immediate resolution of apneas.
Explanation_C: Oral appliances are for mild-to-moderate OSA or those who fail CPAP.
Explanation_D: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) acts as a pneumatic splint to keep the pharyngeal airway open during sleep, and is the gold standard, most effective treatment for OSA.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is the first-line and most effective therapy for Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), preventing airway collapse during inspiration.
One_Line: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the gold standard treatment for Obstructive Sleep Apnea.

Question: A 28-year-old patient with mild intermittent asthma, has daytime symptoms about once to twice a week, and none at night. Which of the following initial treatment should be given when necessary?
Explanation_A: Mild intermittent asthma (symptoms ≤2 days/week, nighttime awakenings ≤2/month) is treated solely with an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) as needed.
Explanation_B: Inhaled corticosteroids are for persistent asthma.
Explanation_C: Leukotriene modifiers are for persistent asthma.
Explanation_D: Oral aminophylline is rarely used due to toxicity.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Mild intermittent asthma is defined by daytime symptoms ≤ 2 times/week and nighttime symptoms ≤ 2 times/month. Treatment is an as-needed SABA (e.g., Albuterol).
One_Line: PRN short-acting beta-2 agonists are the only treatment needed for mild intermittent asthma.

Question: A 28-year-old woman has had mild intermittent asthma for years. She uses a short-acting bronchodilator, as needed. Over the past 2 months, she has noticed that she is using her inhaler at least 3 times a week, and on occasions has had to wake up in the middle of the night to use her inhaler. Which of the following treatments should be added?
Explanation_A: Leukotriene receptor antagonists are an alternative, but ICS is the preferred first-line controller.
Explanation_B: LABAs should never be used as monotherapy in asthma (black box warning) and are added only if ICS fails.
Explanation_C: The patient has transitioned from intermittent to mild persistent asthma (using inhaler >2 days/week, night awakenings 3-4x/month). The next step is a daily low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid.
Explanation_D: Cromolyn is an alternative but is far less effective than an ICS.
High_Yield_Must_Know: When asthma progresses from intermittent to persistent (>2 daytime episodes per week, >2 nighttime episodes per month), the patient must be started on a daily daily low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid.
One_Line: Daily inhaled corticosteroids are the first-line controller therapy for persistent asthma.

Question: A 55-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and a productive cough. The patient has a history of smoking. On auscultation, there is wheezing throughout the chest (see reports). Chest X-ray: Normal. Arterial Blood Gases: Normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Pulmonary fibrosis causes fine inspiratory crackles and a restrictive pattern, not wheezing.
Explanation_B: Occupational lung disease depends on exposure history, but smoking strongly points to COPD.
Explanation_C: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis causes hemoptysis and restrictive disease.
Explanation_D: A smoker with a chronic productive cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing has classic symptoms of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), specifically chronic bronchitis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: COPD encompasses chronic bronchitis (productive cough for 3 months/year for 2 years) and emphysema (alveolar destruction). Smoking is the primary risk factor. Wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase are common.
One_Line: A chronic productive cough and wheezing in a heavy smoker is classic for COPD.

Question: A 25-year-old patient suddenly develops chest pain and dyspnoea. Vocal and tactile fremitus are reduced, and breath sounds are diminished (see report). Chest X-ray: It shows absent lung markings on the left side. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, diminished breath sounds, and absent lung markings on CXR is the classic triad for a spontaneous pneumothorax.
Explanation_B: Tuberculosis causes chronic cough and upper lobe consolidations/cavities, not absent lung markings.
Explanation_C: Pulmonary embolism causes dyspnea but breath sounds are normal, and CXR is usually normal (or shows Hampton's hump/Westermark sign).
Explanation_D: Emphysema causes hyperlucency bilaterally, not a sudden unilateral complete loss of lung markings.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in tall, thin, young males. Signs include sudden dyspnea, unilateral absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and an absent pleural line on CXR.
One_Line: Unilateral absent breath sounds with absent lung markings on CXR indicates a pneumothorax.

Question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of lobar pneumonia in adults?
Explanation_A: Klebsiella causes lobar pneumonia classically in alcoholics and diabetics (currant jelly sputum).
Explanation_B: Haemophilus influenzae typically causes exacerbations of COPD.
Explanation_C: Staphylococcus pyogenes (Streptococcus pyogenes) causes pharyngitis, rarely pneumonia.
Explanation_D: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is by far the most common cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia in adults.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common etiology of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in adults, classically presenting with sudden onset fever, chills, lobar consolidation, and rust-colored sputum.
One_Line: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of typical lobar community-acquired pneumonia.

Question: A 45-year-old man is admitted with general tiredness and fever. There is a past history of a chest infection of 4-week duration, for which he was given oral antibiotics. He felt better initially. but never fully recovered and is now becoming worse (see report). Chest X-ray: It shows a right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Lung cancer can cause an effusion but the history of a recent chest infection and fever strongly favors an infectious etiology.
Explanation_B: Tuberculosis is possible, but a para-pneumonic effusion following a partially treated typical bacterial pneumonia is more common here.
Explanation_C: PE causes effusions but not typically following a 4-week history of a chest infection.
Explanation_D: A pleural effusion developing during or shortly after a bout of pneumonia is a parapneumonic effusion, which can become infected (empyema) if not treated adequately.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Parapneumonic effusions arise secondary to bacterial pneumonia. If they become loculated, purulent, or have a pH < 7.2, they are termed an empyema and require chest tube drainage.
One_Line: A pleural effusion developing after a recent respiratory infection is a parapneumonic effusion.

Question: A 45-year-old nurse working in the pulmonary clinic, complains of fever and a productive cough for the last 3 months. She has received 2 courses of oral antibiotics, but showed no improvement (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: A healthcare worker (pulmonary clinic) with a prolonged (3 month) fever and productive cough unresponsive to standard antibiotics is highly suspicious for Tuberculosis.
Explanation_B: H. influenzae pneumonia is acute and responds to antibiotics.
Explanation_C: Infectious mononucleosis causes fatigue, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy, not a 3-month productive cough.
Explanation_D: Streptococcal pneumonia is acute and resolves with antibiotics.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Chronic cough (> 3 weeks), fever, night sweats, and weight loss, especially in high-risk populations (healthcare workers, homeless, immigrants), should immediately raise suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis.
One_Line: A chronic productive cough and fever unresponsive to standard antibiotics in a healthcare worker suggests Tuberculosis.

Question: A 55-year-old patient presents to the clinic with shortness of breath and a cough productive of yellow sputum for the past 2 days. There has also been blood-stained sputum for the last 3 hours. The patient has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes a day for the past 35 years. On examination, there are rhonchi, wheezing, and crepitations heard over the right hemothorax (see report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 84 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Temperature 38.8° C Oxygen saturation 95% on room air Chest X-ray: It shows a dense infiltrate in the right lower lobe. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: The patient has an acute onset of fever, blood-stained (rust-colored) sputum, focal crackles, and a dense infiltrate on CXR. This is classic for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP).
Explanation_B: Acute bronchitis does not cause focal dense infiltrates on CXR.
Explanation_C: Tuberculosis is chronic and typically causes upper lobe infiltrates/cavitations.
Explanation_D: COPD causes chronic symptoms; an acute infiltrate indicates a superimposed pneumonia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Typical CAP (often S. pneumoniae) presents acutely with fever, productive cough (rust-colored), pleuritic chest pain, and a focal lobar infiltrate on chest X-ray.
One_Line: Acute fever, productive cough, and a dense lobar infiltrate on CXR define community-acquired pneumonia.

Question: A 27-year-old woman with asthma has not had a severe attack for the last 3 months. However she has a history of cough and wheezing 2-3 times each week. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
Explanation_A: Ipratropium is for COPD and acute asthma flares, not chronic maintenance.
Explanation_B: The patient has symptoms > 2 days a week (mild persistent asthma). The appropriate controller medication is a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid.
Explanation_C: Salbutamol (SABA) is used PRN, but she needs a controller medication because her symptoms are persistent (>2x/week).
Explanation_D: Salmeterol (LABA) is never used as monotherapy without an ICS.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Mild persistent asthma (>2 daytime symptoms/week but not daily) requires the initiation of a daily maintenance controller medication: a low-dose Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS).
One_Line: Mild persistent asthma requires daily inhaled corticosteroids for maintenance.

Question: A 21-year-old woman comes to the clinic with episodes of shortness of breath on exertion for one year. She has to stop after 15-20 minutes of exercise, because of dyspnoea and coughing, which get better after about one hour of rest. There are no symptoms at rest. Physical examination and spirometry are normal. Blood pressure 125/75 mmH Heart rate 80 /min Respiratory rate 12 /min Temperature 37.0° C Which of the following is the most appropriate inhaled treatment before exercise?
Explanation_A: Salmeterol is a LABA, used for chronic control with ICS, not for acute pre-exercise prophylaxis.
Explanation_B: The patient has Exercise-Induced Bronchoconstriction (EIB). The treatment of choice is a short-acting beta-2 agonist (Salbutamol/Albuterol) 10-15 minutes prior to exercise.
Explanation_C: Budesonide (ICS) is a controller, not a rapid-onset prophylactic for exercise.
Explanation_D: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic not used for EIB.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Exercise-induced asthma (EIB) presents with bronchospasm during or immediately after exercise. It is best managed by administering a Short-Acting Beta Agonist (SABA) 15 minutes before exertion.
One_Line: Exercise-induced asthma is prevented by using a SABA (Salbutamol) 15 minutes before exercise.

Question: A 42-year-old man with asthma presents with daily symptoms despite regularly using a long acting -agonist inhaler and an inhaled high-dose corticosteroid. He also uses a short acting - agonist inhaler as "rescue" medication. These episodes also wake him from sleep 2-3 times a week. Physical examination shows bilateral (see table). Blood pressure 140/85 mmH Heart rate 90 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 36.7° C Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 Second Normal value Before bronchodilator 65 % 25-75 % After bronchodilators 91 % Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Option_C: Observe the patient using his inhaler
Explanation_A: Theophylline is a toxic last-resort drug.
Explanation_B: While a leukotriene inhibitor could be added, checking inhaler technique is crucial when a patient on maximal therapy remains uncontrolled.
Explanation_C: Before stepping up therapy (e.g., oral steroids) for a patient with poorly controlled asthma on high-dose ICS + LABA, the physician MUST ensure adherence and proper inhaler technique.
Explanation_D: GERD can exacerbate asthma, but checking technique is the most direct first step.
High_Yield_Must_Know: In any patient with poorly controlled asthma despite seemingly adequate prescribed therapy, always assess medication adherence and inhaler technique before stepping up pharmacological treatment.
One_Line: Always check inhaler technique and adherence before stepping up asthma medications in poorly controlled patients.

Question: A 67-year-old patient presents to the Emergency Department with chest pain, shortness of breath, and haemoptysis following a car trip for more than 5 hours (see report). ECG: Right axis deviation, an S1-Q3-T3 pattern, and a right bundle branch block. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: MI causes chest pain but not hemoptysis, and the classic PE ECG findings are absent.
Explanation_B: Lung cancer doesn't have an acute 5-hour onset post-travel.
Explanation_C: Prolonged immobilization (car trip) leads to DVT, which embolized to the lungs (PE). The ECG findings of S1Q3T3 (S wave in I, Q wave in III, inverted T in III) indicate acute right heart strain, classic for PE.
Explanation_D: Pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The classic ECG finding for Pulmonary Embolism is the S1Q3T3 pattern, indicating acute right ventricular strain (cor pulmonale). Prolonged travel is a major risk factor.
One_Line: Sudden dyspnea, hemoptysis, and an S1Q3T3 pattern on ECG after prolonged travel defines a pulmonary embolism.

Question: A 55-year-old smoker presents to a clinic with progressive shortness of breath (see report). Chest X-ray: It reveals a massive right pleural effusion. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
Explanation_A: A massive, new pleural effusion requires diagnostic sampling to determine the etiology (exudate vs. transudate, cytology for cancer). A diagnostic thoracentesis is the immediate next step.
Explanation_B: CT scan is useful later, but thoracentesis gives an immediate tissue/fluid diagnosis and symptom relief.
Explanation_C: Intercostal tube (chest tube) is for pneumothorax, hemothorax, or empyema. A diagnostic tap must precede tube insertion for a simple effusion.
Explanation_D: Bronchodilators do not treat pleural effusions.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Any new, unexplained pleural effusion requires a diagnostic thoracentesis to differentiate between a transudate (heart/liver/kidney failure) and an exudate (infection, malignancy) using Light's criteria.
One_Line: The first step in evaluating a new, unexplained pleural effusion is a diagnostic thoracentesis.

Question: A 28-year-old patient develops the sudden onset of dyspnoea and tachycardia 5 days post a knee surgery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Pulmonary embolism classically presents with sudden onset dyspnea and tachycardia, especially in high-risk patients such as those immobilized after major orthopedic (knee/hip) surgery.
Explanation_B: Myocardial infarction can cause dyspnea, but sudden dyspnea post-orthopedic surgery is overwhelmingly due to PE.
Explanation_C: Ventricular tachycardia causes palpitations and syncope, not primarily isolated sudden dyspnea.
Explanation_D: Pulmonary emphysema is a chronic disease and does not present with sudden acute dyspnea 5 days post-surgery.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Major orthopedic surgery (hip, knee) carries a very high risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and subsequent pulmonary embolism (PE).
One_Line: Sudden dyspnea and tachycardia a few days after knee or hip surgery is classic for a pulmonary embolism.

Question: A patient with stage IIIB small cell lung cancer complains of new onset of back pain for the past 12 hours. Initial neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action to take?
Option_D: High dose IV corticosteroids and MRI
Explanation_A: MRI is the imaging modality of choice, but in suspected malignant spinal cord compression, high-dose IV corticosteroids must be administered immediately, even before the MRI.
Explanation_B: Radiation therapy is the definitive treatment but requires imaging and steroid administration first.
Explanation_C: Taking no immediate action could result in permanent paralysis.
Explanation_D: New-onset back pain in a patient with lung cancer represents epidural spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. Immediate high-dose IV corticosteroids (dexamethasone) reduce edema and preserve neurologic function while awaiting an urgent MRI.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Malignant epidural spinal cord compression is an oncologic emergency. The first step, even before imaging, is to give high-dose IV dexamethasone to prevent permanent paralysis.
One_Line: New back pain in a cancer patient requires immediate high-dose IV corticosteroids followed by an urgent spinal MRI.

Question: On a follow-up consultation of a patient with a squamous cell carcinoma, some abnormalities are noted in blood analysis (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Parathyroid hormone 1.0 1.1-5.3 pmol/L Calcium 3.30 2.15-2.62 mmol/L Calcium ionised 1.6 1.1-1.3 mmol/L Sodium 140 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 4.3 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the metabolic abnormality?
Option_D: Secretion of PTH-related peptide by the tumour
Explanation_A: Renal failure can cause secondary hyperparathyroidism (low calcium, high PTH), not hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.
Explanation_B: Primary hyperparathyroidism would show HIGH calcium and HIGH (or inappropriately normal) PTH.
Explanation_C: Secondary hyperparathyroidism presents with low calcium and high PTH in response.
Explanation_D: Squamous cell carcinomas commonly secrete PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), which acts like PTH to raise serum calcium but does not cross-react in standard PTH assays, leading to hypercalcemia with suppressed endogenous PTH.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung classically causes paraneoplastic hypercalcemia via the secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP).
One_Line: Hypercalcemia with a suppressed PTH in a patient with squamous cell carcinoma is caused by PTHrP secretion.

Question: A 78-year-old man and current smoker, with 50 pack-year smoking history, complains of shortness of breath, dry cough and fatigue progressing over the past 8 weeks. The patient also reports a significant weight loss, corresponding to approximately 15% of body weight over the last 12 weeks. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: COPD causes progressive SOB but does not typically cause massive (15%) weight loss unless in end-stage cachexia, and a new onset at 78 favors malignancy.
Explanation_B: Pneumonia causes acute fever and productive cough, not an 8-12 week progression of weight loss and fatigue.
Explanation_C: A heavy smoking history coupled with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and significant weight loss is the hallmark clinical presentation of lung cancer.
Explanation_D: Interstitial lung disease causes dry cough and dyspnea but is less strongly associated with massive weight loss and 50 pack-year smoking history as the primary driver compared to lung cancer.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Unintentional weight loss, chronic cough, and dyspnea in an older heavy smoker should be considered lung cancer until proven otherwise.
One_Line: Significant weight loss, progressive dyspnea, and a chronic cough in an elderly heavy smoker indicate lung cancer.

Question: A 20-year-old man with sickle cell anemia presents with right sided chest pain and shortness of breath for 2 days. It was associated with pain in both legs and back. On examination, fine crackles were heard in right middle and lower zones (see image). Blood pressure 125/75 mmHg Heart rate 92 /min Respiratory rate 25/min Temperature 37.9° C Oxygen saturation 91% on room air Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Viral pericarditis causes positional chest pain but does not cause lung crackles or hypoxia.
Explanation_B: Pulmonary embolism can cause chest pain and hypoxia, but in a sickle cell patient with concurrent vaso-occlusive pain (legs/back) and lung crackles, Acute Chest Syndrome is the primary diagnosis.
Explanation_C: Acute chest syndrome is a life-threatening complication of sickle cell disease characterized by chest pain, fever, hypoxia, and a new pulmonary infiltrate (crackles). It is often triggered by a vaso-occlusive crisis or infection.
Explanation_D: PCP pneumonia affects immunocompromised patients (HIV), presenting with bilateral ground-glass infiltrates, not focal acute chest pain and bone pain.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Acute Chest Syndrome in sickle cell disease is defined by a new radiodensity on CXR accompanied by fever, respiratory distress, or chest pain. It is the leading cause of death among adult sickle cell patients.
One_Line: Chest pain, hypoxia, and a lung infiltrate in a patient with sickle cell disease signifies Acute Chest Syndrome.

Question: A 20-year-old man with sickle cell anemia presents with right sided chest pain and shortness of breath for 2 days. It is associated with pain in both legs and back. On examination, fine crackles are heard in right middle and lower zones (see image). Blood pressure 125/75 mmHg Heart rate 92 /min Respiratory rate 25 /min Temperature 37.9° C Oxygen saturation 91% on room air What is the most effective drug to reduce this incidence?
Explanation_A: Folic acid is supplemented in sickle cell due to high RBC turnover but does not prevent vaso-occlusive crises or acute chest syndrome.
Explanation_B: Hydroxyurea increases the production of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which dilutes HbS, decreases polymerization, and significantly reduces the frequency of vaso-occlusive crises and acute chest syndrome.
Explanation_C: 5-azacytidine can increase HbF but is not the standard or FDA-approved first-line agent (hydroxyurea is).
Explanation_D: Erythropoietin is used for anemia of chronic kidney disease, not for preventing acute chest syndrome.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Hydroxyurea is the primary disease-modifying therapy for severe sickle cell disease. It works by increasing fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels, thereby reducing sickling.
One_Line: Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of acute chest syndrome and pain crises in sickle cell disease by increasing HbF.

Question: Which of the following is the antidote for an opiate overdose?
Explanation_A: Naloxone is a competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist used to rapidly reverse respiratory depression in opiate overdose.
Explanation_B: Flumazenil is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose.
Explanation_C: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine used for seizures/agitation.
Explanation_D: Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist used for maintenance treatment of opioid use disorder, not acute overdose reversal.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The classic triad of opioid overdose is pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and coma. The immediate antidote is Naloxone.
One_Line: Naloxone is the definitive antidote for acute opiate overdose.

Question: A 17-year-old man with history of intravenous drug abuse presents to the clinic for clinical evaluation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
Explanation_A: MRSA screening is not the standard priority routine screen for asymptomatic IV drug users compared to bloodborne viruses.
Explanation_B: Intravenous drug abuse involves sharing needles, putting the patient at an extraordinarily high risk for bloodborne pathogens, most notably HIV, Hepatitis C, and Hepatitis B. Screening for HIV is critical.
Explanation_C: Streptococcus viridans causes endocarditis, but screening is for infectious agents, not an asymptomatic blood culture for viridans.
Explanation_D: Viral hepatitis B screening is important, but HIV testing is a primary, universally required screening for high-risk behaviors.
High_Yield_Must_Know: All patients with a history of intravenous drug use must be screened for bloodborne viruses: HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C.
One_Line: History of intravenous drug abuse mandates immediate screening for HIV and Hepatitis B/C.

Question: A 17-year-old high school athlete presents to the clinic for an annual physical check-up. On examination, he has gained 20 Kg in the past 4 months and has very well developed musculature of the upper body, acne over the face and back and foul breath. Heart rate 94 /min Temperature 37.6° C Blood pressure 138/89 mmHg Respiratory rate 14 /min Which of the following the patient should be screened for?
Explanation_A: Depression does not cause massive muscular hypertrophy and acne.
Explanation_B: Cocaine use causes weight loss, sympathetic overdrive, and mucosal damage.
Explanation_C: Thyroid tumors do not cause 20 kg of rapid muscle mass gain and severe acne.
Explanation_D: Anabolic steroid abuse in athletes classically presents with rapid, massive gains in muscle mass, severe cystic acne, mood swings (roid rage), and eventually testicular atrophy and gynecomastia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Signs of anabolic steroid abuse in males include rapid muscle growth, severe acne, behavioral changes, testicular atrophy, and decreased HDL.
One_Line: Rapid muscle gain combined with severe acne in an athlete is the hallmark of anabolic steroid abuse.

Question: A 40-year-old drug addict man presents to the Emergency Department with 1-hour history of unconsciousness. On examination, he has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 8/minute. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
Explanation_A: Atropine is used for organophosphate poisoning or bradycardia, not opiate overdose.
Explanation_B: The patient exhibits the classic opiate overdose triad: coma, pinpoint pupils (miosis), and severe respiratory depression (RR=8). Naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist, is the life-saving antidote.
Explanation_C: Furosemide is a diuretic for fluid overload.
Explanation_D: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The classic triad of opioid overdose is respiratory depression, altered mental status (coma), and miosis (pinpoint pupils). The immediate treatment is IV Naloxone.
One_Line: Naloxone rapidly reverses the respiratory depression and coma of an opiate overdose.

Question: A 53-year-old woman with history of depression presents to the Emergency Department with history of nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, tinnitus, and shortness of breath 6 hours after consuming 50 tablets of aspirin (see lab result). Test Result Normal Value Plasma salicylate concentration 54 15-30 mg/dL which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
Explanation_A: Hemodialysis is used for massive, life-threatening salicylate overdoses (e.g., severe CNS dysfunction, renal failure, pulmonary edema), but alkalinization is the first step for moderate-to-severe toxicity.
Explanation_B: Gastric lavage is rarely used and only if the patient presents within 1 hour of ingestion.
Explanation_C: Activated charcoal is useful early but urine alkalinization definitively enhances systemic elimination of the drug.
Explanation_D: Aspirin (salicylate) is a weak acid. Alkalinizing the urine with IV sodium bicarbonate ion-traps the salicylate in the renal tubules, massively increasing its excretion and resolving the toxicity.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Salicylate (Aspirin) overdose causes a mixed respiratory alkalosis (due to hyperventilation/tinnitus) and high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Treatment is IV Sodium Bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine.
One_Line: Urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate enhances the renal excretion of aspirin in overdoses.

Question: Which of the following systems is stimulated by stressful situation?
Explanation_A: The urinary system is not the primary driver of the stress response.
Explanation_B: The respiratory system responds to stress (tachypnea) but is not the control system.
Explanation_C: The Sympathetic nervous system (fight-or-flight) is massively stimulated by stress, leading to catecholamine release, tachycardia, and pupil dilation.
Explanation_D: The Parasympathetic nervous system (rest-and-digest) is inhibited, not stimulated, during acute stress.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The acute stress response is mediated by the Sympathetic Nervous System (releasing epinephrine/norepinephrine) and the HPA axis (releasing cortisol).
One_Line: The sympathetic nervous system drives the 'fight or flight' stress response.
Accuracy_Review: Corrected provided answer in source (D). The correct answer is C (Sympathetic). Source material had a gross error.

Question: Which of the following clinical signs caused by a lesion in Wernicke's area?
Option_A: Can understand but unable to say words easily
Option_B: Cannot understand spoken or written words
Option_C: Loss of ability to recognize faces
Explanation_A: This describes Broca's (expressive) aphasia, caused by a lesion in the frontal lobe (inferior frontal gyrus).
Explanation_B: Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia is caused by a lesion in the superior temporal gyrus. Patients cannot understand spoken or written words, and their own speech is fluent but nonsensical ('word salad').
Explanation_C: Loss of ability to recognize faces is prosopagnosia, typically due to lesions in the fusiform gyrus (occipitotemporal lobe).
Explanation_D: Loss of short-term memory is related to bilateral hippocampal lesions.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Wernicke's aphasia (superior temporal gyrus) is a receptive aphasia = fluent, nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension. Broca's aphasia (inferior frontal gyrus) is expressive = broken, non-fluent speech with intact comprehension.
One_Line: A lesion in Wernicke's area results in an inability to comprehend spoken or written language.

Question: Which of the following is the lowest fatal dose of tricyclic antidepressant?
Explanation_A: 500 mg can cause toxicity but is rarely fatal in adults.
Explanation_B: 1 gm can cause severe toxicity.
Explanation_C: 2 gm is a massive overdose.
