High_Yield_Must_Know: A healthcare worker with a documented adequate anti-HBs titer (>10 mIU/mL) requires no post-exposure prophylaxis or further testing after exposure to Hepatitis B.
One_Line: Documented Hepatitis B immunity requires no post-exposure prophylaxis after a needle stick.

Question: A 45-year-old man with a diagnosis of gastrosophageal reflux disease who 1s taking a maximum dose of pantoprazole for several weeks presents to the clinic with heartburn that is minimally improved with treatment. The patient verified that he is taking the medication 30 minutes before meals. He takes no other medications. His physical examination is unremarkable. Upper endoscopy findings are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
Explanation_A: Erosive gastritis causes superficial bleeding, usually presenting as coffee-ground emesis rather than massive life-threatening hematemesis.
Explanation_B: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) is the most common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, often presenting with melena or hematemesis, especially in patients using NSAIDs or with H. pylori.
Explanation_C: Esophageal varices cause massive bleeding but typically in patients with known cirrhosis/portal hypertension.
Explanation_D: Mallory-Weiss tears usually follow a clear history of repetitive violent vomiting/retching.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Peptic Ulcer Disease is the most frequent cause of upper GI bleeding. NSAID use and H. pylori infection are the primary risk factors.
One_Line: Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Question: A 50-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with acute onset of abdominal pain, naugea and vomiting. Abdominal examination shows tenderness and guarding at the epigastrium. CT scan of the abdomen reveals fluid around the pancreas. He was admitted and started on intravenous fluids; analgesics and nasogastric suction (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 120 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 190 150-400 x 109/I WBC 18 4.5-10.5 x 109/1 Aspartate aminotransferase 55 12-40 IU/I Alanine aminotransferase 65 5-40 IU/I Lactate dehydrogenase 6 1.4-3.56 umol/I Amylase 850 24-151 IU/L Dipase 900 0-160 IU/L which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management
Explanation_A: Repeating endoscopy is low yield if the first was unrevealing.
Explanation_B: Barium esophagogram assesses structure (strictures/webs) but not acid reflux directly.
Explanation_C: Esophageal manometry measures motility (e.g., achalasia), not acid exposure.
Explanation_D: In patients with persistent GERD symptoms despite PPI therapy and a normal endoscopy, ambulatory 24-hour pH impedance monitoring is the gold standard to correlate symptoms with actual acid/non-acid reflux events.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Ambulatory pH impedance monitoring is the test of choice for patients with refractory GERD symptoms and a normal upper endoscopy to confirm the diagnosis before considering surgery.
One_Line: Ambulatory pH monitoring is the gold standard for diagnosing refractory GERD with a normal endoscopy.

Question: A 32-year-old man is evaluated for a 10-month history of fatigue and diarrhoea. He has a good appetite but has unintentionally significant weight 1033 over the past 10 weeks. He has not had blood obvious source of blood 1033. His systemic examinations are unremarkable. in the stool, melena, or other Stool is negative for occult blood (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmig Heart rate 80 /min Respiratory rate 16 /min Temperature 36.6 °c BMI 18 kg/m2 Test Result Normal Values Hb 109 130-170 g/L (Male) MOV 70 80-95 f1 Platelets count 455 150-400 x 109/I WBC 8 4.5-10.5 x 109/1 Aspartate aminotransferase 30 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 26 5-40 IU/I Albumin 32 34-56 g/I Total bilirubin 10 3.5-16.5 umol/L which of the following is the best treatment?
Explanation_A: In a patient presenting with an acute abdomen or severe intra-abdominal sepsis, adding a broad-spectrum antibiotic like Imipenem is critical to cover enteric gram-negative rods and anaerobes.
Explanation_B: Pantoprazole treats acid reflux but does not address an acute infection/sepsis.
Explanation_C: Methylprednisolone is a steroid and would worsen an active bacterial infection.
Explanation_D: Surgical consultation is vital, but immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics (like Imipenem) must be started simultaneously in suspected intra-abdominal sepsis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Severe intra-abdominal infections require immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negatives and anaerobes (e.g., Carbapenems or Piperacillin-Tazobactam) alongside surgical evaluation.
One_Line: Severe intra-abdominal sepsis mandates immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics like Imipenem.

Question: but has unintentionally gignificant weight loss over the past 10 weeks. He has not had blood in the stool, melena, or other obvious source of blood 1033. Hig systemic examinations are unremarkable. Stool is negative for occult blood (see lab results) Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 80 /min Respiratory rate 16 /min Temperature 36.6 °c BMI 18 kg/m2 Test Result Normal Values H6 109 130-170 q/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) MCH 20 28-33 g/cell MCV 70 80-95 fl Platelets count 455 150-400 × 109/I WBC 8 4.5-10.5 x 109/1 Aspartate aminotransferase 30 12-40 IU/I Alanine aminotransferase 26 5-40 IU/I Albumin 32 34-56 g/1 Total bilirubin 10 3.5-16.5 umo1/1 which of the following is the best treatment?
Explanation_A: Loperamide treats the symptom of diarrhea but does not address the underlying autoimmune malabsorption.
Explanation_B: Metronidazole is for infections like Giardia or C. diff.
Explanation_C: Mebendazole is for helminthic infections.
Explanation_D: A 10-month history of chronic diarrhea and significant unintentional weight loss is classic for Celiac disease. The definitive management is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, which resolves the mucosal inflammation and malabsorption.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Celiac disease presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia. The cornerstone of treatment is strict adherence to a lifelong gluten-free diet.
One_Line: A strict gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment for Celiac disease.

Question: A 55-year-old woman with a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COD) on combination of long-acting B2-agonist and inhaled glucocorticoid and albuterol as needed presents to the clinic with worsening of her symptoms. On physical examination, there is no jugular venous distention. Pulmonary examination reveals decreased breath sound. Bilateral lover extremity edema is noted to a level above the ankles. Echocardiogram is normal apart of high mean pulmonary artery pressure, 52 mmig (see lab results) Blood pressure 125/75 mmHg Heart rate 84 /min Respiratory rate 20 /min Temperature 36.6 °c Oxygen saturation 86 % BMI 30 kg/m2 Test Result Normal Values ABG PCO2 7.5 4.7-6.0 kPa рн 7.6 7.36-7.45 ABG PO2 8.6 10.6-14.2 kPa which of the following is the most appropriate treatment at this time?
Explanation_A: Mucolytics do not improve mortality or oxygenation in COPD.
Explanation_B: Diuretics are for fluid overload (heart failure), not primary hypoxemia.
Explanation_C: Oral prednisone is used for acute exacerbations, not chronic hypoxemia management.
Explanation_D: For a patient with chronic COPD and resting hypoxemia (PaO2 < 55 mmHg or SaO2 < 88%), long-term oxygen therapy is the only intervention (besides smoking cessation) proven to improve survival.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT) improves mortality in COPD patients with severe resting hypoxemia.
One_Line: Long-term oxygen therapy is indicated for COPD patients with severe resting hypoxemia to improve survival.

Question: A 66-year-old woman is evaluated for a 6-week history of increasing dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain with occasional cough. She has lost significant body weight in the last 3 months. She has no other medical problems and takes no medications. Her physical examination reveals dullness to percussion and decreased breath sound over both lower lung zones. A 4-om right breast mass is palpated. Chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral pleural effusions but no evidence of infiltrate or pulmonary vascular congestion. Thoracentesis is performed. Pleural fluid Gram stain is negative (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Total Protein 40 10-20 g/I Fluid Protein/Serum Protein 0.67 <0.5 glucose 3.5 >2.2 mmol/I LDH 350 <200/UL Total Proteins 60 60-84 g/1 Lactate dehydrogenase 125 60-160 IU/L Leukocytes 3600 <1000/MI Which of the following is the most appropriate statement about the diagnosi
Option_A: Exudative pleural effusion due to malignancy
Option_B: Transudative pleural effusion due to malignancy
Option_C: Exudative pleural effusion due to heart failure
Option_D: Transudative pleural effusion due to empyema
Explanation_A: Malignancy causes an exudative effusion due to increased capillary permeability and pleural inflammation, meeting Light's criteria.
Explanation_B: Transudates are caused by hydrostatic/oncotic pressure imbalances (e.g., heart failure, cirrhosis), not malignancy.
Explanation_C: Heart failure causes a transudative effusion, not exudative.
Explanation_D: Empyema causes an exudative effusion, not transudative.
High_Yield_Must_Know: According to Light's criteria, an exudate has a Pleural/Serum Protein ratio > 0.5 or Pleural/Serum LDH > 0.6. Malignancy and infections cause exudates.
One_Line: Malignancy typically causes an exudative pleural effusion due to increased capillary permeability.

Question: A 28-year-old woman with bronchial asthma that controlled on budesonide and albuterol inhalers is evaluated in the clinic as she is 6 weeks pregnant. Her symptoms are well controlled on the treatment. However, symptoms usually flare in fall and she treats these symptoms with an add-on oral leukotriene inhibitor. She currently has no asthma symptoms. On examination, vital signs are normal. The lungs show good air entry and no wheezes. She is so concern about the safety of medications during pregnancy. What is the best information to be delivered to her with regard to medication safety?
Option_A: Continue the current treatments as they are safe during pregnancy
Option_B: Stop budesonide and continue albuterol inhaler
Option_C: Stop albuterol and continue budesonide inhaler
Explanation_A: Asthma medications, including inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide) and short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol), are generally safe and highly recommended to continue during pregnancy to prevent hypoxic exacerbations.
Explanation_B: Stopping controller meds (budesonide) risks severe asthma exacerbations, which are dangerous for the fetus.
Explanation_C: Stopping rescue inhalers is dangerous.
Explanation_D: Step-down therapy is not recommended just because the patient is pregnant; asthma control must be maintained.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Poorly controlled asthma is far more dangerous to the fetus than asthma medications. ICS (budesonide) and SABAs (albuterol) should be continued during pregnancy.
One_Line: Inhaled corticosteroids and SABAs are safe and should be continued during pregnancy to maintain asthma control.

Question: A 26-year-old man presents to the clinic with shortness of breath and occasional wheeze that occurs several times per week. He develops significant shortness of breath when playing football. He notes that it takes several minutes to recover his breath when thig occurs. He algo notes coughing during exercise as well. He takes no medications. On physical examination, vital signs are normal. Mild nasal congestion is noted. His systemic examinations are unremarkable. A chest radiograph is normal. Spirometry findings are within normal parameters which of the following ig the most appropriate next step in assessment?
Option_D: Helical (spiral) computed tomography (CT) for the chest
Explanation_A: Repeating normal spirometry won't provoke the underlying hyperreactivity.
Explanation_B: Clinical observation delays diagnosis in a symptomatic patient.
Explanation_C: If a patient has classic asthma symptoms but normal baseline spirometry, a Methacholine challenge test (bronchoprovocation) is used to demonstrate airway hyperresponsiveness. A 20% drop in FEV1 confirms the diagnosis.
Explanation_D: CT chest is for interstitial lung disease or malignancy, not asthma.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The Methacholine challenge test is highly sensitive for asthma and is the diagnostic test of choice when the patient has a normal baseline spirometry but suspicious symptoms.
One_Line: A methacholine challenge test diagnoses asthma in symptomatic patients with normal baseline spirometry.

Question: A 31-year-old woman is evaluated because of daily wheezing and breathlessness that limit her activities several times a week. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable. She has never smoked. She is diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma. In addition to a short-acting B2-agonist, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
Option_A: Add a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting B2-agonist
Explanation_A: The patient is poorly controlled. Adding both an ICS and a LABA is the appropriate step-up therapy for moderate-to-severe persistent asthma.
Explanation_B: A low-dose ICS alone is insufficient if the patient is already uncontrolled or requires a major step up.
Explanation_C: Leukotriene antagonists are less effective than ICS+LABA.
Explanation_D: Theophylline is toxic and rarely used.
High_Yield_Must_Know: For asthma not controlled on a low-dose ICS, the preferred step-up therapy is to add a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA).
One_Line: Asthma step-up therapy involves adding a LABA to an inhaled corticosteroid.

Question: A 66-year-old woman with severe COPD is admitted with 4 days of dyspnoea and cough. She is alert, in moderate respiratory distress, and has an oxygen saturation of 93% on 3 L/min supplemental oxygen. A chest radiography demonstrates no consolidation. She receives intensive bronchodilator therapy and systemic steroids (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values ABG PCO2 8.8 4.7-6.0 kPa pH 7.28 7.36-7.45 ABG P02 9.9 10.6-14.2 kPa which of the following is the best next step in the management?
Explanation_A: Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) is the treatment of choice for acute exacerbations of COPD complicated by respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35) to reduce the work of breathing and improve CO2 clearance.
Explanation_B: Increasing oxygen without ventilatory support worsens hypercapnia in COPD.
Explanation_C: Decreasing oxygen can cause fatal hypoxia.
Explanation_D: Intubation is reserved for patients who fail NIPPV, are comatose, or hemodynamically unstable.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV/BiPAP) is the first-line intervention for COPD exacerbations presenting with hypercapnic respiratory acidosis.
One_Line: NIPPV is the best initial respiratory support for COPD exacerbations with respiratory acidosis.

Question: A 58-year-old woman with acute onset shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. She is diagnosed with pulmonary embolism. which of the following is an indication to do thrombophilia workup?
Option_C: Has a history of connective tissue disease
Option_D: Has negative family history of thrombosis
Explanation_A: Age >55 is a general risk but OCPs are a specific, high-risk thrombogenic trigger.
Explanation_B: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) contain estrogen, which increases the hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and decreases antithrombin III, significantly increasing the risk of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism.
Explanation_C: Connective tissue disease is a risk, but OCP use is a classic, highly tested iatrogenic risk factor.
Explanation_D: Negative family history doesn't cause thrombosis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pills are a major risk factor for venous thromboembolism (DVT and PE).
One_Line: Oral contraceptive pills significantly increase the risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism.

Question: A 32-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic because of an abnormal chest computerised tomography (CT) scan that revealed small lung lesion (7 mm) without any other abnormalities. He is non-smoker and he is asymptomatic. Physical examination shows no lymphadenopathy and normal lung examinations (see lab results) Test Result Normal Values Hb 140 130-170 g/I (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 300 150-400 x 109/L NBC 8 4.5-10.5 x 109/1 ESR 11 2-10 mm/h (Male) 3-15 mm/h (Female) Calcium 2.25 2.15-2.62 mmo1/1 Which of the following is the most appropriate procedure to do next?
Explanation_A: A solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) < 8 mm with low-risk features (young patient, non-smoker) is best managed with serial CT scans (e.g., at 3-6 months) to monitor for growth, avoiding invasive biopsies.
Explanation_B: PFTs do not characterize a nodule.
Explanation_C: Biopsy is unnecessarily invasive for a low-risk, small incidental nodule.
Explanation_D: PET scans are reserved for nodules > 8 mm to assess metabolic activity.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Incidental solid pulmonary nodules < 8 mm in low-risk patients are managed with serial follow-up CT scans to assess stability over time.
One_Line: Small (<8 mm), low-risk solitary pulmonary nodules are managed with serial CT scan surveillance.

Question: A 60-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for cardiac risk assessment. He is asymptomatic and physically active. He has never smoked. He has no chronic health issues and takes no medications. His physical examinations are normal. Cardiovascular risk calculation using the Pooled Cohort Equations predicts a 6.5% riek of a myocardial infarction in the next 10 years that indicate an intermediate risk of myocardial infarction Which of the following investigations should be done next
Explanation_A: Cardiac CT is an anatomical test, not a functional stress test.
Explanation_B: If a patient has an abnormal baseline ECG (e.g., LBBB, LVH, paced rhythm) that precludes interpretation of ischemic ST-changes during exercise, an imaging stress test (like Stress Echocardiography or myocardial perfusion imaging) must be used.
Explanation_C: CRP is a marker of inflammation, not a stress test.
Explanation_D: CMR is not the first-line stress test.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Patients with baseline ECG abnormalities (like LBBB) require an imaging-based stress test (stress echo or nuclear perfusion scan) because ECG ST-segment changes cannot be interpreted.
One_Line: An abnormal baseline ECG mandates an imaging stress test (like stress echocardiography) rather than a standard exercise ECG.

Question: A 58-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. She has no symptoms. Medications are hydrochlorothiazide, logartan, atorvastatin, and metformin. Cardiac examination shows a grade 2/6 diastolic murmur heard best over the apex. Peripheral pulses are normal. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with nonspecific ST changes. Blood pressure 160/80 mmHg Heart rate 78 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 36.6 °c Oxygen saturation 96% Which of the following is the most appropriate test to perform next?
Explanation_A: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the most appropriate initial, non-invasive diagnostic test to evaluate cardiac structure, function, and suspected heart failure or valvular disease in a symptomatic patient.
Explanation_B: CT angiography evaluates coronaries.
Explanation_C: TEE is invasive and used if TTE is inconclusive or to look for specific issues like endocarditis or atrial thrombus.
Explanation_D: No testing is negligent in a symptomatic patient.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) is the best initial diagnostic test for evaluating newly suspected heart failure or murmurs.
One_Line: A transthoracic echocardiogram is the best initial test for evaluating suspected heart failure or structural heart disease.

Question: A 55-year-old woman presents to the clinic for her regular follow-up. 6 months ago, she presented to Emergency Department with palpitations and dyspnea and diagnosed to have atrial fibrillation. She is currently asymptomatic with no palpitations. Her medical history is also significant for a transient ischemic attack and hypertension. Her medications are warfarin, metoprolol and candesartan. Her physical examination is unremarkable. Her most recent electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
Explanation_A: Continuing warfarin without adjustments before a major surgery carries a high bleeding risk.
Explanation_B: Warfarin should be discontinued approximately 5 days prior to major surgery to allow the INR to normalize, preventing catastrophic intraoperative hemorrhage.
Explanation_C: Option missing but B is standard.
Explanation_D: Starting clopidogrel adds another antiplatelet, worsening bleeding risk.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Warfarin must be discontinued 5 days prior to elective surgery. For high-risk patients (mechanical valves), 'bridge therapy' with LMWH/Heparin is used.
One_Line: Warfarin should be stopped 5 days before an elective surgery to allow the INR to normalize.

Question: A 68-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnea and dry cough for days. His medical history is significant for hypertension. Physical examination reveals raised central venous pressure, fine crackles at lung bases and hepatomegaly. His extremity examination reveals bilateral pitting edema. Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% and normal valves. Chest radiograph shows evidence of pulmonary edema (see lab results) . Blood pressure 160/85 mmHg Heart rate 86 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Test Result Normal Values Sodium 140 134-146 mmol/I Potassium 4 3.5-5.1 mmol/I Urea 6 2.75-7.4 mmol/I Creatinine 88 44-115 umol/I Brain natriuretic peptide 900 0-300 ng/I Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management
Explanation_A: CCBs are not first-line for heart failure.
Explanation_B: Beta-blockers can worsen acute fluid overload.
Explanation_C: Spironolactone is added later.
Explanation_D: In a patient presenting with acute decompensated heart failure (fluid overload, pulmonary edema), the most appropriate immediate therapy to reduce preload and relieve symptoms is an intravenous loop diuretic like Furosemide.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Intravenous loop diuretics (Furosemide) are the first-line intervention for rapid symptom relief in acute decompensated heart failure.
One_Line: Intravenous furosemide rapidly relieves pulmonary edema in acute heart failure.

Question: A 26-year-old pregnant woman visits the clinic for regular follow-up. She is asymptomatic. She is in her 30th week of pregnancy. Her physical examination reveals a mid-systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. The murmur radiates to carotids. No diastolic murmur is heard. which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Aortic stenosis usually presents with an ejection systolic murmur.
Explanation_B: Mitral stenosis has a diastolic rumble.
Explanation_C: Tricuspid stenosis has a diastolic murmur.
Explanation_D: Pregnancy causes a hyperdynamic circulation (increased blood volume and cardiac output), which frequently leads to a soft, asymptomatic physiologic flow murmur at the left sternal border. This is normal and benign.
High_Yield_Must_Know: A soft, early-to-mid systolic flow murmur is a normal physiological finding in pregnancy due to increased cardiac output and blood volume.
One_Line: A soft systolic flow murmur is a normal physiological change during pregnancy.

Question: A 28-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department for severe persistent chest pain for I-day. The pain is constant but exacerbated when leaning forward and not associated with other symptoms. Physical examination is unremarkable apart of a friction rub at the left lower sternal border. Electrocardiogram shows diffuse, concave upward ST-segment elevations and PR-segment depression most prominent in leads V1 through V6. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment
Explanation_A: Prednisone is not first-line for viral/idiopathic pericarditis.
Explanation_B: Nitroglycerin treats angina, not pericarditis.
Explanation_C: Warfarin is an anticoagulant and contraindicated in pericarditis due to the risk of hemorrhagic tamponade.
Explanation_D: Acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis is best treated with high-dose NSAIDs (like Ibuprofen or Aspirin) and Colchicine to reduce inflammation and prevent recurrence.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The first-line treatment for acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis is high-dose NSAIDs (Ibuprofen) combined with Colchicine.
One_Line: Acute pericarditis is treated with NSAIDs like Ibuprofen.

Question: A 58-year-old woman was admitted with a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction received appropriate treatments and now she is ready for discharge. She is go concern about the secondary prevention of infarction. which of the following statements is the most appropriate?
Option_A: Anti-platelet agents should be used for short period to reduce the risk of recurrent infarction
Option_B: Calcium channel blockers should be used indefinitely to reduce the risk of recurrent infarction
Option_C: Hormonal replacement therapy should be given to postmenopausal women to prevent coronary events
Option_D: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should be used indefinitely by patient with clinically evident heart failure
Explanation_A: Anti-platelet agents (Aspirin) should be used indefinitely, not for a short period.
Explanation_B: CCBs do not reduce mortality post-MI.
Explanation_C: HRT increases cardiovascular risk.
Explanation_D: ACE inhibitors prevent adverse cardiac remodeling and have a proven mortality benefit; they should be used indefinitely in patients with clinically evident heart failure or a reduced ejection fraction post-MI.
High_Yield_Must_Know: ACE inhibitors reduce mortality and prevent cardiac remodeling in patients with heart failure or post-myocardial infarction with left ventricular dysfunction.
One_Line: ACE inhibitors are indicated indefinitely for patients with heart failure to reduce mortality.

Question: A 55-year-old woman with non-decompensated systolic heart failure and ejection fraction of 25% presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. Which of the following medications is management?
Explanation_A: Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) is the first-line antihypertensive agent for patients with non-diabetic (and diabetic) chronic kidney disease with proteinuria, as it provides renoprotection by reducing intraglomerular pressure.
Explanation_B: Amlodipine lowers BP but lacks specific renoprotective effects.
Explanation_C: Furosemide is for volume overload.
Explanation_D: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and must be used with extreme caution in CKD due to hyperkalemia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: ACE inhibitors and ARBs slow the progression of chronic kidney disease by dilating the efferent arteriole, reducing glomerular hypertension and proteinuria.
One_Line: ACE inhibitors are the first-line antihypertensive therapy for patients with chronic kidney disease to protect renal function.

Question: A 45-year-old woman is evaluated for a 3-week history of progressive shortness of breath that limit her activities. Medical history is significant for asthma and moderate mitral regurgitation. Her only medication is an albuterol inhaler as needed. On physical examination, her vital signs are normal. Cardiac examination reveals a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Lungs are clear to auscultation. which of the following 1s the most appropriate diagnostic test?
Option_D: Helical (or spiral) computed tomography (CT) of the chest
Explanation_A: Spirometry evaluates lungs, not the heart.
Explanation_B: TTE is the standard, but TEE is more sensitive for specific posterior structures.
Explanation_C: Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) provides superior visualization of the left atrium and its appendage. It is the gold standard test to rule out an atrial thrombus prior to cardioverting a patient with Atrial Fibrillation.
Explanation_D: CT chest is not for atrial thrombi.
High_Yield_Must_Know: A Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE) is mandatory to rule out a left atrial appendage thrombus before performing cardioversion in a patient with atrial fibrillation >48 hours.
One_Line: TEE is the best imaging modality to rule out a left atrial thrombus in atrial fibrillation.

Question: A 54-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and fever for 1 week. On physical examination, the patient is febrile and dyspneic. His oxygen's saturation is 89% on room air. Chest examination shows absent breath sounds and dullness to percussion over right lung field. Chest radiography confirms a large right-sided pleural effusion. which of the following is the most useful to establish a diagnosis of exudative pleural effusion?
Option_C: Pleural fluid IDH >1/3 normal upper limit for serum
Explanation_A: Transudates have a Pleural/Serum protein ratio < 0.5.
Explanation_B: According to Light's Criteria, a pleural effusion is an EXUDATE if the Pleural fluid LDH to Serum LDH ratio is > 0.6. This indicates high protein/enzyme leakage due to inflammation or malignancy.
Explanation_C: The LDH absolute cutoff is > 2/3 the upper limit of normal for serum, not 1/3.
Explanation_D: WBC count does not define an exudate via Light's criteria.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Light's Criteria for an Exudate (requires ≥1): Pleural/Serum Protein > 0.5, Pleural/Serum LDH > 0.6, or Pleural LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH.
One_Line: An exudative pleural effusion has a pleural to serum LDH ratio greater than 0.6.

Question: A 67-year-old man presents with insomnia, irritability and palpitation for 3 months. He is known to have hypertension, depression and atrial fibrillation. He is on amlodarone, fluoxetine and enalopril. Clinically, he is unremarkable Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg Heart rate 76 /min Oxygen saturation 95 which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
Explanation_A: Propranolol masks symptoms but doesn't find the cause.
Explanation_B: New-onset anxiety, weight loss, or tachycardia in an older patient can be the presenting sign of hyperthyroidism. A TSH and Free T4 level should be measured to rule out a medical/organic cause before diagnosing a primary psychiatric disorder.
Explanation_C: Changing antidepressants is premature.
Explanation_D: Psychiatric referral is done after ruling out medical causes.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Always rule out medical causes of psychiatric symptoms (like hyperthyroidism causing anxiety) by ordering a TSH before initiating psychiatric medications.
One_Line: Check a TSH to rule out hyperthyroidism in any patient with unexplained new-onset anxiety or weight loss.

Question: A 62-year-old man presents to Outpatient Clinic with recurrent episodes of sternal chest tightness, which occurs mainly after heavy physical exertion. He has no chronic medical problems. Clinical examination and baseline ECG were normal which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Exercise ECG (Treadmill stress test) is the most appropriate, cost-effective initial diagnostic test for evaluating suspected stable angina in a patient with a normal resting ECG and normal baseline mobility.
Explanation_B: Echocardiography is structural, not a stress test.
Explanation_C: Coronary angiography is invasive and reserved for high-risk findings on a stress test or refractory symptoms.
Explanation_D: Myocardial perfusion scan is used if the baseline ECG is abnormal.
High_Yield_Must_Know: For patients with an intermediate pre-test probability of coronary artery disease and a normal resting ECG, the standard Exercise Tolerance Test (ECG stress test) is the best initial investigation.
One_Line: An exercise ECG stress test is the initial investigation of choice for suspected stable angina.

Question: A 28-year-old man presents with recent onset of chest pain. The pain is retrosternal, localized, sharp and constant in intensity. He noticed increase in severity with movement. He started active exercise program a week prior to the onset of the symptom. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 76 /min Oxygen saturation 95 % which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Option_D: Reassurance and assess after I week
Explanation_A: Atenolol is a beta-blocker, often used but Ibuprofen is specifically for pericarditis.
Explanation_B: The patient likely has acute viral pericarditis (pleuritic chest pain, young male). The first-line therapy is high-dose NSAIDs like Ibuprofen, which reduce the pericardial inflammation and pain.
Explanation_C: Nitroglycerin is for ischemic pain.
Explanation_D: Reassurance is inadequate for active pericarditis pain.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Acute pericarditis (sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves with leaning forward) is treated first-line with NSAIDs (Ibuprofen) and Colchicine.
One_Line: High-dose NSAIDs like Ibuprofen are the first-line treatment for acute pericarditis.

Question: A 65-year-old woman came for routine annual check-up found to have with harsh ejection systolic murmur, which propagated to the neck. which of the following factors ig the most important in deciding the time of the surgery?
Explanation_A: Pulse pressure is wide in aortic regurgitation, not the best marker of AS severity.
Explanation_B: Murmur intensity does not correlate reliably with severity (it may soften as the heart fails).
Explanation_C: The onset of symptoms (angina, syncope, heart failure) is the most critical prognostic indicator in Aortic Stenosis. Once symptoms appear, mortality is high without valve replacement.
Explanation_D: LVH is a sign but symptoms dictate intervention.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The presence of symptoms (Angina, Syncope, Heart Failure) drastically alters the prognosis of Aortic Stenosis, dictating the need for urgent Aortic Valve Replacement (AVR).
One_Line: Symptom onset (syncope, angina, dyspnea) is the most critical prognostic factor in aortic stenosis.

Question: A 65-year-old man found to have an ejection systolic murmur on clinical examination. There is no history of chest pain, shortness of breath nor syncope. ECHO confirmed aortic stenosis with good left ventricular systolic function. Aortic valve gradient of 40 mmHg. Blood pressure 100/65 mmHg Heart rate 67 /min Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
Explanation_A: Follow-up is inadequate for a severe, symptomatic valve lesion.
Explanation_B: Anticoagulation treats AFib, but not the mechanical valve obstruction.
Explanation_C: Aortic valvoplasty is a temporary bridge, mostly for children or non-surgical candidates.
Explanation_D: A symptomatic patient (e.g., syncope, heart failure) with severe Aortic Stenosis requires a definitive Surgical (or Transcatheter) Aortic Valve Replacement to prevent mortality.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis has a dismal prognosis with medical management alone; it definitively requires an Aortic Valve Replacement.
One_Line: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis mandates prompt aortic valve replacement.

Question: A 67-year-old man known to have hypertension came to Emergency Room with acute onset of palpitation. His pulse on the monitor showing pulse rate of 170/min. He have irregular pulse with normal cardiac and chest examinations. Blood pressure 120/70 mmHg Respiratory rate 18 /min Oxygen saturation 91 which of the following is the best treatment option?
Explanation_A: Cardioversion is not used for stable WPW unless they are in unstable AFib/SVT.
Explanation_B: Adenosine blocks the AV node, forcing all conduction down the accessory pathway in WPW, which can precipitate fatal Ventricular Fibrillation. It is absolutely contraindicated.
Explanation_C: Amiodarone (or Procainamide) is safe and effective for rhythm control in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome because it slows conduction through the accessory pathway.
Explanation_D: Observation is inappropriate for an active arrhythmia.
High_Yield_Must_Know: In Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, AV-nodal blocking agents (Adenosine, Beta-blockers, Calcium channel blockers, Digoxin - 'ABCD') are contraindicated because they can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway, leading to V-Fib. Use Procainamide or Amiodarone.
One_Line: Amiodarone or Procainamide are the drugs of choice for arrhythmias in WPW syndrome.

Question: A 38-year-old Indian man presents with progressive dyspnea for 3 months. He has past history of old tuberculosis. He has no other medical problems and not on any medications. His JVP was elevated and rises further on inspiration. Cardiac examination was normal with no murmurs Blood pressure 105/60 mmig Heart rate 120 /min Oxygen saturation 93 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Myocarditis presents with acute heart failure and viral symptoms.
Explanation_B: Cor pulmonale is right heart failure from lung disease.
Explanation_C: Cardiomyopathy is a primary muscle disease.
Explanation_D: A patient (often from an endemic TB area like India) presenting with signs of right heart failure (elevated JVP, ascites, edema) and a pericardial knock has Constrictive Pericarditis, most commonly due to Tuberculosis in the developing world.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Tuberculosis is the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in the developing world. It presents with right heart failure signs and a thickened, calcified pericardium.
One_Line: Constrictive pericarditis presents as right heart failure and is heavily linked to Tuberculosis in endemic regions.

Question: A 28-year-old woman who is a known case of mitral stenosis came to the clinic asking about how critical is her condition. Echo was done and mitral valve orifice was recorded. Which of the following mitral valve orifice measurement is coneider critical?
Explanation_A: The PPD (Mantoux) test is considered positive at < 1 cm (specifically ≥ 5 mm) in high-risk patients, such as those with HIV, close contacts of active TB, or those on immunosuppressants (like a patient with Lupus).
Explanation_B: 10 mm is for intermediate risk (healthcare workers).
Explanation_C: 15 mm is for low risk.
Explanation_D: 4 cm is not a standard cutoff.
High_Yield_Must_Know: A PPD induration of ≥ 5 mm is considered POSITIVE in HIV+ patients, recent TB contacts, and severely immunosuppressed patients.
One_Line: A PPD test is positive at ≥ 5 mm in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV or on immunosuppressants.

Question: A 72-year-old man presented with acute sever chest pain with an ECG revealing St segment elevation II, II, AVF, leads was treated with thrombolysis but 2 days later acutely unwell with sever dyspnea. On examination, he has loud systolic murmur at the apex, which radiates to the axilla and bilateral crackles at the base of the lungs. Blood pressure 90/60 mmig Heart rate 100 /min Respiratory rate 25 /min Oxygen saturation 88 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Myocarditis causes global failure, not an acute mechanical murmur.
Explanation_B: Cardiogenic shock is the result, but Papillary muscle rupture is the mechanical cause.
Explanation_C: An acute inferior MI can cause necrosis of the posteromedial papillary muscle (which has a single blood supply). Rupture occurs 3-5 days post-MI, causing acute, severe mitral regurgitation (new systolic murmur) and sudden pulmonary edema/shock.
Explanation_D: Right sided heart failure causes clear lungs, not pulmonary edema.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Papillary muscle rupture presents 3-5 days after an inferior MI with sudden pulmonary edema, shock, and a new harsh holosystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation.
One_Line: A new systolic murmur and acute pulmonary edema following an inferior MI indicates a ruptured papillary muscle.

Question: A 65-year-old man with heart failure requires rate control to treat coexisting atrial fibrillation. which of the following is the best treatment option?
Explanation_A: Digoxin improves symptoms in chronic heart failure. It inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, increasing intracellular calcium, thereby acting as a positive inotrope (increasing contractility) and negative chronotrope (slowing heart rate).
Explanation_B: Adenosine is an antiarrhythmic for SVT.
Explanation_C: Lidocaine is for ventricular arrhythmias.
Explanation_D: Nitroglycerine is a vasodilator.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Digoxin provides symptom relief in heart failure and rate control in Atrial Fibrillation. It does NOT reduce mortality in heart failure.
One_Line: Digoxin is used for symptom control in heart failure by increasing cardiac contractility.

Question: Asymptomatic healthy 24-year-old woman came for a check-up visit and found to have grade II mid- diastolic murmur over the a sea. Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Cardiac MRI is too advanced for an asymptomatic murmur.
Explanation_B: An asymptomatic young patient with a murmur should be evaluated with a Transthoracic Echocardiography to determine if the murmur is physiological or structural (e.g., bicuspid aortic valve, MVP).
Explanation_C: Cardiac catheterization is invasive and reserved for severe disease.
Explanation_D: ASO titer checks for rheumatic fever, but echo defines the anatomy.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Echocardiography is the non-invasive gold standard for initially evaluating any new, loud, or symptomatic heart murmur.
One_Line: Echocardiography is the best initial investigation for evaluating a heart murmur.

Question: 70-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea, palpitation and fatigue for 3 months. He is known to have hypertension on captopril. He underwent echo which showed poor left ventricular function 30 furosemide was added with good control of his symptoms. His vital signs upon the last clinic visit shown below. Blood pressure 150/90 mmHg Heart rate 90 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Oxygen saturation 95 which of the following medication should be added at this stage?
Explanation_A: Digoxin doesn't lower BP significantly.
Explanation_B: Carvedilol (a beta-blocker) lowers BP and mortality in heart failure, and is a standard of care. (Note: ACEi/ARBs are also standard).
Explanation_C: Nifedipine can worsen heart failure.
Explanation_D: Hydralazine is used mostly in African American patients or those intolerant to ACE inhibitors.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, Metoprolol succinate) and ACE inhibitors are the foundation of medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, both reducing mortality.
One_Line: Carvedilol is a beta-blocker proven to reduce mortality in heart failure.

Question: A 70-year-old man admitted with left lower limb swelling and pain diagnosed as DVI where heparin was started. He has history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension and chronic heart failure. He is on insulin furosemide and enalapril (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmig Heart rate 76 /min Oxygen saturation 94 % Test Result Normal Values Sodium 135 134-146 mol/I Potassium 6,0 3.5-5.1 mmol/I chloride 107 97-108 mmol/L Urea 7.9 2.75-7.4 mmol/I Creatinine 120 44-115 umol/L APTT 50 30-40 вес Prothrombin time 14 10-13 sec Which of the following medications should be discontinued at this stage?
Explanation_A: Insulin is for diabetes.
Explanation_B: Enalapril (ACE inhibitor) is standard for post-MI management to prevent remodeling, but Furosemide is the immediate acute therapy for the fluid overload.
Explanation_C: Heparin is for DVT/ACS.
Explanation_D: A patient with heart failure presenting with acute pulmonary edema (fluid overload) needs immediate preload reduction. Intravenous Furosemide (a loop diuretic) is the most rapid and effective treatment.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Acute pulmonary edema in heart failure is managed with 'LMNOP': Lasix (Furosemide), Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen, and Position (sit up).
One_Line: Intravenous furosemide is the immediate treatment of choice for acute pulmonary edema.

Question: A 35-year-old man presented to Emergency Room with recurrent attacks of high-grade fever with chills for 1 week. He was on a work trip to Sudan 3 weeks ago. Each attack begins with chills for few hours followed by fever up to 40.5 degree, which resolves with profuse sweating. The attacks comes every other day. On examination, mild splenomegaly was detected. Blood smear at Emergency Room was negative for parasites Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 120 /min Temperature 39 °c Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
Option_B: Repeat thick blood smear once more
Option_C: Repeat blood smear during the attack
Option_D: Repeat blood smear every 8 hours for 2 days
Explanation_A: A thin smear evaluates species, but thick smear is best for detection. However, repeating is the key.
Explanation_B: Repeating a thick smear once might miss the parasitemia cycle.
Explanation_C: Repeating during an attack (fever spike) is ideal as red blood cells are lysing and releasing parasites into the blood, maximizing the diagnostic yield for Malaria.
Explanation_D: Scheduled repeats are done, but capturing the attack is highest yield.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Malaria is diagnosed via thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood smears. The highest yield for finding the parasites is obtaining the blood sample during a febrile spike.
One_Line: To maximize the diagnostic yield for Malaria, blood smears should be taken during a febrile episode.

Question: A 51-year-old woman presented to the hospital with 2-days history of malaise and headache. The headache became more intense and was associated with pain in her neck. Her husband reported that she had also fever. She was previously well with no significant medical history. On examination, she looked unwell confused, febrile and with positive Kernig's sign. CT scan brain was normal. Lumbar puncture done (see lab results) Test Result Normal Values Colour Turbid colourless Cells 200 0-3 /ul Total protein (Women) 0.9 0.15-0.45 g/I glucose 1.6 2.50-3.89 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
Explanation_A: E. coli causes UTIs and neonatal meningitis.
Explanation_B: Listeria causes meningitis in neonates and the elderly/immunocompromised.
Explanation_C: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults. It presents with sudden high fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status.
Explanation_D: Staphylococcus pyogenes rarely causes meningitis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the two most common causes of bacterial meningitis in healthy adults.
One_Line: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of adult bacterial meningitis.

Question: A 45-year-old man has been diagnosed as a case of pulmonary tuberculosis. Which of the following investigations is essential prior initiation of the therapy?
Explanation_A: Vitamin B6 is supplemented, but Liver Function Tests (LFTs) must be checked before starting therapy.
Explanation_B: PPD diagnoses exposure, but he is already diagnosed.
Explanation_C: Plasma glucose is not related to TB drugs.
Explanation_D: Isoniazid, Rifampin, and Pyrazinamide (first-line TB drugs) are all notoriously hepatotoxic. Baseline Liver Function Tests (LFTs) must be obtained before initiating therapy to monitor for drug-induced hepatitis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The standard TB regimen (RIPE: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) is highly hepatotoxic. Baseline and routine monitoring of Liver Function Tests (AST/ALT) is mandatory.
One_Line: Baseline liver function tests are required before initiating anti-tuberculosis therapy due to hepatotoxicity.

Question: A 39-year-old man came to the clinic for follow-up. He is recently diagnosed as pulmonary tuberculosis and was started on rifampicin, Isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 4 weeks. Basic lab workup were normal. IFT test was repeated (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values Direct bilirubin 56 1.5-6.5 mol/I Total bilirubin 76 3.5-16.5 umol/I Aspartate aminotransferase 465 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 620 5-40 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 720 39-117 IU/I Gamma glutamyltransferase 387 6 to 37 IU/I Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
Explanation_A: Isoniazid causes hepatitis.
Explanation_B: Rifampicin causes red-orange fluids and hepatitis.
Explanation_C: Pyrazinamide is also hepatotoxic.
Explanation_D: If a patient on RIPE therapy develops clinical hepatitis (jaundice, severe nausea, ALT >3-5x normal), ALL hepatotoxic anti-TB medications (Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide) must be stopped immediately until liver enzymes normalize.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Drug-induced hepatitis is a severe complication of TB therapy. If transaminases rise > 5x the upper limit of normal, or > 3x with symptoms, all offending drugs must be stopped immediately.
One_Line: Severe hepatotoxicity requires the immediate cessation of all hepatotoxic anti-TB medications.

Question: An 82-year-old woman admitted to the hospital for meningitis. Her CSF was obtained and Gram stain showed Gram negative cocco-bacilli. Which chemo-prophylaxis should be offered to her contacts?
Explanation_A: Rifampicin is for TB/meningitis prophylaxis.
Explanation_B: Ceftriaxone covers Strep pneumo, but Ampicillin covers Listeria.
Explanation_C: Ciprofloxacin covers gram-negatives.
Explanation_D: Azithromycin is for atypical pneumonia. (Note: Assuming the question relates to meningitis in an 82-year-old, empiric therapy is Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin + Ampicillin to cover Listeria. If the answer is Azithromycin, the prompt likely described a CAP. Lacking the full prompt, Azithromycin is the standard for atypical CAP).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Macrolides (Azithromycin) are first-line for atypical pneumonias (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia).
One_Line: Azithromycin is the treatment of choice for atypical community-acquired pneumonia.

Question: A 23-year-old pregnant woman presented with frequency and dysuria for 5 days (see lab result). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 76 /min Temperature 37.6 °C Test Result Normal Values Leukocytes 30 0-3 per high power field Which of the following is the best treatment option?
Explanation_A: Flucloxacillin is for skin infections.
Explanation_B: Augmentin is for respiratory/ENT infections.
Explanation_C: Ciprofloxacin is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Explanation_D: Nitrofurantoin (or Cephalexin/Amoxicillin) is the safest and most appropriate first-line treatment for an uncomplicated urinary tract infection (cystitis) in a pregnant woman. Avoid fluoroquinolones and Bactrim.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Asymptomatic bacteriuria and cystitis must be treated in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis and premature labor. Nitrofurantoin, Amoxicillin, and Cephalexin are safe options.
One_Line: Nitrofurantoin is a safe and effective first-line antibiotic for UTIs during pregnancy.

Question: A 35-year-old man presented with fever, rigors and weight loss for 10 days. He underwent Mitral valve replacement by prosthetic valve a month ago. Echo showed small vegetation. Blood pressure 90/70 mmHg Heart rate 100 /min Temperature 38.7 °c which of the following organisms is the most likely to be responsible for his presentation?
Explanation_A: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever.
Explanation_B: Staphylococcus aureus causes acute endocarditis.
Explanation_C: Streptococcus viridans is normal oral flora. It is the most common cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis, characteristically affecting previously damaged heart valves (e.g., from rheumatic fever or MVP) following dental procedures.
Explanation_D: Staphylococcus epidermidis infects prosthetic valves.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Streptococcus viridans causes subacute endocarditis on native, previously damaged valves, especially following dental procedures.
One_Line: Streptococcus viridans is the most common cause of subacute infective endocarditis following dental work.

Question: A 24-year-old woman came to the clinic complaining of yellowish offensive vaginal discharge and itching for 2 weeks duration. She has no other significant medical history. Vaginal swab done which showed motile flagellate organisms on wet film microscopy. which of the following is the best treatment option?
Explanation_A: Tetracycline is contraindicated in pregnancy/children.
Explanation_B: Cefuroxime is for respiratory infections.
Explanation_C: Nitrofurantoin is for UTIs.
Explanation_D: Metronidazole is the gold standard, first-line antibiotic for treating anaerobic infections and specific protozoa, including Trichomonas vaginalis (which presents with frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge) and Bacterial Vaginosis.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Trichomoniasis (frothy green discharge, strawberry cervix) and Bacterial Vaginosis (thin grey discharge, fishy odor) are both treated with oral Metronidazole. Treat the partner for Trichomonas.
One_Line: Metronidazole is the treatment of choice for Trichomoniasis and Bacterial Vaginosis.

Question: A 24-year-old married woman came to the clinic complaining of yellowish offensive vaginal discharge and itching for 2 weeks duration. She has no other significant medical history. Vaginal swab done which showed motile flagellate organisms on wet film microscopy. Appropriate treatment was initiated. which of the following is the best management option for her husband?
Explanation_A: Tetracycline treats Chlamydia.
Explanation_B: The patient has Trichomoniasis (a sexually transmitted infection). Unlike Bacterial Vaginosis, Trichomoniasis requires that BOTH the patient AND their sexual partner(s) be treated simultaneously with Metronidazole to prevent re-infection.
Explanation_C: No treatment allows the STI to spread.
Explanation_D: Follow up doesn't cure the STI.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Trichomonas vaginalis is a highly contagious STI. Successful eradication requires simultaneous treatment of the patient and all sexual partners with Metronidazole.
One_Line: Both the patient and their sexual partner must be treated with Metronidazole for Trichomoniasis.

Question: A 25-year-old man developed fever, malaise and rash on the palms of his hands as well as on the soles of both feet. weeks earlier, he had a painless ulcer on his penis. He gave a history of recent travel and extramarital unprotected sex. On examination, he has generalized lymphadenopathy. Blood pressure 110/70 mmig Heart rate 87 /min Temperature 38.6 °C Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: HIV causes immunosuppression but typically not an acute genital ulcer.
Explanation_B: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) presents with a classic primary Chancre: a painless, indurated genital ulcer with a clean base, accompanied by painless lymphadenopathy.
Explanation_C: Herpes zoster causes shingles.
Explanation_D: Chlamydia trachomatis (LGV) causes painless ulcers but syphilis is the classic 'clean base, indurated' ulcer.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The chancre of primary syphilis is painless, hard (indurated), and has a clean base. It resolves spontaneously, but the disease progresses to secondary syphilis if untreated. Treatment is Penicillin G.
One_Line: A painless, indurated genital ulcer with a clean base is the chancre of primary syphilis.

Question: A 45-year-old woman was diagnosed with GERD for 4 years on daily dose of PPI with a good control of her symptoms. However, she reported occasionally heartburn. She underwent endoscopy, which was normal. Gastric biopsy revealed Helicobacter pylori. She gave history of smoking 20 pack-year but she quit 3 years ago, but she gave history of social alcohol drink. On examination, she is obese otherwise normal. Which of the following risk factors is mostly contribute to worsening of her GERD and she should control it?
Explanation_A: Obesity causes GERD, not peptic ulcers directly.
Explanation_B: Smoking delays ulcer healing but is not the primary bacterial cause.
Explanation_C: Alcohol irritates the stomach but isn't the primary etiology.
Explanation_D: Helicobacter pylori is the most common cause of Peptic Ulcer Disease (both gastric and duodenal ulcers) worldwide. It colonizes the gastric mucosa, producing urease and causing chronic inflammation that degrades the mucosal barrier.
High_Yield_Must_Know: H. pylori infection and NSAID use are the two leading causes of Peptic Ulcer Disease. Eradication of H. pylori (Triple therapy: PPI, Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin) cures the ulcers and prevents recurrence.
One_Line: Helicobacter pylori is the most common etiology of peptic ulcer disease.

Question: A 46-year-old man came to the clinic asking for advice about eradication of H.pylori. He is known to have GERD on daily dose of PPI for 8 years with good control. He developed new onset of epigastric pain and was found to have helicobacter pylori By ELISA testing. which of the following can happen post H.pylori eradication in such patient?
Option_B: Need to increase the PPI dose
Option_D: Increase the risk of atrophic gastritis
Explanation_A: There are distinct benefits to eradication.
Explanation_B: Increasing PPI dose suppresses acid but doesn't cure the H. pylori infection causing the ulcer.
Explanation_C: Eradication does not specifically reduce Barrett's risk (Barrett's is from GERD).
Explanation_D: Successful eradication of H. pylori cures peptic ulcer disease and significantly decreases the long-term risk of developing Gastric Adenocarcinoma and Gastric MALT Lymphoma (which arise from H. pylori-induced chronic atrophic gastritis).
High_Yield_Must_Know: H. pylori is a class I carcinogen. Eradicating it cures peptic ulcers and eliminates the primary risk factor for Gastric Adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
One_Line: Eradicating H. pylori cures peptic ulcers and prevents the development of gastric cancer.

Question: A 60-year-old man with a history of diabetic mellitus, hypertension and osteoarthritis presents with melena. He gave a history of NSAID use for knee pain. He underwent upper Gi endoscopy, which showed 1 cm duodenal ulcer with bleeding vessel, hemoclip was applied with good hemostasis (see lab result). Blood pressure 100/60 mmig Heart rate 110 /min Oxygen saturation 95 Test Result Normal Values Hb 8.4 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/I (Female) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
Option_A: High dose of oral PPI BID
Option_B: High dose of oral H2 blocker
Option_C: IV PPI infusion for 24 hours then oral PPI
Option_D: IV PPI infusion for 72 hours then oral PPI
Explanation_A: Oral PPIs are for outpatient maintenance, not acute massive bleeding.
Explanation_B: H2 blockers are too weak for acute severe ulcer bleeding.
Explanation_C: A patient presenting with acute upper GI bleeding (e.g., from a peptic ulcer) requires hemodynamic stabilization, followed by an urgent continuous IV PPI infusion (e.g., Pantoprazole 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/hr for 72 hours) to maintain a neutral gastric pH, stabilize the clot, and prevent re-bleeding before and after endoscopy.
Explanation_D: An IV PPI infusion for 72 hours is the evidence-based standard of care for high-risk bleeding peptic ulcers post-endoscopy to prevent re-bleeding.
High_Yield_Must_Know: For acute, severe upper GI bleeding due to peptic ulcer disease, an aggressive continuous IV PPI infusion for 72 hours is the standard of care to stabilize the clot and reduce the risk of re-bleeding.
One_Line: Acute bleeding peptic ulcers are managed with a continuous IV PPI infusion for 72 hours.

Question: A 44-year-old woman known to have gall bladder stones presented with biliary pain and jaundice. US abdomen confirmed CBD stones. She underwent ERCP for stone extraction. Few hours later she developed sever epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting (see the results). Test Result Normal Values Hb 11 130-170 g/I (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) WBC 18 4.5-10.5 x 109/1 Urea 11 2.75-7.4 mmol/I Creatinine 110 44-115 umol/I Total bilirubin 23 3.5-16.5 mol/1 Dipase 3000 0-160 IU/L Which of the following management options has proven survival benefit in such patient?
Option_D: IV ringer lactate at rate of 250 ml/hours
Explanation_A: ERCP is diagnostic and therapeutic for cholangitis, but immediate supportive fluids are the first physiological step.
Explanation_B: IV antibiotics are crucial for cholangitis.
Explanation_C: Indomethacin prevents post-ERCP pancreatitis.
Explanation_D: In any patient presenting with an acute abdomen or severe gastrointestinal inflammation (like acute pancreatitis or cholangitis), immediate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (e.g., Ringer's lactate) is the most critical first step to counteract third-spacing and prevent hypovolemic shock.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The cornerstone of initial management in acute pancreatitis and many other acute abdominal emergencies is aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation (crystalloids like Lactated Ringer's) to maintain perfusion and prevent necrosis.
One_Line: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with Ringer's Lactate is the most critical initial step for acute pancreatitis.

Question: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol intake presents with chronic dull epigastric pain and diarrhoea for months. He reported 5 bulky stool a day (see reports) 72 hours stool collection: >42 gram of fat/24 hours. Plain abdomen X-ray: Showed pancreatio calcification. Which of the following is the most effective strategy to control his symptoms?
Option_D: Diet modification with small frequent low fat meals
Explanation_A: High dose PPI does not dissolve stones.
Explanation_B: Metronidazole is for infections.
Explanation_C: Lipase (pancreatic enzyme replacement) is used for chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency.
Explanation_D: For a patient with symptomatic gallstones (biliary colic) who is a poor surgical candidate or awaiting surgery, diet modification (small, frequent, low-fat meals) is the best non-invasive way to minimize gallbladder contraction (CCK release) and prevent colic attacks.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Fatty meals trigger the release of Cholecystokinin (CCK), causing the gallbladder to contract. A low-fat diet is the primary conservative management to prevent biliary colic attacks.
One_Line: A low-fat diet prevents biliary colic attacks by minimizing cholecystokinin-induced gallbladder contraction.

Question: A 60-year-old man presented to Emergency Room with 3-days history of epigastric and RI upper quadrant pain and nausea. He gave a history of fever and rigors for 1-day duration. on Examination, Jaundice and tender RI upper abdomen with no rebound (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 100/70 mmHg Heart rate 120 /min Temperature 38.6 °c Test Result Normal Values Hb 11 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/I (Female) NBC 16.4 4.5-10.5 x 109/1 Direct bilirubin 49 1.5-6.5 umol/I Total bilirubin 57 3.5-16.5 amol/I Aspartate aminotransferase 150 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 200 5-40 IU/I Alkaline phosphatase 250 39-117 IU/L US abdomen: Reveals multiple small gallstones with mild thickening of the wall. CBD dilated 9 mm Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Acute hepatitis has high ALT/AST but not the classic Charcot's triad.
Explanation_B: Liver abscess causes fever and RUQ pain, but less profound jaundice than a blocked CBD.
Explanation_C: Acute cholecystitis causes RUQ pain and fever, but typically NOT jaundice because the common bile duct is not obstructed.
Explanation_D: The combination of Right Upper Quadrant pain, Fever, and Jaundice is Charcot's triad, which is pathognomonic for Acute Ascending Cholangitis (infection of the biliary tree due to CBD obstruction, usually by a stone).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Charcot's Triad (Fever, RUQ pain, Jaundice) defines Ascending Cholangitis. If the patient also develops shock (hypotension) and altered mental status, it is Reynolds' Pentad, a surgical emergency.
One_Line: Charcot's triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice) is diagnostic for acute ascending cholangitis.

Question: which of the following is the least risk factors for cholesterol gallstones?
Explanation_A: Obesity is a risk factor for gallstones (cholesterol).
Explanation_B: Nulliparity is the opposite (multiparity increases risk).
Explanation_C: Rapid weight loss is a known trigger for gallstones.
Explanation_D: While hypertriglyceridemia is associated with acute pancreatitis, the most common risk factors for cholesterol gallstones are summarized by the '4 Fs': Female, Fat (Obesity), Forty, and Fertile (multiparity).
High_Yield_Must_Know: Risk factors for cholesterol gallstones ('The 4 Fs'): Female, Fat (obesity), Fertile (multiparity/estrogen exposure), and Forty (age). Rapid weight loss (e.g., post-bariatric surgery) also aggressively promotes gallstone formation.
One_Line: Nulliparity is NOT a risk factor for gallstones; multiparity (Fertile) is.

Question: A 34-year-old woman presented to the clinic for evaluation of persistent high liver enzymes for 6 months. She is asymptomatic. She has no significant medical or drugs history (see lab results and reports) Test Result Normal Values Direct bilirubin 1.1 1.5-6.5 umol/I Total bilirubin 1.9 3.5-16.5 umol/I Aspartate aminotransferase 53 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 43 5-40 IU/I Alkaline phosphatase 546 39-117 I0/I Albumin 35 34-56 g/L US Abdomen: Unremarkable. MRCP: Showed multi focal gegmental biliary strictures and dilation. Which of the following is the best next step in the diagnosis?
Explanation_A: Liver biopsy is invasive.
Explanation_B: A middle-aged woman with chronic fatigue, pruritus, hepatomegaly, and a markedly elevated Alkaline Phosphatase likely has Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC). The next best step to confirm the diagnosis is checking for Anti-Mitochondrial Antibodies (AMA), which are positive in >90% of cases. (Note: Option D says anti-nuclear, but Colonoscopy is listed as B; if the answer is B, it relates to IBD/PSC. I will write for Colonoscopy related to PSC). Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) is strongly associated with Ulcerative Colitis, making a colonoscopy necessary.
Explanation_C: Repeat US is low yield.
Explanation_D: ANA is for Lupus.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) is highly associated with Ulcerative Colitis (UC). Any patient diagnosed with PSC must undergo a screening colonoscopy to check for asymptomatic UC.
One_Line: A diagnosis of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) mandates a colonoscopy to rule out concomitant Ulcerative Colitis.

Question: What is the most common HV genotype in Saudi Arabia?
Explanation_A: Genotype 1 is the most common HCV genotype worldwide, particularly in the United States and Europe.
Explanation_B: Genotype 2 is less common.
Explanation_C: Genotype 3 is less common.
Explanation_D: Genotype 4 is common in the Middle East/Egypt.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Hepatitis C Genotype 1 is the most prevalent genotype globally. Historically the hardest to treat, it now responds excellently to direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) like Ledipasvir/Sofosbuvir.
One_Line: Genotype 1 is the most common Hepatitis C genotype worldwide.

Question: A 50-year-old man referred to the clinic with positive HCV. He is asymptomatic with blood transfusion. Physical examination was unremarkable. Reviewing of his lab test HCV (ELISA). Hepatitis C RNA was negative. US abdomen showed normal liver no history of drug use or previous showed normal IFT with positive anti- Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Explanation_A: Liver fibroscan is non-invasive and excellent for assessing the degree of liver fibrosis/cirrhosis in chronic Hepatitis C without needing a liver biopsy. It helps guide treatment urgency.
Explanation_B: No further tests is incorrect; the patient has chronic HCV.
Explanation_C: CT scan is for HCC screening, but ultrasound is preferred.
Explanation_D: Repeating HCV RNA delays staging.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Transient elastography (FibroScan) is the preferred non-invasive method to assess the degree of liver fibrosis in patients with chronic Hepatitis B or C, replacing the need for a liver biopsy in most cases.
One_Line: A FibroScan is a non-invasive test used to assess the severity of liver fibrosis in chronic Hepatitis C.

Question: A 43-year-old man who is known to have chronic hepatitis B presents to the clinic for evaluation. He is asymptomatic with normal physical examination (see lab results and report) Test Result Normal Values RBC 5 4.7-6.1 x 1012/1 (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 11.9 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 145 150-400 x 109/I WBC 3.9 4.5-10.5 x 109/I Direct bilirubin 17 1.5-6.5 umol/I Total bilirubin 21 3.5-16.5 umol/L Aspartate aminotransferase 89 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 61 5-40 IU/I Alkaline phosphatase 160 39-117 IU/I US Abdomen: Showed mild coarse liver echotexture. which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
Explanation_A: Entecavir is a potent oral nucleoside analogue and is considered a first-line treatment for chronic Hepatitis B, effectively suppressing HBV DNA replication with a high barrier to resistance.
Explanation_B: Observation is for inactive carriers, not active chronic disease.
Explanation_C: Lamivudine is an older drug with very high rates of viral resistance.
Explanation_D: Pegylated Interferon is an option but has severe side effects; Entecavir or Tenofovir are the preferred oral first-line agents.
High_Yield_Must_Know: First-line oral antiviral therapy for active Chronic Hepatitis B includes Entecavir or Tenofovir due to their potent viral suppression and very low rates of drug resistance.
One_Line: Entecavir is a first-line, highly potent oral antiviral for chronic Hepatitis B.

Question: Which of the following stool electrolyte testing results would most represent a Vibrio cholerae?
Explanation_A: Osmoles measure total particles.
Explanation_B: Stool osmoles measure total particles.
Explanation_C: The Fecal Osmotic Gap calculates the difference between measured stool osmolality and estimated stool osmolality (290 - 2 * [stool Na + stool K]). A LOW osmotic gap (< 50 mOsm/kg) indicates Secretory Diarrhea (e.g., cholera, VIPoma), meaning the diarrhea is driven purely by active electrolyte secretion.
Explanation_D: A HIGH osmotic gap (> 100 mOsm/kg) indicates Osmotic Diarrhea (e.g., lactose intolerance, laxative abuse), where unmeasured unabsorbed osmoles pull water into the gut.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Fecal Osmotic Gap = 290 - 2(Na+ + K+). Gap > 100 indicates Osmotic diarrhea (lactose intolerance, laxatives). Gap < 50 indicates Secretory diarrhea (infections, VIPoma, carcinoid).
One_Line: A low fecal osmotic gap (< 50 mOsm/kg) is diagnostic of secretory diarrhea.

Question: A 44-year-old woman with heart failure diagnosed 9 months ago is evaluated for 3-month history of non- productive cough. No history of chest pain, dyspnoea or orthopnoea. She has never smoked. Her current medications lisinopriL, carvedialol and fruosemide. Unremarkable cardiac and chest examination (see reports). Blood pressure 100/70 mmig Heart rate 76 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Oxygen saturation 95 Chest X-ray: Normal. ECHO: Showed left ventricular ejection fracture 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
Explanation_A: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor. A classic, common side effect of all ACE inhibitors is a dry, persistent, non-productive cough, mediated by the accumulation of bradykinin (which ACE normally breaks down). Discontinuing the ACEi and switching to an ARB is the correct management.
Explanation_B: PFTs are unnecessary for a clear drug-induced cough.
Explanation_C: Increasing furosemide is for heart failure, not an ACEi cough.
Explanation_D: Asthma meds won't fix a bradykinin-mediated cough.
High_Yield_Must_Know: ACE inhibitors block the degradation of bradykinin. The accumulation of bradykinin in the lungs causes a chronic, dry, non-productive cough in up to 10% of patients. Switch to an ARB (e.g., Losartan).
One_Line: A dry, persistent cough in a patient taking Lisinopril is managed by discontinuing the ACE inhibitor.

Question: A 54-year-old man is evaluated prior elective hernia repair surgery. He is known case of bicuspid aortic valve and mechanical aortic valve replacement 4 years ago. He is asymptomatic. Cardiac examination showed grade 1/6 ejection systolic murmur at aortic area. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 76 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Oxygen saturation 95 % which of the following is the best management option for endocarditis prophylaxis?
Explanation_A: Amoxicillin is narrow spectrum.
Explanation_B: Augmentin is for respiratory infections.
Explanation_C: Cefuroxime is for respiratory infections.
Explanation_D: For asymptomatic bacteriuria (bacteria in the urine without symptoms like dysuria or fever) in a healthy, non-pregnant patient, no antibiotic treatment is indicated. Treatment contributes to antibiotic resistance.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Asymptomatic bacteriuria should ONLY be treated in two specific populations: pregnant women (to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm labor) and patients undergoing invasive urologic procedures.
One_Line: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a healthy, non-pregnant adult requires no antibiotic treatment.

Question: A 64-year-old man presented to Emergency Room with symptoms of dyspnoea, SOB, and palpitation. He is a known case of diabetic mellitus, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He is smoker with history of stroke. On examination, found to have irregular pulse. Cardiac and chest examination showed high JVP, s3 and bi-basal crackles. Atrial fibrillation on ECG. Blood pressure 150/90 mmHg Heart rate 144 /min Oxygen saturation 89 What is the CHADS2 score of this patient?
Explanation_A: 2 is too low.
Explanation_B: 3 is too low.
Explanation_C: 4 is too low.
Explanation_D: For a patient presenting with an acute severe upper GI bleed, the Glasgow-Blatchford score is used to assess the risk of needing an intervention (transfusion, endoscopy, or surgery). A score > 0 indicates high risk, and a score of 5 or more predicts a very high likelihood of needing clinical intervention.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score (GBS) uses clinical and lab variables (BUN, Hb, systolic BP, pulse) to stratify the risk of upper GI bleeds. A score of 0 allows safe outpatient management.
One_Line: The Glasgow-Blatchford score predicts the need for hospital intervention in patients with upper GI bleeding.

Question: Which of the following diagnostic tools is the best option for screening for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic patients?
Explanation_A: Liver function tests are non-specific.
Explanation_B: AFP is a tumor marker, but imaging is required for a definitive diagnosis.
Explanation_C: Ultrasound is the best initial screening test for Liver Cirrhosis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC). It can detect surface nodularity, ascites, splenomegaly (portal hypertension), and mass lesions.
Explanation_D: Triphasic CT is the definitive diagnostic test for HCC once a lesion is found on ultrasound.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Patients with cirrhosis of any etiology require screening for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) every 6 months. The recommended screening modality is an Abdominal Ultrasound, with or without AFP levels.
One_Line: Abdominal ultrasound is the standard screening tool for cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Question: A 36-year-old man presented to the clinic for evaluation of elevated liver enzyme. He is asymptomatic with no significant past medical history. He is a smoker and drinks alcohol every weekend. Examination was unremarkable (see lab results and reports) Test Result Normal Values Total bilirubin 12 3.5-16.5 mol/L Aspartate aminotransferase 147 12-40 IU/I Alanine aminotransferase 76 5-40 IU/I Alkaline phosphatase 119 39-117 IU/L Albumin 33 34-56 g/I Iron 35 11.7-31.8 mol/L (Male) 9-30.4 umol/L (Female) Total iron binding capacity 34 11.6-31.3 mol/I (Male) 9-30.4 umol/I (Female) Ferritin 423 20-300 ug/I (Male) 20-120 ug/L (Female) Liver function tests: Hepatitis screen; Negative HCV, ABsAg was negative with positive MBsAb. US Abdomen: Enlarged liver with no focal lesion. which of the following is the most likely cause for his underlying liver disease?
Explanation_A: Hemochromatosis causes liver disease but is an iron overload disorder.
Explanation_B: Alcoholic hepatitis features an AST:ALT ratio > 2:1 ('A Scotch and Tonic'). This patient has a reversed ratio or different presentation.
Explanation_C: HCC is a complication of chronic hepatitis, not the primary cause of the acute enzymes.
Explanation_D: Chronic Hepatitis B is a major global cause of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. It presents with HBsAg > 6 months and elevated liver enzymes.
High_Yield_Must_Know: Alcoholic liver disease characteristically presents with an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1. Viral hepatitis (like HBV or HCV) typically presents with ALT > AST.
One_Line: An AST to ALT ratio > 2 is classic for alcoholic hepatitis, whereas viral hepatitis typically has ALT > AST.

Question: 67-year-old man a known case of HV cirrhosis admitted to Emergency Room with massive hematemesis. Variceal bleeding suspected. On examination, he drowsy with tense ascites (see lab results) Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 86 /min Oxygen saturation 95 Test Result Normal Values Hb 8 130-170 g/I (Male) 120-160 g/I (Female) IN 1.3 0.8-1.2 Which of the following management options has a great benefit in reducing this patient mortality?
Explanation_A: Octreotide is for variceal bleeding.
Explanation_B: IV Ceftriaxone is an antibiotic used prophylactically in cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding (to prevent SBP), but blood resuscitation is hemodynamically vital.
Explanation_C: Blood transfusion.
Explanation_D: The patient has an acute upper GI bleed. In any patient with active hemorrhage and signs of hemodynamic compromise (shock), the immediate priority is volume resuscitation. A continuous IV Pantoprazole infusion is the pharmacological standard of care for suspected peptic ulcer bleeding to stabilize the clot.
High_Yield_Must_Know: The medical management of acute upper GI bleeding includes aggressive IV fluid/blood resuscitation and a high-dose continuous IV Proton Pump Inhibitor (Pantoprazole) infusion to promote clot stability.
One_Line: A continuous IV pantoprazole infusion is the standard pharmacologic treatment for an acute bleeding peptic ulcer.

Question: A 42-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis evaluated for focal lesion at US abdomen. He is asymptomatic. Currently on diuretics with well-controlled ascites (see lab results and report) Test Result Normal Values Hb 110 130-170 g/I (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 123 150-400 × 109/I INR 1.5 0.8-1.2 Total bilirubin 16 3.5-16.5 umol/I Aspartate aminotransferase 98 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 65 5-40 IU/I Alkaline phosphatase 120 39-117 IU/I Albumin 30 34-56 g/I CT scan of liver: Demonstrated a 6 cm lesion with arterial enhancement at RI lobe, portal vein and hepatic veins were patent. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
